National Credit Union Administration
12 CFR Part 740
RIN 3133-AF75
AGENCY:
National Credit Union Administration (NCUA).
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
The NCUA Board (Board) is issuing this final rule to streamline its regulations governing advertising and the notice of insured status. This final
(
printed page 73431)
rule eliminates provisions concerning the official advertising statement. This action is undertaken to reduce regulatory complexity, and the intended effect is to reduce the administrative burden and costs for federally insured credit unions (FICUs) and provide them with greater flexibility in their advertising activities. The final rule does not amend requirements related to displaying the official sign.
DATES:
This final rule is effective on December 16, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Office of General Counsel:
Rachel Ackmann, Senior Attorney, Office of General Counsel, at (703) 518-6540 or at 1775 Duke Street, Alexandria, VA 22314.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Introduction
A. Background
The Board comprehensively revised and streamlined part 740 in a 2003 final rule.
[
1
]
The primary purpose of the 2003 revision was to modernize the regulation for clarity, address the growing use of the internet for member transactions, and clarify the use of trade names in advertising. The NCUA's goal was to ensure members were adequately informed of their federal share insurance coverage while imposing a minimal regulatory burden.
Over the subsequent years, the NCUA amended these regulations several times. In the 2006 final rule, the NCUA revised the official sign to reflect statutory changes from the Federal Deposit Insurance Reform Act of 2005,
[
2
]
which included adding a statement in the official NCUA sign that insured accounts are backed by the full faith and credit of the United States Government. The Federal Deposit Insurance Reform Act of 2005 also removed a requirement for FICUs to include a statement in their advertisements that their member accounts are insured by the NCUA. The 2006 final rule did make any changes to part 740 to reflect this statutory change.
A subsequent 2008 final rule provided credit unions with additional flexibility by permitting the use of a shortened advertising statement, “Federally insured by NCUA,” or the official sign itself in advertisements.
[
3
]
In a 2011 final rule, the Board made the advertising rules more stringent.
[
4
]
This amendment, among other changes, reduced the time exemption for radio and television advertisements from 30 seconds to 15 seconds. It also introduced the requirement to include the official advertising statement in annual reports and statements of condition, clarified that the statement's font size in print must be no smaller than the smallest font used for other consumer information, and defined the term “advertisement” for the first time.
However, in a 2018 final rule, the NCUA reversed the 2011 change to the broadcast advertisement exemption to provide regulatory relief and restore parity with regulations for banks insured by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC).
[
5
]
The 2018 rule expanded the radio and television exemption back to 30 seconds and introduced a shorter advertising statement option: “Insured by NCUA.” Most recently, a 2020 final rule made technical corrections to improve clarity.
[
6
]
On December 29, 2025, the Board published a proposed rule to streamline its regulations governing advertising and the notice of insured status by removing the requirement for an official advertising statement.
[
7
]
The proposed rule applied to all FICUs.
B. Legal Authority
Section 205(a) of the Federal Credit Union Act (FCU Act) (
12 U.S.C. 1785(a)
) requires each FICU to display a sign relating to the insurance of its share accounts.
[
8
]
The NCUA implements this requirement in part 740 of its rules (part 740).
[
9
]
Part 740 also requires that each FICU include an official advertising statement related to share insurance in all advertisements.
[
10
]
This requirement originated from a historic statutory provision in section 1785(a). Before 2005, section 1785(a) required every FICU to include a statement in all advertisements reiterating that its member accounts are insured by NCUA. Section 1785(a) also provided that NCUA may exempt advertisements from this requirement if the advertisements do not relate to member accounts or when it is impractical to include such a statement.
The 2005 statutory amendment retained the requirement for FICUs to post official signs but removed the requirement to include official advertising statements. The Board issued a final rule implementing changes associated with the 2005 statutory amendments in 2006 but did not remove the portions of part 740 that implemented the historical requirement to include an official advertising statement.
[
11
]
Part 740 currently includes both the requirements for an official sign and advertising statement.
[
12
]
II. Final Rule
A. Overview
This final rule follows publication of the proposed rule and takes into consideration the comments received on the proposal. By the close of the public comment period on February 27, 2026, the Board had received 19 public comments. Comments were submitted by individuals, FICUs, state credit union leagues, a national association of state credit union supervisors, a national banking trade organization, and national credit union trade associations. After careful consideration of the issues raised by the commenters, the Board has decided to adopt the proposal without change.
B. Discussion of Public Comments
This section of the preamble discusses the significant issues raised by the commenters, and the Board's responses to the comments.
Commenters were mixed in whether they supported the proposed rule. Several commenters objected to the proposal and raised concerns related to consumer confusion on insured status and parity with the FDIC. Other commenters supported the proposal and discussed the enhanced efficiency the proposal would achieve without compromising consumer protection. However, a few commenters who supported the proposed rule also raised the importance of consumer confidence in share insurance and offered additional suggestions.
Two individual commenters and a banking trade organization were opposed to the proposed amendments. These commenters expressed concern
(
printed page 73432)
that removing the advertising statement might result in consumer confusion between federally insured and non-insured entities. In particular, one commenter noted that the rule would remove safeguards at a time when fraud in digital financial markets continues to rise, along with the prevalence of non-insured platforms that closely resemble traditional credit union services. The commenter noted that a CFPB study concluded that it is not always clear to consumers when they are dealing directly with a bank or a nonbank. The Board understands that there is a potential for additional consumer confusion. However, the Board believes that ensuring members are aware of their federal insurance coverage is more adequately achieved through other, more direct means. Specifically, the requirements in § 740.4, which are not being amended by this rule, mandate the display of the official NCUA sign at each station or window where insured account funds or deposits are normally received in a FICU's principal place of business and in all its branches. Each FICU must also display the official sign on its internet page, if any, where it accepts deposits or open accounts
[
13
]
Additionally, all insured credit unions must provide notice to members concerning NCUA insurance coverage, which may be accomplished in a variety of ways.
[
14
]
These existing requirements ensure that members receive prominent notice of their insured status at the key points of transaction and interaction.
Additionally, the requirements in § 740.2 mandate that FICU advertising be accurate and not deceptive. This provision helps to ensure that, if a FICU references its federal share insurance in advertisements, it does so accurately. For example, if a FICU states it is NCUA-insured in an advertisement that includes noninsured products, the advertisement should be clear that the product is not insured. The additional requirement in current § 740.5 to include a specific statement in all advertisements on share insurance may contribute to some consumers' understanding of federal share insurance, but the Board does not believe it materially enhances member protection in a way that justifies the associated compliance costs.
One banking trade association commenter stated that due to concerns around consumer confusion from non-insured entities in the financial marketplace, the FDIC recently updated its signage rules to make clear what is and is not insured across digital and traditional banking spaces. The commenter included several specific suggestions, including coordinating with the FDIC on insured status- communication principles. The Board acknowledges that parity with the FDIC's signage rules had previously been one of its stated goals.
[
15
]
Additionally, the Board is aware that the FDIC recently amended its signage rules, in part, to reflect that consumers are increasingly relying on internet and mobile banking channels to access banking services, which may make it more difficult for consumers to understand when they are conducting business with an insured institution.
[
16
]
However, the FDIC's amended signage rules primarily related to insured institutions' official signs and ensuring consumer awareness when accessing online and mobile banking accounts. These amendments were generally unrelated to the mandated advertising statement. Additionally, part 740 addresses these primary concerns related to online and mobile access and requires each FICU to display the official sign on its internet page, if any, where it accepts deposits or open accounts, including mobile banking pages.
[
17
]
Most commenters supported eliminating the requirement to include an official advertising statement. Many commenters expressed frustration that the current rules have become increasingly difficult to apply consistently across diverse digital channels. Commenters noted that modern advertising often involves character limits, responsive layouts, and automated placements, making compliance burdensome and unclear. Commenters appreciated that the proposal would allow for more creative and targeted marketing efforts without the constraints of mandatory disclosures in every advertisement. The Board agrees that the highly prescriptive nature of the rule, with its specific textual requirements and complex list of exceptions for items ranging from radio spots to promotional pens, forces FICUs to dedicate administrative resources to compliance. This approach is inflexible and poorly suited to the modern, fast-paced advertising landscape, particularly in the context of digital and social media, where space is often limited and communication must be concise. Additionally, many commenters stated that additional flexibility can be achieved while maintaining meaningful disclosure through existing signage, including that the insured status be clearly displayed on the credit union's website and in branches, and truth-in-advertising standards. Commenters stated that the requirement to display the official NCUA sign under § 740.4, and the general accuracy requirement in § 740.2, are not changed by the proposal. The Board agrees that these provisions continue to help ensure that members receive clear notice of federal share insurance and that any reference to insurance in advertising is accurate and not deceptive, thereby helping to ensure adequate consumer protection.
A few commenters also discussed the importance of federal insurance awareness. One commenter in favor of the proposal stated that the removal of a standardized advertising reference may, over time, reduce insurance awareness. Commenters included various suggestions related to public awareness of federal share insurance, including encouraging NCUA to continue proactive public education efforts regarding federal share insurance coverage and to remain attentive to the confidence-building role that federal share insurance messaging plays during periods of economic uncertainty. One commenter recommended that the Board provide additional guidance on best practices for communicating insured status in digital format, and another commenter encouraged NCUA to make a digital sign comparable to the FDIC's available for online and mobile platforms. This could be a voluntary tool; or NCUA could consider developing a smaller, digital seal that FICUs could use on social media profiles. The Board notes that NCUA's website includes downloaded graphics currently that can be used on FICU web pages and mobile apps.
[
18
]
The Board does not believe it is necessary to include additional guidance or consumer-education material at this time but may do so in the future. The Board intends to closely monitor implementation to ensure that the final rule does not result in consumer confusion regarding share insurance or whether members are engaging with an FICU or a non-insured third-party. The Board also notes that FICUs may continue to include the official
(
printed page 73433)
advertising statement, provided the inclusion is not inaccurate or deceptive, and believes many FICUs will do so on a voluntary basis as part of their advertising strategy.
Finally, a national trade association recommended that NCUA consolidate all NCUA-related insurance requirements into a single, modern comprehensive publication. This suggestion is beyond the scope of this rulemaking, but the Board is committed to providing regulatory clarity and will take this recommendation under advisement.
III. Regulatory Procedures
A. Executive Orders 12866, 13563, and 14192
Pursuant to
Executive Order 12866
(“Regulatory Planning and Review”), a determination must be made whether a regulatory action is significant and therefore subject to review by the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA), within the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) in accordance with the requirements of the Executive Order.
[
19
]
Executive Order 13563
(“Improving Regulation and Regulatory Review”) supplements and reaffirms the principles, structures, and definitions governing contemporary regulatory review established in
Executive Order 12866
.
[
20
]
This final rule was drafted and reviewed in accordance with
Executive Order 12866
and
Executive Order 13563
. OIRA has determined that this final rule is not a “significant regulatory action” as defined by section 3(f) of
Executive Order 12866
.
Executive Order 14192
(“Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation”) requires that any new incremental costs associated with new regulations shall, to the extent permitted by law, be offset by the elimination of existing costs associated with at least 10 prior regulations.
[
21
]
This final rule is not an
Executive Order 14192
regulatory action because this rule is not significant under
Executive Order 12866
. This final rule is considered an
Executive Order 14192
deregulatory action.
B. Regulatory Flexibility Act
The Regulatory Flexibility Act
[
22
]
generally requires an agency to conduct a regulatory flexibility analysis of any rule subject to notice and comment rulemaking requirements, unless the agency certifies that the rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities. If the agency makes such a certification, it shall publish the certification at the time of publication of either the proposed rule or the final rule, along with a statement providing the factual basis for such certification.
[
23
]
For purposes of this analysis, NCUA considers small credit unions to be those having under $100 million in assets.
[
24
]
The Board fully considered the potential economic impacts of the regulatory amendments on small credit unions.
This rule is narrow in scope and purely deregulatory. Further, FICUs may voluntarily continue to include the official advertising statement in their advertisements and may choose not to change their current practices. Accordingly, NCUA certifies the final rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small credit unions.
C. Paperwork Reduction Act
The Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (PRA) generally provides that an agency may not conduct or sponsor, and not withstanding any other provision of law, a person is not required to respond to, a collection of information, unless it displays a currently valid OMB control number. The PRA applies to rulemaking in which an agency creates new or amends existing information collection requirements. For purposes of the PRA, an information collection requirement may take the form of a reporting, recordkeeping, or third-party disclosure requirement. The NCUA has determined that the changes described in this final rule do not create a new information collection or revise an existing information collection as defined by the PRA.
D.
Executive Order 13132
on Federalism
Executive Order 13132
encourages independent regulatory agencies to consider the impact of their actions on state and local interests.
[
25
]
NCUA, an agency as defined in
44 U.S.C. 3502(5)
, voluntarily complies with the executive order to adhere to fundamental federalism principles. This final rule applies to all FICUs, including state-chartered credit unions. The Board expects that any effect on states or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government will be minor. The changes remove an existing requirement on state-chartered credit unions and do not affect the division of responsibilities between the NCUA and state regulatory authorities with oversight of federally insured, state-chartered credit unions. These changes relate to the NCUA's insurance of member accounts, which is a distinct federal function. The rulemaking therefore does not have a direct effect on the states, the relationship between the national government and the states, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government.
E. Assessment of Federal Regulations and Policies on Families
NCUA has determined that this final rule will not affect family well-being within the meaning of Section 654 of the Treasury and General Government Appropriations Act, 1999.
[
26
]
The rule relates to FICUs' advertisements, but the Board does not believe it will cause member confusion regarding share insurance coverage. Therefore, any effect on family well-being is expected to be indirect.
F. Congressional Review Act
Subtitle E of the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act of 1996, also known as the Congressional Review Act (CRA), generally provides for congressional review of agency rules.
[
27
]
NCUA must submit a report to Congress and the Comptroller General when it issues a final rule, as defined by the CRA.
[
28
]
An agency rule, in addition to being subject to congressional oversight, may also be subject to a delayed effective date if the rule is a “major rule.” OIRA has determined that this rule is not a “major rule” within the meaning of the relevant sections of the CRA. NCUA will also file appropriate reports with Congress and the Comptroller General so this rule may be reviewed.

National Credit Union Administration
12 CFR Part 716
RIN 3133-AG13
AGENCY:
National Credit Union Administration (NCUA).
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
The NCUA Board (Board) is issuing a final rule to make technical corrections to provisions of the NCUA's regulations. The technical amendments improve clarity by removing obsolete references to the privacy of consumer financial information regulation, which the NCUA no longer administers.
DATES:
The final rule is effective on November 16, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
John H. Brolin, Senior Staff Attorney, Division of Regulations and Legislation, Office of General Counsel, at (703) 518-6540 or at 1775 Duke Street, Alexandria, VA 22314.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Introduction
A. Background
Historically the NCUA, along with the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, Treasury; Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System; Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation; Office of Thrift Supervision, Treasury; and Farm Credit Administration (collectively, the Agencies) maintained regulations
[
1
]
implementing the privacy provisions of subtitle A of title V of the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act (GLB Act). These rules required financial institutions to provide initial and annual privacy notices to their customers under section 728 of the Financial Services Regulatory Relief Act of 2006.
The Dodd-Frank Act was signed into law in 2010.
[
2
]
The Dodd-Frank Act substantially changed the federal legal framework for consumer financial protection regulation. Among the many changes, title X of the Dodd-Frank Act transferred the NCUA's GLB Act rulemaking authority to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB).
[
3
]
As a result, the NCUA rescinded its rule governing consumer financial information privacy,
12 CFR part 716
.
[
4
]
CFPB republished consumer financial protection requirements as interim final rules at
12 CFR part 1016
.
[
5
]
To assist federally insured credit unions during the transition, the NCUA retained part 716 under its original heading and amended it to replace the requirements with a cross-citation to the CFPB's interim final rules as described above.
[
6
]
The Board periodically issues rules as technical amendments to remove outdated information. Consistent with the treatment of other consumer financial protection laws, this final rule removes obsolete cross-citations to the CFPB's regulations governing the privacy of consumer financial information because NCUA no longer has rulemaking authority in this area. Because these changes are technical in nature, the Board adopts these amendments as final rules without the opportunity for notice and comment typically required by the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).
[
7
]
This final rule makes technical amendments that do not require affected parties to adjust their behavior before the final rule takes effect.
[
8
]
Therefore, the Board is issuing this final rule to address the types of matters described in this paragraph with an immediate effective date and without notice and comment.
B. Legal Authority
The Board has the legal authority to issue this final rule pursuant to its plenary rulemaking authority under the Federal Credit Union Act and its specific rulemaking authority under the various acts the Board administers.
[
9
]
II. Final Rule
The final rule amends current part 716 to remove the cross-citation to the CFPB's regulations governing the privacy of consumer financial information. The section currently provides that the NCUA's rule, formerly published at
12 CFR part 716
, has been republished by the CFPB at
12 CFR part 1016
, “Privacy of Consumer Financial Information (Regulation P).” As explained in the Background of this preamble, this part merely cross-references the applicable consumer financial protection regulation, which is maintained by the CFPB. Because this part, as amended in 2011, was intended only to assist credit unions with the 2011 transfer of NCUA's rules to the CFPB, this part is no longer necessary. Accordingly, this final rule removes current part 716 in its entirety and reserves the part.
III. Regulatory Procedures
A. Executive Orders 12866, 13563, 14192
Pursuant to
Executive Order 12866
(“Regulatory Planning and Review”), a determination must be made whether a regulatory action is significant and therefore subject to review by the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA), within the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) in accordance with the requirements of the Executive Order.
[
10
]
Executive Order 13563
(“Improving Regulation and Regulatory Review”) supplements and reaffirms the principles, structures, and definitions governing contemporary regulatory review established in
(
printed page 73430)
Executive Order 12866
.
[
11
]
This final rule was drafted and reviewed in accordance with
Executive Order 12866
and
Executive Order 13563
. OIRA has determined that this final rule is not a “significant regulatory action” as defined by section 3(f) of
Executive Order 12866
.
Executive Order 14192
(“Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation”) requires that any new incremental costs associated with new regulations shall, to the extent permitted by law, be offset by the elimination of existing costs associated with at least 10 prior regulations.
[
12
]
This final rule is not an
Executive Order 14192
regulatory action because this rule is not significant under
Executive Order 12866
. This final rule is considered an
Executive Order 14192
deregulatory action.
B. The Regulatory Flexibility Act
The Regulatory Flexibility Act requires the Board to prepare an analysis of any significant economic impact a regulation may have on a substantial number of small entities.
[
13
]
The Board has designated federally insured credit unions with less than $100 million in assets as small entities for this purpose.
[
14
]
As discussed previously, consistent with the APA,
[
15
]
the Board has determined for good cause that general notice and opportunity for public comment is unnecessary, and therefore the Board is not issuing a notice of proposed rulemaking. Rules for which notice and comment procedures are not required are not subject to the Regulatory Flexibility Act's requirements, including conducting a regulatory flexibility analysis. Accordingly, the Board has concluded that the Regulatory Flexibility Act's requirements relating to initial and final regulatory flexibility analyses do not apply.
Nevertheless, if these requirements applied, the Board would determine that the final rule does not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities because it does not impose or alter any rights or obligations on non-agency parties. The final rule simply removes certain obsolete regulations.
C. The Paperwork Reduction Act
The Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (PRA) generally provides that an agency may not conduct or sponsor, and not withstanding any other provision of law, a person is not required to respond to, a collection of information, unless it displays a currently valid Office of Management and Budget control number. The PRA applies to rulemakings in which an agency creates a new or amends existing information collection requirements. For purposes of the PRA, an information-collection requirement may take the form of a reporting, recordkeeping, or a third-party disclosure requirement. The NCUA has determined that the changes addressed in this notice do not create a new information collection or revise an existing information collection as defined by the PRA.
D.
Executive Order 13132
on Federalism
Executive Order 13132
encourages certain agencies to consider the impact of their actions on state and local interests.
[
16
]
The NCUA, an agency as defined in
44 U.S.C. 3502(5)
, voluntarily complies with the executive order to adhere to fundamental federalism principles. The final rule does not have substantial direct effects on the states, on the relationship between the national government and the states, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government. The final rule does not create or alter existing rights or requirements that apply to federally insured, state-chartered credit unions or affect the ability of state regulatory agencies to examine, supervise, or regulate such credit unions. The NCUA has therefore determined that this final rule does not constitute a policy that has federalism implications for purposes of the executive order.
E. Assessment of Federal Regulations and Policies on Families
The NCUA has determined that this rule will not affect family well-being within the meaning of section 654 of the Treasury and General Government Appropriations Act.
[
17
]
F. Congressional Review Act
Subtitle E of the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act of 1996 (also known as the Congressional Review Act or CRA) generally provides for congressional review of agency rules.
[
18
]
NCUA must submit a report to Congress and the Comptroller General when it issues a final rule, as defined by the CRA.
[
19
]
An agency rule, in addition to being subject to congressional oversight, may also be subject to a delayed effective date if the rule is a “major rule.” OIRA has determined that this final rule is not a major rule as defined by the CRA.
[
20
]
The delayed effective date required by the CRA does not apply to any rule for which an agency for good cause finds (and incorporates the finding and a brief statement of reasons therefor in the rule issued) that notice and public procedure thereon are impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest.
[
21
]
For the same reasons noted above with respect to forgoing notice and comment in adopting this final rule, NCUA is adopting the final rule without the delayed effective date generally prescribed under the CRA.

Project Description:
The project includes an approximately 252.6-foot-long, 29-foot-high dam that includes two spillway sections that are overtopped with inflatable rubber crest gates with maximum crest elevations of 136 feet National Geodetic Vertical Datum of 1929 (NGVD 29) and a powerhouse that includes an intake structure with a trashrack with 0.8-inch clear bar spacing for the upper 8 feet of the trashrack and 2-inch clear bar spacing on the bottom section, and three 2.485-MW Kaplan turbine-generator units, for a total installed capacity of 7.455 MW.
The dam creates an impoundment that has a normal surface area of 6.7 acres at 136.0 feet NGVD 29. From the impoundment, water flows through the powerhouse to a 190-foot-long tailrace, where it returns to the Winooski River. Water also flows through the intake structure to a downstream fishway that includes a collection chamber behind the trashracks and a 3-foot-diameter pipe that discharges to the tailrace on the east side of the powerhouse. The project creates an approximately 230-foot-long bypassed reach of the Winooski River.
The project includes an upstream fish passage facility that consists of a trap and truck facility with a concrete fish lift located on the west side of the powerhouse. Project recreation facilities include: (1) an approximately 660-foot-long paved walkway on the north shoreline of the impoundment; (2) an approximately 745-foot-long public access trail on the north shoreline of the Winooski River, to the west of the project dam; and (3) a public access and overlook area on top of the powerhouse. The project includes a 200-foot-long access road on the northern bank of the impoundment.
Electricity generated at the project is transmitted to the electric grid via an underground 400-foot-long, 13.8-kilovolt transmission line.

AGENCY:
National Credit Union Administration (NCUA).
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
The NCUA Board (Board) is publishing this final rule to remove a redundant and outdated regulation regarding nondiscrimination in lending. The regulation was intended to summarize the Fair Housing Act (FHA) prohibitions on discrimination related to real estate related loans, appraisals, and advertising. The Board's last substantive amendment to the regulation was finalized in 2001. Thus, the regulation does not reflect all case law or regulatory developments under the FHA, a statute that primarily falls under the jurisdiction of the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and continues to apply to federal credit unions (FCUs) regardless of this regulation. For these reasons, the Board is removing the regulation in its entirety.
DATES:
This final rule is effective on December 16, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Office of General Counsel:
Gira Bose, Senior Staff Attorney, at (703) 518-6540 or at 1775 Duke Street, Alexandria, VA 22314.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Introduction
A. Background
Section 701.31 was first promulgated in 1972, and its purpose was to centralize and summarize the lending discrimination requirements applicable to FCUs.
[
1
]
The regulation includes nondiscrimination requirements for loans and appraisals; advertising, notices, and logos related to nondiscrimination; and guidelines for compliance with the FHA.
[
2
]
While § 701.31 has been updated periodically, it has not kept pace with regulatory and case law changes regarding lending discrimination or fair housing. In addition, § 701.31 is duplicative of other, more comprehensive, federal laws—principally the FHA and the Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA)—and their implementing regulations, such as the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's Regulation B. Some changes were made to § 701.31 in the 1980s and again in 2001; however, in the intervening years, the regulation has not kept pace with current law.
B. Legal Authority
The Board is issuing this final rule pursuant to its authority under the FCU Act. Under the FCU Act, NCUA is the chartering and supervisory authority for FCUs and the federal supervisory authority for federally insured credit unions (FICUs).
[
3
]
The FCU Act grants NCUA a broad mandate to issue regulations governing both FCUs and all FICUs. Section 120 of the FCU Act is a general grant of regulatory authority and authorizes the Board to prescribe rules and regulations for the administration of the FCU Act.
[
4
]
Section 207 of the FCU Act is a specific grant of authority over share insurance coverage, conservatorships, and liquidations.
[
5
]
Section 209 of the FCU Act is a plenary grant of regulatory authority to issue rules and regulations necessary or appropriate to carry out its role as share insurer for all FICUs.
[
6
]
Accordingly, the FCU Act grants the Board broad rulemaking authority to ensure that the federally insured credit union industry and the Share Insurance Fund remain safe and sound.
While the FCU Act authorizes the Board to adopt such regulations as it deems appropriate to administer the Act, it does not require the agency to promulgate regulations to assist credit unions in their compliance with the FHA or ECOA. Neither the FHA nor ECOA require any such NCUA rulemaking. Thus, the Board has determined that § 701.31 should be rescinded.
II. Final Rule
A. Overview
This final rule follows publication of the proposed rule and takes into consideration the comments received on the proposal. By the close of the public comment period on March 16, 2026, the Board received 16 public comments. Comments were submitted by three credit unions, seven state and regional credit union leagues, two national credit union trade associations, three individuals who did not disclose a group affiliation, and one think tank. After careful consideration of the issues raised by the commenters, the Board has decided to adopt the proposal without change.
B. Discussion of Public Comments
This section of the preamble discusses the significant issues raised by the commenters, and the Board's responses to the comments.
Twelve commenters expressed support for the proposal. Nine of these commenters supported the proposal without any conditions. The other three commenters expressed support but noted the importance of ensuring that eliminating this provision does not unintentionally reduce clarity regarding fair lending obligations. One commenter requested four clarifications in the event that NCUA removes the regulation: (1) that the preamble to the final rule confirm that removal of § 701.31 does not alter or weaken existing fair lending and nondiscrimination obligations, and that examiners will continue to evaluate compliance directly against FHA, ECOA, and Regulation B standards; (2) clarification that credit unions may update internal policies, procedures, and control documentation that reference § 701.31 through their normal governance and policy refresh cycles; (3) that the final rule preamble clearly state that fair housing poster and notice requirements established under HUD regulations remain fully applicable to FCUs; and (4) confirmation that nondiscrimination expectations related to appraisals remain fully governed by existing FHA and ECOA standards after removal of § 701.31 as clarification that
(
printed page 73428)
the change is structural rather than substantive.
Two commenters opposed the proposal, one interpreting revocation of the rule to mean the agency supports discrimination in lending and the other commenter stating that revocation will lead to an increase in discrimination in lending. Finally, two commenters stated that, rather than just eliminating the rule, the agency should: (1) provide cross-references to Fair Housing Act regulations if § 701.31 is removed; (2) issue updated supervisory guidance explaining fair-lending expectations; and (3) clarify in the final rule that removal of § 701.31 does not alter credit unions' substantive obligations under federal nondiscrimination laws.
To be clear, this final rule is designed only to remove an outdated and redundant regulation that has not kept pace with current law. It does not reflect any reduction in NCUA's estimation of the importance of FCUs adhering to fair lending and nondiscrimination laws. And it does not in any way alter FCUs' legal obligations under the FHA, ECOA, or regulations promulgated by HUD or CFPB pursuant to those statutes. Those laws have applied, and continue to apply, to FCUs regardless of § 701.31. FHA's fair housing poster and notice requirements remain fully applicable to FCUs.
[
7
]
In order to accomplish this change without undue burden, when removing references to § 701.31, FCUs may rely on the methods and timeframes they typically use to update their systems. It is the Board's understanding that FCUs have not generally relied on § 701.31 to meet their obligations under FHA and ECOA. Therefore, the Board does not deem it necessary to issue cross-references to those statutes or issue updated supervisory expectations at this time. NCUA's website already hosts a Fair Lending Guide, which includes information and resources for compliance with FHA and ECOA.
[
8
]
III. Regulatory Procedures
A. Executive Orders 12866, 13563, and 14192
Pursuant to
Executive Order 12866
(“Regulatory Planning and Review”), a determination must be made whether a regulatory action is significant and therefore subject to review by the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA), within the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) in accordance with the requirements of the Executive Order.
[
9
]
Executive Order 13563
(“Improving Regulation and Regulatory Review”) supplements and reaffirms the principles, structures, and definitions governing contemporary regulatory review established in
Executive Order 12866
.
[
10
]
This final rule was drafted and reviewed in accordance with
Executive Order 12866
and
Executive Order 13563
. OIRA has determined that this final rule is not a “significant regulatory action” as defined by section 3(f) of
Executive Order 12866
.
Executive Order 14192
(“Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation”) requires that any new incremental costs associated with new regulations shall, to the extent permitted by law, be offset by the elimination of existing costs associated with at least 10 prior regulations.
[
11
]
This final rule is not an
Executive Order 14192
regulatory action because this rule is not significant under
Executive Order 12866
. This final rule is considered an
Executive Order 14192
deregulatory action.
B. Regulatory Flexibility Act
The Regulatory Flexibility Act
[
12
]
generally requires an agency to conduct a regulatory flexibility analysis of any rule subject to notice and comment rulemaking requirements, unless the agency certifies that the rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities. If the agency makes such a certification, it shall publish the certification at the time of publication of either the proposed rule or the final rule, along with a statement providing the factual basis for such certification.
[
13
]
For purposes of this analysis, NCUA considers small credit unions to be those having under $100 million in assets.
[
14
]
The Board fully considered the potential economic impacts of the regulatory amendments on small credit unions.
This final rule does not substantively alter credit unions' regulatory obligations. It is expected that removing § 701.31 will simplify FCU compliance with fair lending and nondiscrimination requirements because it is eliminating an outdated regulation and a potential source of confusion. Accordingly, NCUA certifies the final rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small credit unions.
C. Paperwork Reduction Act
The Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (PRA) generally provides that an agency may not conduct or sponsor, and not withstanding any other provision of law, a person is not required to respond to, a collection of information, unless it displays a currently valid OMB control number. The PRA applies to rulemaking in which an agency creates a new or amends existing information collection requirements. For purposes of the PRA, an information collection requirement may take the form of a reporting, recordkeeping, or a third-party disclosure requirement. NCUA has determined that the changes in the final rule do not create a new information collection or revise an existing information collection as defined by the PRA.
D.
Executive Order 13132
on Federalism
Executive Order 13132
encourages independent regulatory agencies to consider the impact of their actions on state and local interests.
[
15
]
NCUA, an agency as defined in
44 U.S.C. 3502(5)
, voluntarily complies with the executive order to adhere to fundamental federalism principles. Section 701.31 applies to FCUs and not state-chartered credit unions. Therefore, this rulemaking will not have a direct effect on the states, the relationship between the national government and the states, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government.
E. Assessment of Federal Regulations and Policies on Families
The removal of § 701.31 from NCUA's regulations does not constitute a substantive change. Nondiscrimination and fair lending laws continue to apply to FCUs regardless of § 701.31. Therefore, NCUA has determined that this final rule will not affect family well-being within the meaning of Section 654 of the Treasury and General Government Appropriations Act, 1999.
[
16
]
F. Congressional Review Act
Subtitle E of the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act of 1996, also known as the Congressional Review Act (CRA), generally provides for congressional review of agency rules.
[
17
]
NCUA must submit a report to Congress and the Comptroller General when it issues a final rule, as defined by the CRA.
[
18
]
An agency rule, in addition
(
printed page 73429)
to being subject to congressional oversight, may also be subject to a delayed effective date if the rule is a “major rule.” OIRA has determined that this rule is not a “major rule” within the meaning of the relevant sections of the CRA. NCUA will also file appropriate reports with Congress and the Comptroller General so this rule may be reviewed.

AGENCY:
National Credit Union Administration (NCUA).
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
The NCUA Board (Board) is issuing a final rule to make technical corrections to provisions of the NCUA's regulations. The technical amendments in this final rule improve clarity by removing obsolete references to the registration of mortgage loan originators.
DATES:
The final rule is effective on November 16, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
John H. Brolin, Senior Staff Attorney, Office of General Counsel, by telephone at (703) 518-6540 or at 1775 Duke Street, Alexandria, VA 22314.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Introduction
A. Background
In July of 2010, the NCUA, in conjunction with the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, Office of Thrift Supervision, and Farm Credit Administration (FCA) (collectively, the Agencies), adopted final rules
[
1
]
to implement the Secure and Fair Enforcement for Mortgage Licensing Act (the SAFE Act).
[
2
]
The SAFE Act requires an employee of a bank, savings association, credit union or Farm Credit System institution and certain of their subsidiaries that are regulated by a federal banking agency or the FCA (collectively, Agency-regulated institutions) who acts as a residential mortgage loan originator to register with the Nationwide Mortgage Licensing System and Registry, obtain a unique identifier, and maintain this registration.
[
3
]
The final rule further provided that Agency-regulated institutions must:
Require that their employees who act as residential mortgage loan originators comply with the SAFE Act's requirements to register and obtain a unique identifier; and
Adopt and follow written policies and procedures designed to assure compliance with these requirements.
The NCUA codified its SAFE Act regulations under
12 CFR part 761
.
The Dodd-Frank Act was signed into law in 2010.
[
4
]
The Dodd-Frank Act substantially changed the federal legal framework with respect to consumer financial protection regulation. Among the many changes, title X of the Dodd-Frank Act transferred the NCUA's rulemaking authority under the SAFE Act to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB).
[
5
]
As a result, the NCUA rescinded its regulation at part 761, which established the requirements described previously for registration of residential mortgage loan originators.
[
6
]
The CFPB republished these requirements as interim final at
12 CFR part 1007
.
[
7
]
To assist federally insured credit unions during the transition, the rescinded parts of the NCUA's regulations were retained under their original heading and were amended to include a cross-citation to the CFPB's republished version of the regulation.
[
8
]
The Board periodically issues technical amendments rules to remove outdated information. Consistent with the treatment of other consumer financial protection laws, this final rule removes obsolete cross-citations to the CFPB's regulations governing the registration of residential mortgage loan originators. As explained previously, rulemaking authority for these regulations no longer rests with the NCUA, so the Board is removing historic cross-citations to the CFPB's regulations. Because these changes are technical in nature, the Board adopts these amendments as final rules without the opportunity for notice and comment typically required by the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).
[
9
]
This final rule makes technical amendments that do not require affected parties to adjust their behavior before the final rule takes effect.
[
10
]
Therefore, the Board is issuing this final rule to address the types of matters described in this paragraph with an immediate effective date and without notice and comment.
B. Legal Authority
The Board has the legal authority to issue this final rule pursuant to its plenary rulemaking authority under the Federal Credit Union Act and its specific rulemaking authority under the various acts the Board administers.
[
11
]
II. Final Rule
A. Section 741.223 Registration of Residential Mortgage Loan Originators
The final rule amends current § 741.223 to remove the cross-citation to the CFPB's regulations governing the registration of residential mortgage loan originators. The section currently provides that any credit union that is insured pursuant to title II of the Federal Credit Union Act must adhere to the requirements stated in part 1007 of title 12 (Regulation G). As explained in the Background part of this preamble, this section merely cross-references the applicable consumer financial protection regulation, which is maintained by the CFPB. Because this section was intended only to assist federally insured, state-chartered credit unions, given the transfer of the NCUA's 2013 regulations to the CFPB—which occurred more than 13 years ago—the cross-citation is no longer necessary to remedy any confusion about where to find the applicable regulations. Accordingly, the final rule removes current § 741.223 and reserves the section.
B. Part 761 Registration of Residential Mortgage Loan Originators
The final rule amends current part 761 to remove the cross-citation to the CFPB's regulations governing the
(
printed page 73435)
registration of residential mortgage loan originators. The section currently provides that the rules formerly at
12 CFR part 761
have been republished by the CFPB at
12 CFR part 1007
, “S.A.F.E. Mortgage Licensing Act—Federal Registration of Residential Mortgage Loan Originators (Regulation G)”. As explained in the Background of this preamble, this part merely cross-references the applicable consumer financial protection regulation, which is maintained by the CFPB. Because this part was intended only to assist credit unions given the transfer of the NCUA's 2013 regulations to the CFPB—which occurred more than 12 years ago—the part is no longer necessary to remedy any confusion about where to find the applicable regulations. Accordingly, the final rule removes current part 761 in its entirety and reserves the part.
III. Regulatory Procedures
A. Executive Orders 12866, 13563, 14192
Pursuant to
Executive Order 12866
(“Regulatory Planning and Review”), a determination must be made whether a regulatory action is significant and therefore subject to review by the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA), within the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) in accordance with the requirements of the Executive Order.
[
12
]
Executive Order 13563
(“Improving Regulation and Regulatory Review”) supplements and reaffirms the principles, structures, and definitions governing contemporary regulatory review established in
Executive Order 12866
.
[
13
]
This final rule was drafted and reviewed in accordance with
Executive Order 12866
and
Executive Order 13563
. OIRA has determined that this final rule is not a “significant regulatory action” as defined by section 3(f) of
Executive Order 12866
.
Executive Order 14192
(“Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation”) requires that any new incremental costs associated with new regulations shall, to the extent permitted by law, be offset by the elimination of existing costs associated with at least 10 prior regulations.
[
14
]
This final rule is not an
Executive Order 14192
regulatory action because this rule is not significant under
Executive Order 12866
. This final rule is considered an
Executive Order 14192
deregulatory action.
B. The Regulatory Flexibility Act
The Regulatory Flexibility Act requires the Board to prepare an analysis of any significant economic impact a regulation may have on a substantial number of small entities.
[
15
]
The Board has designated federally insured credit unions with less than $100 million in assets as small entities for this purpose.
[
16
]
As discussed previously, consistent with the APA,
[
17
]
the Board has determined for good cause that general notice and opportunity for public comment is unnecessary, and therefore the Board is not issuing a notice of proposed rulemaking. Rules for which notice and comment procedures are not required are not subject to the Regulatory Flexibility Act's requirements, including conducting a regulatory flexibility analysis. Accordingly, the Board has concluded that the Regulatory Flexibility Act's requirements relating to initial and final regulatory flexibility analyses do not apply.
Nevertheless, if these requirements applied, the Board would determine that the final rule does not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities because it does not impose or alter any rights or obligations on non-agency parties. The final rule simply removes certain obsolete regulations.
C. The Paperwork Reduction Act
The Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (PRA) generally provides that an agency may not conduct or sponsor, and not withstanding any other provision of law, a person is not required to respond to, a collection of information, unless it displays a currently valid Office of Management and Budget control number. The PRA applies to rulemakings in which an agency creates a new or amends existing information collection requirements. For purposes of the PRA, an information-collection requirement may take the form of a reporting, recordkeeping, or a third-party disclosure requirement. The NCUA has determined that the changes in the final rule do not create a new information collection or revise an existing information collection as defined by the PRA.
D.
Executive Order 13132
on Federalism
Executive Order 13132
encourages certain agencies to consider the impact of their actions on state and local interests.
[
18
]
The NCUA, an agency as defined in
44 U.S.C. 3502(5)
, voluntarily complies with the executive order to adhere to fundamental federalism principles. The final rule does not have substantial direct effects on the states, on the relationship between the national government and the states, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government. The final rule does not create or alter existing rights or requirements that apply to federally insured, state-chartered credit unions or affect the ability of state regulatory agencies to examine, supervise, or regulate such credit unions. The NCUA has therefore determined that this final rule does not constitute a policy that has federalism implications for purposes of the executive order.
E. Assessment of Federal Regulations and Policies on Families
The NCUA has determined that this rule will not affect family well-being within the meaning of § 654 of the Treasury and General Government Appropriations Act.
[
19
]
F. Congressional Review Act
Subtitle E of the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act of 1996 (also known as the Congressional Review Act or CRA) generally provides for congressional review of agency rules.
[
20
]
NCUA must submit a report to Congress and the Comptroller General when it issues a final rule, as defined by the CRA.
[
21
]
An agency rule, in addition to being subject to congressional oversight, may also be subject to a delayed effective date if the rule is a “major rule.” OIRA has determined that this final rule is not a major rule as defined by the CRA.
[
22
]
The delayed effective date required by the CRA does not apply to any rule for which an agency for good cause finds (and incorporates the finding and a brief statement of reasons therefor in the rule issued) that notice and public procedure thereon are impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest.
[
23
]
For the same reasons noted above with respect to forgoing notice and comment in adopting this final rule, NCUA is adopting the final rule without the delayed effective date generally prescribed under the CRA.
(
printed page 73436)

Specifically, this final rule removes requirements related to wages and benefits that the Administration believes are not in line with the plain language of the Head Start Act and are costly and overly prescriptive for Head Start programs and staff. ACF estimates these changes will result in over $2 billion in future cost savings for Head Start programs. The rescissions in this final rule impact the costliest parts of the final rule published by the Office of Head Start (OHS) in 2024, Supporting the Head Start Workforce and Consistent Quality Programming.

AGENCY:
Office of Head Start (OHS), Administration for Children and Families (ACF), Department of Health and Human Services (HHS).
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
In this final rule, the Administration for Children and Families (ACF) removes requirements from the Head Start Program Performance Standards (Performance Standards) to restore local flexibility to Head Start programs and improve access to quality services. Specifically, this final rule removes requirements related to wages and benefits that the Administration believes are not in line with the plain language of the Head Start Act and are costly and overly prescriptive for Head Start programs and staff. ACF estimates these changes will result in over $2 billion in future cost savings for Head Start programs. The rescissions in this final rule impact the costliest parts of the final rule published by the Office of Head Start (OHS) in 2024,
Supporting the Head Start Workforce and Consistent Quality Programming.
DATES:
Effective date:
January 15, 2027.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Shawna Pinckney, Office of Head Start, 866-763-6481,
OHS_Policy@acf.hhs.gov
.
I. Background
The Federal Head Start program provides early education and other comprehensive services to low-income pregnant women and children prenatal to age 5 in center- and home-based settings across the country. Since its inception in 1965 as part of the War on Poverty, Head Start has been a leader in providing high-quality services that support the development of children from low-income families, helping them enter kindergarten more prepared to succeed in school and in life. Research shows that the first five years of a child's life are pivotal for brain development, laying the foundation for all future learning, behavior, and health.
[
1
]
For children in poverty, this period is even more crucial, as they often face additional stressors—such as inadequate nutrition or limited access to educational resources—that can hinder brain development.
[
2
]
Research demonstrates that early intervention, including quality early education, is key to disrupting the cycle of poverty and supporting the development of young children so they are more prepared to succeed in school and in life. Indeed, a wealth of evidence supports the positive outcomes for low-income children and their families who participate in and graduate from Head Start programs.
[
3
]
The Head Start Program Performance Standards (Performance Standards), first published in the 1970s, are the foundation on which Head Start programs design and deliver high-quality, comprehensive services to children and their families. They set forth the requirements local grant recipients must meet to support the cognitive, social, emotional, and healthy development of children enrolled in the program. They include requirements to provide education, health, mental health, nutrition, and family and community engagement services, as well as requirements for local program governance and Federal administration of the program.
The
Improving Head Start for School Readiness Act of 2007
(the 2007 Reauthorization), which amended the Head Start Act (the Act), required the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) to ensure children and families receive quality Head Start services. The 2007 Reauthorization also required the Secretary of HHS to revise the Performance Standards, as needed. This authority has provided a basis for updates and changes made to the Performance Standards since 2007. HHS conducted a major revision of the Performance Standards through a final rule published in 2016 to implement the statutory changes in the 2007 Reauthorization and to enhance program requirements to reflect the latest science on child development. Subsequently, HHS published a final rule in 2024
[
4
]
that added a number of specific and costly requirements for programs related to supports for the Head Start workforce, among other changes. This final rule makes necessary changes to bring the Head Start regulations in line with the Head Start Act. It restores flexibility to local Head Start programs and improves access for children and families by removing the costly requirements added in 2024. These changes are explained in greater detail in the sections that follow.
II. Statutory Authority
This final rule is being issued under the authority granted to the Secretary of
(
printed page 73471)
Health and Human Services by sections 641A, 645A, and 653 of the Act (
42 U.S.C. 9836a
,
9840a
, and
9848
), as amended by the Improving Head Start for School Readiness Act of 2007 (
Public Law 110-134
). Under these sections, the Secretary is required to establish performance standards and other regulations for Head Start and Early Head Start programs. Specifically, the Act requires the Secretary to “modify, as necessary, program performance standards by regulation applicable to Head Start agencies and programs.”
[
5
]
This final rule meets the statutory requirements Congress put forth in its 2007 bipartisan reauthorization of the Head Start program and addresses Congress's mandate that called for the Secretary to review and revise the Performance Standards. The Secretary has determined that the modifications to the Performance Standards contained in this regulation are appropriate and needed to effectuate the goals of the Performance Standards and the purposes of the Act.
III. Summary Description of Regulatory Provisions
The following is a summary of the regulatory changes included in this final rule. This rule removes the wage and benefit requirements in § 1302.90(e) and (f) that were introduced in the 2024 final rule, restoring greater flexibility to local Head Start programs. Specifically, it eliminates prescriptive requirements that would have required programs to develop or update a pay scale for all staff; provide education staff with wages comparable to public preschool teachers; provide all staff a salary sufficient to cover basic costs of living; and promote wage comparability across Head Start Preschool and Early Head Start. This final rule also eliminates requirements to provide staff with specified benefits.
The staff wage and benefit requirements introduced by ACF in the 2024 final rule were intended to address persistent workforce instability in Head Start programs. In the 2024 final rule, ACF cited that, at that time, Head Start programs faced historically high levels of staff turnover and vacancies, with low wages and limited benefits identified as key contributors to recruitment and retention challenges. ACF also explained that expectations and qualification requirements for Head Start staff had increased substantially without corresponding growth in compensation. Because staffing shortages may have been preventing some programs' ability to open classrooms and serve children, in the 2024 final rule, ACF identified improved compensation as key to stabilizing the workforce and maintaining program quality.
In the 2024 final rule, ACF recognized that, in the absence of sufficient additional appropriations from Congress, implementing these wage and benefit requirements would require some programs to reduce funded Head Start slots in order to increase staff compensation. ACF estimated that by the time the wage and benefit requirements were fully implemented in 2031, funded enrollment could decline by more than 100,000 slots. At the same time, ACF acknowledged substantial uncertainty in projecting future enrollment, including uncertainty about whether the significant under enrollment that existed at the time would persist. In other words, ACF recognizes that the ultimate impact of these requirements on the number of children served could be even greater than the estimates ACF presented in the 2024 final rule.
Although ACF recognizes that workforce challenges may persist for Head Start programs, the current Administration has reconsidered the approach adopted in the 2024 final rule and does not believe that a one size fits all approach to staff compensation is the appropriate way to address these challenges, particularly when doing so may reduce access to Head Start services. Instead, ACF has determined that programs should have maximum local flexibility to design compensation packages and provide services that best meet the needs of their communities. ACF encourages programs to provide compensation according to salary scales based on training and experience, per Sec. 653 of the Act.
Through this final rule, ACF is rescinding the 2024 wage and benefit requirements well in advance of the 2031 compliance deadline to avoid programs making further operational and financial changes in anticipation of requirements that will no longer apply. ACF recognizes that some programs have already begun taking steps to comply with these requirements, including through requests to reduce their funded Head Start enrollment slots. ACF also recognizes that some Head Start staff may have remained in their jobs in anticipation of receiving wage or benefit increases as part of implementation of the 2024 final rule. However, ACF anticipates that most programs have not yet undertaken substantial implementation efforts, given that multiple years remain before compliance is required. Recent PIR data indicate that, after adjusting for inflation, education staff wages have increased by a small amount since the 2024 final rule, suggesting some progress toward implementing the wage requirements.
Further, Head Start programs can still voluntarily choose to implement much of what the 2024 final rule required for staff wages and benefits, regardless of this final rule. For instance, if a program has determined that more competitive wages are necessary to retain their staff, they can choose to make these changes within their budgets regardless of these Federal regulatory requirements being removed. Additionally, there is no requirement that programs who have made salary increases for staff to reduce those increases as a result of this rule.
As discussed in the Regulatory Impact Analysis (RIA) of this final rule, ACF considered and assessed several policy alternatives to this final rule. Alternatives such as extending the implementation timeline for the 2024 wage and benefit requirements would delay, but not resolve, ACF's concerns that prescriptive Federal compensation requirements limit local flexibility and could require programs to reduce the number of funded slots or otherwise redirect resources from services to children and families. For this reason, ACF determined that rescinding the 2024 wage and benefit requirements is the appropriate approach. This final rule reduces regulatory burden, provides local programs with more discretion over compensation and benefits, and preserves funding for services to children and families.
ACF has evaluated this final rule against Sec. 641A(a)(2)(C)(ii) of the Act which requires that any revision to the Performance Standards will not result in the elimination of or any reduction in quality, scope, or types of health, educational, parental involvement, nutritional, social, or other services required to be provided under such standards as in effect on December 12, 2007. Congress did not provide that every regulation later promulgated by HHS becomes independently protected against revision. While the provisions implicated in this rule were added nearly 17 years after the protected baseline, HHS none-the-less reviewed them and considered the substance of the underlying 2007 service obligation. The 2007 standards did not include any Federal regulations related to staff wages and benefits, and therefore HHS has determined this rescission does not reduce the 2007 level of quality, scope, or types standard.
