IV. Discussion of Comments and Regulatory Provisions
General Comments
ACF received nearly 300 public comments on the proposed changes in the NPRM. Several of these comments include signatories from multiple individuals or large organizations, including two multi-signatory letters from Members of Congress. Some commenters expressed strong support for the NPRM and appreciated the flexibility it offers programs, the relief from burdensome Federal regulation, and the removal of an unfunded mandate. Many comments expressed concern about the proposed removal of wage and benefit requirements in § 1302.90, including the two multi-signatory congressional letters. These comments reflected several themes including concerns about workforce stability, compensation, equity with public schools, and overall advocacy for teachers and the Head Start workforce. We heard from a variety of commenters about the specific impacts this final rule will have on their communities.
Commenters who wrote in support, opposition, or neutrally about the policy changes outlined in the NPRM consistently reflected value for Head Start and deep care for the future of the program. Commenters including staff, parents, alumni and community members expressed the deep and lasting impact Head Start has had on individuals and communities. While no response to these comments is needed, ACF acknowledges and appreciates these comments.
ACF thanks commenters that responded to ACF's invitation to comment on other changes from the 2024 final rule that ACF should consider for rescission or modification in a future NPRM, particularly changes that were burdensome for programs. These comments have been reviewed and will be used to inform future regulatory action but are not discussed in detail in this final rule.
Below we summarize the comments that pertain to the proposed rule, organized by topic, and respond to them accordingly.
Wages and Benefits
Comment:
Many commenters stated that Head Start educators deserve higher pay, livable wages, and benefits. Commenters emphasized that compensation should reflect the important role Head Start staff play in supporting children's learning and development and expressed concern that current compensation levels make it difficult to attract and retain qualified staff.
Response:
ACF recognizes the important contributions of the Head Start workforce, particularly that a stable workforce is essential to delivering high-quality Head Start services and that competitive wages and benefits are important tools for recruiting and retaining that workforce. At the same time, Head Start grant recipients operate in diverse labor markets, face different workforce needs and must balance investments in compensation with the resources necessary to maintain enrollment and deliver comprehensive services to children and families. The compensation requirements established in the 2024 final rule would have required, among other provisions, specified wage benchmarks for education staff, pay structures for all staff, and minimum standards related to wages and benefits. ACF has determined that maintaining these prescriptive Federal requirements without corresponding additional increases in appropriations would place substantial financial pressure on Head Start programs. ACF estimates that absent additional appropriations, approximately 106,000 funded Head Start slots would need to be eliminated for programs to meet the requirements by the applicable compliance deadline. Accordingly, retaining the requirements could force many grant recipients to make significant tradeoffs among increasing compensation, reducing staffing or funded enrollment, and maintaining existing levels of service. This rule removes a burdensome unfunded mandate that would impact programs' ability to continue operating at current levels and would have necessitated laying off staff.
This final rule provides grant recipients with greater flexibility to determine compensation approaches that reflect local workforce conditions, organizational priorities, and available funding while continuing to meet applicable statutory requirements. To be clear, the final rule does not prohibit the maintenance of current compensation structures, nor does it encourage grant recipients to reduce compensation for program staff. Through this rule, ACF merely seeks to give programs the ability to make compensation decisions that impact their staff with maximum flexibility, while still complying with Federal law.
Comment:
Some commenters stated that improving compensation supports higher-quality services by strengthening workforce stability, improving child and family outcomes, and increasing trust among families served by Head Start programs.
Response:
The changes to the Performance Standards through this final rule do not diminish the importance of program quality. Rather, this final rule removes Federal requirements that prescribe specific approaches and provides grant recipients with greater discretion to determine how best to support program quality and their workforce based on local needs, resources, and circumstances.
Comment:
A number of commenters emphasized that Head Start educators should be valued as professionals and expressed support for greater equity with other early childhood educators and public school personnel. Several commenters noted the education, qualifications, and expertise required of the Head Start workforce.
Response:
This final rule does not alter the important role that Head Start staff play in delivering quality education and comprehensive services to children and families. By reducing prescriptive Federal requirements, the rule provides grant recipients with greater discretion to make personnel and workforce decisions that reflect their organizational needs and local priorities. This final rule does not remove the requirements found in
2 CFR 200.430
Compensation—personal services, which states that wages paid to staff hired by Federal recipients will be considered reasonable to the extent that it is comparable to that paid for similar work in the labor market in which the recipient or subrecipient competes for the kind of employees involved. ACF also reminds grant recipients of the statutory requirement in Sec. 653 of the Act which states that the Secretary shall take such action as necessary to assure that people employed to carry out the Head Start program are not paid in excess of the average rate of compensation in the same area where the program is carried out to a substantial number of persons providing comparable services; nor are paid less than the minimum wage rate prescribed in section 6(a)(1) of the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938. Programs that operate in areas where there is significant competition for staff, from other early childhood or kindergarten programs, may establish pay scales and benefits packages that are competitive based on their local labor market. This final rule reflects trust in Head Start program leaders to run their programs, value staff, and make decisions on staff compensation given the local context and on their own timeline, meaning Head Start programs may choose to
(
printed page 73473)
implement wage and benefit increases in a more extended timeframe, or not at all.
Comment:
Many commenters discussed the economic pressures facing Head Start staff, including rising costs of living, increased financial hardship, strains on employee well-being, and the importance of competitive benefits to address these challenges.
Response:
ACF recognizes the economic challenges affecting the Head Start workforce, including rising costs of living, financial hardship, and the impact these challenges can have on employee well-being, recruitment, and retention. ACF also recognizes that offering competitive compensation and benefits can be an important strategy for supporting and sustaining a qualified workforce. At the same time, local labor markets, costs of living, and program resources vary considerably across communities, and grant recipients are best positioned to determine how to structure compensation and benefits within their available funding. Therefore, this final rule reduces Federal requirements thereby providing grant recipients with greater flexibility to respond to changing local economic and workforce conditions and to make staffing and resource allocation decisions that best meet the needs of their programs and communities. However, this flexibility does not relieve programs of their obligation to comply with applicable Federal, State, and local minimum wage laws. ACF further notes that, subject to available appropriations, programs have discretion in using annual cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) funding to support staff salaries.
ACF acknowledges that while Head Start staff face economic pressures, so too do families eligible for Head Start services. Implementing rigid Federal standards without increased appropriations would have limited the number of children and families that have access to Head Start services; this trade off was not one ACF is willing to make at a national level, using a one-size fits all approach. Instead, with the implementation of this final rule, local communities have the ability to weigh these factors to determine a path forward.
Comment:
Several commenters expressed concern that the proposed rule would result in reductions to current staff wages or otherwise require grant recipients to decrease employee compensation. Commenters stated that lowering wages would exacerbate existing workforce challenges and negatively affect recruitment, retention, and program quality.
Response:
This final rule does not require or encourage grant recipients to reduce wages or compensation of current Head Start employees. ACF knows it is important to maintain a qualified and stable Head Start workforce. Several commenters appear to have misunderstood the effect of these changes. This final rule does not require programs to reduce current wages; the rule removes certain Federal regulatory requirements and provides grant recipients with greater flexibility in making workforce and operational decisions consistent with applicable law and available resources. Compensation decisions remain the responsibility of individual grant recipients, and nothing in this final rule requires changes to current employee wages or benefits.
Comment:
A few commenters addressed the NPRM's statement that the proposed requirements “would likely exceed” the requirements of the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA). Commenters expressed concern that the statement reflects that teacher wages would be tied to minimum wage benchmarks. Other commenters requested clarification regarding the relationship between the proposed requirements and existing Federal labor laws.
Response:
The statement in the NPRM was intended to distinguish the proposed regulatory requirements from the baseline requirements established under the FLSA. This final rule does not modify, supersede, or affect the rights and obligations established under the FLSA or any other applicable Federal, State, Tribal, or local labor law. Grant recipients remain responsible for complying with all applicable employment and labor laws. By removing the regulatory requirements, this final rule eliminates Federal requirements that would have gone beyond existing statutory labor protections while leaving all underlying legal obligations unchanged.
Comment:
Several commenters stated that, over many years, Head Start has encouraged and, in some cases, required increased educational qualifications and professional credentials for its workforce, including bachelor's degrees, Child Development Associate (CDA) credentials, and other specialized training. These commenters expressed concern that compensation has not kept pace with these increasing expectations and argued that removing the compensation provisions would further widen the gap between the qualifications expected of Head Start staff and their compensation. Commenters encouraged OHS to maintain regulatory provisions that support compensation commensurate with the education, credentials, and expertise required of the Head Start workforce.
Response:
This final rule does not modify the qualification or credentialing requirements applicable to Head Start staff or diminish the importance of maintaining a qualified workforce. Rather, it removes Federal regulatory requirements related to compensation and benefits while providing grant recipients with greater flexibility to determine workforce policies that reflect local labor market conditions, organizational priorities, and available resources. Decisions regarding employee compensation remain the responsibility of individual grant recipients, consistent with applicable law and the Head Start Act.
Workforce Stability and Access
Comment:
A large number of commenters, including both congressional letters, described ongoing challenges related to recruiting and retaining qualified staff, workforce shortages, and employee turnover. Commenters expressed concern that these challenges affect program operations and the ability to keep classrooms open.
Response:
ACF recognizes that workforce recruitment and retention remain significant challenges across the early childhood sector. However, ACF does not believe this final rule will impede programs from addressing recruitment and retention issues as it gives programs flexibility to implement wages and benefits that meet the needs of their specific communities. Workforce conditions vary considerably across communities, and grant recipients are best positioned to assess local labor markets and develop strategies that respond to those conditions. This final rule reduces Federal regulatory requirements and provides programs with increased flexibility to address workforce challenges in ways that are appropriate for their individual circumstances. This final rule prevents the enactment of an unfunded mandate that would destabilize the sector and likely force many classrooms and programs to close. Through this final rule, ACF has weighed the tradeoffs, and has decided ensuring access to services for children and families is more important than enforcing a one-size fits all approach to national requirements on wages and compensation.
Comment:
Several commenters emphasized that stable relationships between children and caregivers are fundamental to healthy development
(
printed page 73474)
and expressed concern that workforce turnover disrupts continuity of care for children and families. Commenters stated that maintaining compensation requirements supports workforce stability and, in turn, promotes continuity of care and positive child outcomes.
Response:
This final rule does not alter the statutory mission of the Head Start program or programs' responsibility to provide high-quality services to enrolled children and families. ACF remains committed to the principles of continuity of care that are fundamental to early childhood education. Instead, the rule removes Federal requirements prescribing specific workforce practices and provides grant recipients with greater discretion to determine the strategies that best support workforce stability and program operations in their communities. ACF believes that prioritizing access to stable, high-quality early care and education services through Head Start that offer continuity of care is more critical than implementing a one-size fits all wage and compensation policy that would limit access to those services for children and families.
Comment:
Commenters emphasized the importance of maintaining access to comprehensive Head Start services for children and families and expressed support for the removal of regulatory requirements that could affect program capacity or enrollment.
Response:
We agree; by reducing Federal regulatory requirements, this final rule provides grant recipients with additional flexibility to manage available resources and make operational decisions that support continued delivery of services consistent with statutory requirements and community needs. By enacting this final rule, ACF is prioritizing access to comprehensive services for as many children and families as possible.
Comment:
Commenters expressed concern that removing the compensation provisions could have unintended long-term effects on the early childhood education workforce by affecting educators' access to degree pathways or student aid. Commenters expressed concern that these effects could reduce the future pipeline of qualified Head Start educators.
Response:
This final rule does not modify the education or qualification requirements applicable to Head Start staff, nor does it affect Federal student aid programs or the eligibility of institutions of higher education to participate in those programs. Rather, this rule removes Federal regulatory requirements related to compensation and benefits within the Performance Standards and provides grant recipients with greater flexibility to make workforce and operational decisions consistent with applicable law and available resources.
Comment:
Several commenters expressed concern that rescinding the compensation and benefits provisions could contribute to workforce instability, resulting in classroom closures, reduced program capacity, or the loss of Head Start services in some communities. Commenters stated that disruptions to Head Start availability could impact family integrity by reducing access to reliable early care and education, limiting parents' ability to work or attend school, and diminishing an important source of support for children and families. Both congressional letters included detailed statements on these themes, particularly the importance of access to services for Head Start children and families.
Response:
This final rule is intended to reduce Federal regulatory requirements and provide grant recipients with greater flexibility to make workforce and operational decisions based on local needs and available resources. ACF continues to recognize the importance of maintaining access to Head Start services and believes that allowing grant recipients greater discretion in allocating resources and managing their workforce best supports their ability to respond to local conditions while continuing to fulfill the Head Start mission consistent with applicable law. If programs need to make adjustments to their wages and compensation in order to ensure classrooms can continue to operate, they can work with their Regional Office to modify their budgets and make those changes under this final rule.
Funding and Program Investment
Comment:
Many commenters stated that the wage and benefit requirements included in the 2024 final rule constituted an unfunded mandate. Other commenters also stated that additional Federal funding is necessary to support workforce investments and expressed concern that regulatory requirements should not impose costs that exceed available resources.
Response:
It is the role of Congress to make decisions regarding Federal appropriations for Head Start. In developing this final rule, ACF has sought to reduce Federal regulatory requirements and associated compliance obligations, providing grant recipients with greater flexibility to determine how best to allocate available resources in support of their programs and workforce. Further, ACF agrees with the important goal of removing unrealistic, unfunded mandates through this final rule.
Comment:
Several commenters expressed concern about uncertainty regarding the future sustainability of Head Start programs and the operational challenges programs face in a changing fiscal and workforce environment.
Response:
This final rule reduces Federal regulatory requirements that currently limit local decision-making and therefore this action provides programs with greater discretion to adapt to evolving circumstances while continuing to carry out the Head Start mission consistent with applicable law.
Comment:
Some commenters framed their feedback in terms of broader values, emphasizing the importance of investing in children, families, and the early childhood workforce. Other commenters expressed views regarding the policy rationale underlying the proposed requirements.
Response:
We appreciate the thoughtful perspectives shared by commenters regarding the mission of the Head Start program and the importance of supporting children, families, and the workforce. In developing this final rule, ACF carefully considered these perspectives while focusing on its objectives of maximizing access to Head Start services for eligible children and families, reducing unnecessary Federal regulation and providing grant recipients with greater flexibility to administer their programs consistent with statutory requirements.
Flexibility and Reduced Burden
Comment:
Many commenters supported increased flexibility for grant recipients, reduced administrative burden, and greater local decision-making. Commenters stated that local programs are best positioned to determine how to meet the needs of their communities.
Response:
We agree that grant recipients benefit from flexibility to respond to local circumstances. One of the primary objectives of this final rule is to reduce unnecessary Federal requirements and administrative burden while preserving the statutory framework of the Head Start program. We believe that providing greater local discretion allows grant recipients to make decisions that best reflect community needs and organizational priorities.
Comment:
Several commenters questioned the assertion that the proposed rule would increase program flexibility. These commenters stated
(
printed page 73475)
that, absent additional Federal funding, programs would continue to face significant constraints in addressing workforce challenges while maintaining access to comprehensive services for children and families. Commenters expressed concern that limited resources restrict the practical ability of grant recipients to make meaningful operational changes, regardless of regulatory flexibility.
Response:
ACF recognizes the workforce challenges many Head Start grant recipients continue to face. This final rule reduces Federal regulatory requirements that currently limit local decision-making and therefore this action provides grant recipients with greater discretion to determine how best to allocate available resources based on their unique circumstances, workforce needs, and community priorities. ACF recognizes that regulatory flexibility does not itself increase available funding; however, reducing prescriptive Federal requirements affords programs greater latitude to make operational and resource decisions consistent with statutory requirements and the needs of the communities they serve. ACF encourages recipients to work with their Regional Offices to work within their budgets to make decisions on wages and benefits that are best for their community.
Policy Pathways
Comment:
Both commenters in support of the rule and those opposed spoke about the ability to implement the proposed regulatory action in accordance with the Act. Commenters supportive of the proposed rule described ways the Act is conducive to such regulatory action. Commenters that wrote in objection to the proposed rule stated that this regulatory action was not in accordance with the Act.
Response:
After considering the comments received, ACF has determined that this final rule appropriately removes the regulatory provisions related to compensation and benefits and restores greater flexibility for grant recipients to make workforce decisions consistent with the Act.
Comment:
Many commenters recommended alternatives to rescinding the compensation and benefits provisions. Rather than removing the requirements, commenters suggested revising them to provide greater flexibility while preserving Federal expectations related to workforce compensation and benefits. Specific recommendations included revising the requirements to be less prescriptive, delaying implementation, phasing in the requirements over time, conditioning implementation on future appropriations, developing regional or locally adjusted compensation models, establishing wage floors or clearer compensation benchmarks, and providing additional technical assistance to support implementation.
Response:
Many of these recommendations reflect a shared interest in supporting the Head Start workforce while providing programs with sufficient flexibility to respond to local circumstances. After considering these comments, and given the resources currently allocated to Head Start, ACF has determined that removing the compensation and benefits requirements is the most appropriate approach to achieving the objectives of this rulemaking. While commenters proposed various modifications that would retain or revise the existing regulatory framework, these approaches would continue to impose Federal regulatory requirements in areas where ACF has concluded that grant recipients are better positioned to make decisions based on local workforce conditions, organizational priorities, and available resources.
ACF does not agree with the idea that this is an area that should be regulated at the Federal level. Even with some of the caveats proposed by commenters, establishing a Federal requirement does not allow local programs to make the choices that are best for their settings. Any Federal requirement would inherently limit access to children and families in areas that may not need to be limited if each program makes their own decisions with the flexibility this final rule allows. This final rule does not prohibit or discourage grant recipients from developing or maintaining wage structures that support their organizational goals. Rather, it removes the Federal regulatory requirement to do so, allowing grant recipients to determine whether and how to structure compensation policies based on their local workforce needs, organizational priorities, and available resources.

VI. Regulatory Impact Analysis
Need for Regulatory Action
The Performance Standards, established and updated as needed through regulation, are the foundation on which Head Start programs design and deliver high-quality, comprehensive services to children and families. The Performance Standards set forth the requirements that local grant recipients must meet to support the cognitive, social, emotional, and healthy development of children enrolled in the program. In August 2024, ACF published in the
Federal Register
a final rule that revised and updated the Performance Standards.
Most notably, OHS added a series of new requirements in the 2024 final rule related to staff wages and benefits in an attempt to support and stabilize the Head Start workforce. However, these requirements were too prescriptive for all communities that Head Start programs serve according to feedback received from stakeholders, both through the public comment process and through other ongoing stakeholder engagement. Therefore, this final rule removes these wage and benefit requirements from the Performance Standards. These changes restore more local flexibility to grant recipients and provide them the ability to determine the compensation packages that best meet the unique needs of their workforce. Furthermore, without additional appropriations from Congress, approximately 106,000 funded Head Start slots would have needed to be cut in order for programs to meet these requirements by the specified deadline.
Establishing one-size-fits-all wage and benefit requirements at the expense of reducing access to high-quality program services may not be most beneficial, especially at a time when access to child care is already lacking.
[
8
]
Furthermore, both under enrollment and classroom teacher turnover across Head Start programs have decreased nationally since the 2024 final rule. More specifically, under enrollment was approximately 8 percent nationally in 2025, as compared to 13 percent nationally, as discussed in the 2024 final rule. Similarly, classroom teacher turnover decreased from 19 percent as of the 2024 final rule to 17 percent by 2025.
Comment and Response
In this section, we summarize and respond to comments we received on the Regulatory Impact Analysis (RIA) in the NPRM.
Comment:
Several commenters questioned the estimate in the RIA of the proposed rule that approximately 106,000 slots would be retained by rescinding the staff wage and benefit requirements. Commenters stated that recent enrollment reductions and classroom closures have been driven primarily by workforce shortages, and they argued that removing the wage and benefit requirements would not improve programs' ability to recruit and retain staff or result in additional children being served.
Response:
We recognize the workforce challenges many Head Start programs continue to experience. The estimate of approximately 106,000 preserved slots reflects the potential effects on future funded enrollment capacity associated with avoiding projected compliance costs under the 2024 final rule. It is not intended to predict actual future enrollment or classroom operations, which depend on a variety of factors, including workforce availability, local labor market conditions, and funding levels.
Comment:
Several commenters stated that the estimate in the RIA of the proposed rule of approximately $2.1 billion in future cost savings is misleading because it does not represent actual Federal expenditures or additional funding available to programs. Commenters asserted that the estimate reflects avoided future compensation costs rather than realized fiscal savings and therefore does not provide programs with additional resources to increase wages, expand services, or address rising operating costs.
Response:
To clarify, the RIA estimates that removing the wage and benefit requirements will yield approximately $2.1 billion in future annual cost savings for programs. This impact is not characterized as reductions in appropriated funding for Head Start or as reductions to overall program funding levels. Instead, this impact represents an eventual annual transfer of $2.1 billion, encompassing effects among Head Start staff (transfers to those who would avoid losing hours or losing employment entirely, from those who would have received higher remuneration per hour in accordance with the 2024 rule) and among Head Start children and families (including transfers to children and families for whom slot unavailability would have been a consequence of the 2024 rule). This approach aligns with Circular A-4 (2003), OMB's guidance to Federal agencies on the development of regulatory analysis and is generally consistent with the findings and the modeling approach of the RIA of the 2024 final rule. Although this final rule removes regulatory requirements, grant recipients retain the flexibility to determine compensation packages consistent with applicable law, available funding, and local circumstances.
Comment:
A few commenters requested that ACF clarify whether the estimated 106,000 slots that would be preserved as a result of this final rule refers to funded enrollment slots or actual children served.
Response:
To clarify, in the absence of an increase in appropriations from Congress, ACF estimates that approximately 106,000 funded Head Start slots would have needed to be cut in order for programs to meet the wage and benefit requirements by the specified deadline in the 2024 final rule.

published in August 2024 included requirements for Head Start programs to provide competitive wages and benefits for staff to address staff recruitment and retention challenges. Without additional regulatory action, programs would have been required to comply with these requirements by August 2028 (for benefits) and August 2031 (for wages). (
printed page 73478)
anticipated expenditures needed to implement the wage and benefit requirements for Head Start staff; or, alternatively, averting the loss of services to children under the requirements of the 2024 final rule. The 2024 final rule RIA estimated that the wage requirements would cost approximately $1.2 billion in nominal dollars when fully implemented in 2031. The RIA estimated that the staff benefit requirements would cost approximately $877 million in nominal dollars in 2031. ACF combines these figures to estimate the total transfers associated with removing these wage and benefit requirements—resulting in a transfer of approximately $2.1 billion in future expenditures.
In order to estimate the number of Head Start slots that are saved by removing these staff wage and benefit requirements, ACF determined the proportion of FY 2024 funded enrollment that are Head Start Preschool slots (73.7 percent), and Early Head Start slots (26.3 percent), respectively. Next, ACF applied this proportion to the total monetary cost associated with this rule in FY 2024 dollars ($1.7 billion) and divided the cost that would be borne by the average cost per slot for Head Start Preschool in FY 2024 ($15,187) and the cost that will be borne in Early Head Start by the average cost per slot for Early Head Start in FY 2024 ($20,460). ACF uses cost per child because it is the best indicator for the number of slots programs will be able to retain following the removal of the staff wages and benefits requirements from the Performance Standards in this final rule.
These calculations result in $1.3 billion in transfers attributed to Head Start Preschool slots and $452 million in transfers attributed to Early Head Start slots (in FY 2024 dollars). When divided by average cost per slot, this results in approximately 84,000 Head Start Preschool slots and 22,000 Early Head Start slots saved. Collectively, the net transfers associated with this final rule reflect a retention of approximately 106,000 Head Start slots (number of children served) nationally. In other words, by removing the wage and benefit requirements from the Performance Standards, and in the absence of appropriation increases for Head Start, programs could save as many as 106,000 slots that would otherwise have been cut in order to implement these wage and benefit requirements in the future. However, ACF also acknowledges that programs may choose to reduce slots, subject to ACF approval, in order to increase staff compensation, which is no longer required, but could result in lower cost savings and fewer slots saved than estimated in this RIA.

Non-Quantified Impacts of Certain Elements of the Final Rule
In addition to the transfers quantified in this RIA, removing the staff wage and benefit requirements from the Performance Standards restores local flexibility for individual programs to design services that are responsive to the individual needs of the communities in which they operate. Many programs continue to face staffing shortages that impact their ability to serve as many children as possible;
[
10
]
however, the changes in this final rule provide programs more discretion to determine how to best address staff recruitment and retention challenges based on their local contexts. The rescission of the wage and benefit requirements restores needed flexibility and autonomy to local programs so they may determine the best path forward for their program. By removing several costly requirements related to staff wages and benefits, these changes will alleviate unnecessary regulatory burden placed on Head Start programs.
Alternatives to the Final Rule
ACF considered and assessed several policy alternatives to this final rule. In the analysis below, we model a full rescission of the 2024 final rule, which included the following policies with quantified economic impacts: staff wages, staff benefits, staff breaks, family service worker family assignments, mental health supports, and preventing and addressing lead exposure, as well as associated administrative costs. All other policies beyond these from the 2024 final rule were not associated with quantified effects. Our modeling approach of separately estimating and reporting the costs associated with each of these policies enabled ACF to assess additional policy alternatives, such as rescinding subsets of policies included with the 2024 final rule.
As noted in our main analysis, in this final rule, ACF is rescinding a particular subset of those policies, rather than a full rescission.
[
11
]
Table 3 and Table 4 summarize the total expenditures needed to implement the 2024 final rule that would represent reductions in expenditures if the 2024 final rule were rescinded, reporting yearly estimates, and present value and annualized values corresponding to a 3% and 7% discount rate (updated from a 2% discount rate applied in the 2024 final rule RIA) for each of the policies. Collectively, the net reduction in expenditures associated with a full rescission of the 2024 final rule reflects a retention of approximately 96,000 Head Start Preschool slots and 25,000 Early Head Start slots nationally. In other words, by rescinding all policies from the 2024 final rule that had economic impacts, Head Start programs would retain approximately 121,000 slots that would otherwise have been cut in order to implement these policies. This represents an additional 15,000 slots that would be saved beyond the 106,000 retained by rescinding the staff wage and benefit policies. International Trade Administration
[A-533-871]
AGENCY:
Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, Department of Commerce.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) preliminarily determines that producers and/or exporters subject to this administrative review made sales of subject merchandise at less than normal value (NV) during the period of review (POR), August 1, 2024, through July 31, 2025. In addition, we are rescinding the review with respect to 27 companies. Interested parties are invited to comment on these preliminary results.
DATES:
Applicable November 16, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Preston Cox, AD/CVD Operations, Office VI, Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1401 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20230; telephone: (240) 956-8630.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
On August 24, 2017, Commerce published in the
Federal Register
the antidumping duty order on finished carbon steel flanges (steel flanges) from India.
[
1
]
On August 1, 2025, Commerce published a notice of opportunity to request an administrative review of the
Order.
[
2
]
On September 25, 2025, based on timely requests for review, in accordance with
19 CFR 351.221(c)(1)(i)
, we initiated an administrative review of the antidumping duty order on steel flanges from India.
[
3
]
On November 26, 2025, Commerce selected Norma Group
[
4
]
and R. N. Gupta & Co., Ltd. (RNG) as mandatory respondents in this administrative review.
[
5
]
Due to the lapse in appropriations and Federal Government shutdown on November 14, 2025, Commerce tolled all deadlines in administrative proceedings by 47 days.
[
6
]
Additionally, due to a backlog of documents that were electronically filed via Enforcement and Compliance's Antidumping and Countervailing Duty Centralized Electronic Service System (ACCESS) during the Federal Government shutdown, on November 24, 2025, Commerce tolled all deadlines in administrative proceedings by an additional 21 days.
[
7
]
Between June 9 and October 27, 2026, Commerce extended the deadline for the preliminary results of this review by 120 days.
[
8
]
Accordingly, the deadline for Commerce to issue these preliminary results is November 9, 2026.
For a complete description of the events that followed the initiation of this review,
see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.
[
9
]
A list of topics included in the Preliminary Decision Memorandum is included as Appendix I to this notice. The Preliminary Decision Memorandum is a public document and is on file electronically via ACCESS, which is available to registered users at
https://access.trade.gov
.
In addition, a complete version of the Preliminary Decision Memorandum can be accessed directly at
https://access.trade.gov/​frnotices
.
Scope of the Order
The merchandise covered by the
Order
is steel flanges. For a complete description of the scope of the
Order, see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.
Rescission of Administrative Review, in Part
Pursuant to
19 CFR 351.213(d)(3)
, it is Commerce's practice to rescind an administrative review of an antidumping duty order where it concludes that there were no suspended entries of subject merchandise during the POR.
[
10
]
Normally, upon completion of an administrative review, the suspended entries are liquidated at the antidumping duty assessment rate for the review period.
[
11
]
Therefore, for an administrative review to be conducted, there must be a reviewable, suspended entry that Commerce can instruct U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to liquidate at the antidumping duty assessment rate calculated for the POR.
[
12
]
(
printed page 73547)
Commerce notified all interested parties of its intent to rescind the instant review regarding the companies listed in Appendix III because there were no reviewable, suspended entries of subject merchandise from these companies during the POR and invited interested parties to comment.
[
13
]
No party commented on this memorandum. In the absence of any suspended entries of subject merchandise from these companies during the POR, we are rescinding this administrative review for the companies listed in Appendix III, in accordance with
19 CFR 351.213(d)(3)
.
Methodology
Commerce is conducting this review in accordance with sections 751(a)(1)(B) and (2) of the Act. Export price is calculated in accordance with section 772 of the Act. NV is calculated in accordance with section 773 of the Act. For a full description of the methodology underlying these preliminary results,
see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.
Rate for Non-Selected Companies
The Act does not address the establishment of a rate to be applied to companies not selected for individual examination when Commerce limits its examination in an administrative review pursuant to section 777A(c)(2) of the Act. However, Commerce's regulation at
19 CFR 351.109(g)
states that Commerce will determine the rate for non-selected companies by following the process set forth in
19 CFR 351.109(f)(1)-(2)
, which generally parallels the process for calculating the all-others rate in a market economy investigation under section 735(c)(5) of the Act. Under section 735(c)(5)(A) of the Act and
19 CFR 351.109(f)(1)(i)
, the all-others rate is normally “an amount equal to the weighted average of the estimated weighted average dumping margins established for exporters and producers individually investigated, excluding any zero or
de minimis
margins, and any margins determined entirely {on the basis of facts available}.”
In this review, we preliminarily calculated a weighted-average dumping margin of 7.15 percent for RNG, which is the only non-
de minimis
dumping margin calculated for this POR. Consistent with the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit's decision in
Albemarle,
[
14
]
and our practice, we have preliminarily assigned to the non-examined companies a dumping margin of 7.15 percent in accordance with section 735(c)(5)(B) of the Act.
[
15
]

Disclosure
Commerce intends to disclose to interested parties the calculations performed in connection with these preliminary results within five days of any public announcement or, if there is no public announcement, within five days of the date of publication of this notice in accordance with
19 CFR 351.224(b)
.
Verification
As provided in section 782(i)(3) of the Act, Commerce intends to verify the information relied upon in making its final results.
Public Comment
Case briefs or other written comments may be submitted to the Assistant Secretary for Enforcement and Compliance no later than seven days after the date on which the last verification report is issued in this review. Rebuttal briefs, limited to issues raised in the case briefs, may be filed not later than five days after the date for filing case briefs.
[
17
]
Interested parties who submit case briefs or rebuttal briefs in this proceeding must submit: (1) a table of contents listing each issue; and (2) a table of authorities.
[
18
]
All briefs must be filed electronically using ACCESS. An electronically filed document must be received successfully in its entirety in ACCESS by 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time on the established deadline.
As provided under
19 CFR 351.309(c)(2)(iii)
and
(d)(2)(iii)
, we request that interested parties provide at the beginning of their briefs a public executive summary for each issue raised in their briefs.
[
19
]
Further, we request that interested parties limit their public executive summary of each issue to no more than 450 words, not including citations. We intend to use the public executive summaries as the basis of the comment summaries included in the issues and decision memorandum that will accompany the final results in this administrative review. We request that interested parties include footnotes for relevant citations in the public executive summary of each issue. Note that Commerce has amended certain of its requirements pertaining to the service of documents in
19 CFR 351.303(f)
.
[
20
]
Pursuant to
19 CFR 351.310(c)
, interested parties who wish to request a hearing must submit a written request to the Assistant Secretary for Enforcement and Compliance, filed electronically via ACCESS by 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time within 30 days after the date of publication of this notice. Requests should contain: (1) the party's name,
(
printed page 73548)
address, and telephone number; (2) the number of participants and whether any participant is a foreign national; and (3) a list of issues to be discussed. Oral presentations at the hearing will be limited to issues raised in the briefs. If a request for a hearing is made, Commerce will inform parties of the scheduled date for the hearing.
[
21
]
Assessment Rates
Upon completion of this administrative review, Commerce shall determine, and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) shall assess, antidumping duties on all appropriate entries. If the weighted-average dumping margin for a mandatory respondent is not zero or
de minimis
in the final results of this review, we will calculate an importer-specific assessment rate on the basis of the ratio of the total amount of dumping calculated for each importer's examined sales and the total entered value of such sales in accordance with
19 CFR 351.212(b)(1)
.
[
22
]
If the weighted-average dumping margin is zero or
de minimis
in the final results of review, or if an importer-specific assessment rate is zero or
de minimis,
Commerce will instruct CBP to liquidate appropriate entries without regard to antidumping duties.
[
23
]
For entries of subject merchandise during the period of review produced by the respondents for which they did not know its merchandise was destined for the United States, we will instruct CBP to liquidate unreviewed entries pursuant to the reseller policy,
i.e.,
the assessment rate for such entries will be the all-others rate established in the investigation if there is no rate for the intermediate company(ies) involved in the transaction.
[
24
]
For the companies which were not selected for individual examination, we intend to assign an antidumping duty assessment rate equal to the weighted-average dumping margin determined for the non-examined companies in the final results of review.
For the companies for which the administrative review is rescinded, antidumping duties shall be assessed at a rate equal to the cash deposit of estimated antidumping duties required at the time of entry, or withdrawal from warehouse, for consumption, in accordance with
19 CFR 351.212(c)(1)(i)
. Commerce intends to issue assessment instructions to CBP no earlier than 35 days after the date of publication of the final results of this review in the
Federal Register
.
Commerce intends to issue assessment instructions to CBP no earlier than 35 days after the date of publication of the final results of this review in the
Federal Register
. If a timely summons is filed at the U.S. Court of International Trade, the assessment instructions will direct CBP not to liquidate relevant entries until the time for parties to file a request for a statutory injunction has expired (
i.e.,
within 90 days of publication). The final results of this review shall be the basis for the assessment of antidumping duties on entries of merchandise covered by the final results of this review and for future cash deposits of estimated antidumping duties, where applicable.
[
25
]
Cash Deposit Requirements
The following cash deposit requirements will be effective upon publication in the
Federal Register
of the final results of this administrative review for all shipments of the subject merchandise entered, or withdrawn from warehouse, for consumption on or after the date of publication, as provided by section 751(a)(2)(C) of the Act: (1) the cash deposit rate for companies subject to this review will be equal to the company-specific weighted-average dumping margin established in the final results of this administrative review; (2) for merchandise exported by a company not covered in this review but covered in a prior segment of the proceeding, the cash deposit rate will continue to be the company-specific rate published in the completed segment for the most recent period; (3) if the exporter is not a firm covered in this review, a prior review, or the less-than-fair-value investigation, but the producer is, then the cash deposit rate will be the rate established in the most recently completed segment of the proceeding for the producer of the merchandise; and (4) the cash deposit rate for all other producers or exporters will continue to be 8.91 percent, the all-others rate established in the less-than-fair-value investigation.
[
26
]
These cash deposit requirements, when imposed, shall remain in effect until further notice.
Notification to Importers
This notice also serves as a preliminary reminder to importers of their responsibility under
19 CFR 351.402(f)(2)
to file a certificate regarding the reimbursement of antidumping and/or countervailing duties prior to liquidation of the relevant entries during this review period. Failure to comply with this requirement could result in Commerce's presumption that reimbursement of antidumping and/or countervailing duties occurred and the subsequent assessment of double antidumping duties, and/or an increase in the amount of antidumping duties by the amount of countervailing duties.
Notification to Interested Parties
These preliminary results of review are issued and published in accordance with sections 751(a)(1) and 777(i)(1) of the Act, and
19 CFR 351.221(b)(4)
.
Dated: November 9, 2026.
Kasey O'Connor,
Deputy General Counsel, performing the non-exclusive functions and duties of the Assistant Secretary for Enforcement and Compliance.

SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) determines that Deacero S.A.P.I. de C.V., I.N.G.E.T.E.K.N.O.S. Estructurales, S.A. de C.V., and Aceros Turia S.A. de C.V. Based on our review of the record and comments received from interested parties regarding the

Disclosure
Commerce intends to disclose its calculations and analysis performed to interested parties for these preliminary results within five days of any public announcement or, if there is no public announcement, within five days of the date of publication of this notice in accordance with
19 CFR 351.224(b)
.
Assessment Rate
Pursuant to section 751(a)(2)(A) of the Act, and
19 CFR 351.212(b)(1)
, Commerce shall determine, and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) shall assess, antidumping duties on all appropriate entries covered by this review. Pursuant to
19 CFR 351.212(b)(1)
, where the respondent reported the entered value of its U.S. sales, we calculated importer-specific AD assessment rates by aggregating the total amount of dumping calculated for the examined sales of each importer and dividing each of these amounts by the total entered value associated with those sales. Where the respondent did not report entered value, we calculated a per-unit assessment rate for each importer by dividing the total amount of dumping calculated for the examined sales made to that importer by the total quantity associated with those sales. To determine whether an importer-specific, per-unit assessment rate is
de minimis,
in accordance with
19 CFR 351.106(c)(2)
, we also calculated an importer-specific
ad valorem
ratio based on estimated entered values. Where either the respondent's weighted-average dumping margin is zero or
de minimis
within the meaning of
19 CFR 351.106(c)(1)
, or an importer-specific assessment rate is zero or
de minimis,
we will instruct CBP to liquidate the appropriate entries without regard to antidumping duties.
Commerce's “automatic assessment” will apply to entries of subject merchandise during the POR produced by the mandatory respondents for which the companies did not know that the merchandise they sold to an intermediary (
e.g.,
a reseller, trading company, or exporter) was destined for the United States. In such instances, we will instruct CBP to liquidate
(
printed page 73526)
unreviewed entries at the all-others rate established in the original less-than-fair value (LTFV) investigation,
i.e.,
20.58 percent,
[
8
]
if there is no rate for the intermediate company(ies) involved in the transaction.
Commerce intends to issue assessment instructions to CBP no earlier than 41 days after the date of publication of the final results of this review in the
Federal Register
in accordance with
19 CFR 356.8(a)
.
Cash Deposit Requirements
The following cash deposit requirements will be effective for all shipments of the subject merchandise entered, or withdrawn from warehouse, for consumption on or after the publication date of the final results of this administrative review, as provided by section 751(a)(2)(C) of the Act: (1) the cash deposit rates for the companies identified above in the “Final Results of Review” section will be equal to the company-specific weighted-average dumping margin established in the final results of this administrative review; (2) for merchandise exported by a company not covered in this administrative review but covered in a completed prior segment of the proceeding, the cash deposit rate will continue to be the company-specific rate published for the most recently completed segment of this proceeding; (3) if the exporter is not a firm covered in this review or completed prior segment of this proceeding but the producer is, the cash deposit rate will be the company-specific rate established for the most recently-completed segment of this proceeding for the producer of the subject merchandise; and (4) the cash deposit rate for all other producers or exporters will continue to be 20.58 percent, the rate established in the LTFV investigation.
[
9
]
These cash deposit requirements, when imposed, shall remain in effect until further notice.
Notification to Importers
This notice serves as a final reminder to importers of their responsibility under
19 CFR 351.402(f)(2)
to file a certificate regarding the reimbursement of antidumping duties prior to liquidation of the relevant entries during this POR. Failure to comply with this requirement could result in Commerce's presumption that reimbursement of antidumping duties has occurred and the subsequent assessment of double antidumping duties.
Administrative Protective Order (APO)
This notice also serves as a final reminder to parties subject to an APO of their responsibility concerning the return or destruction of proprietary information disclosed under APO in accordance with
19 CFR 351.305(a)(3)
, which continues to govern business proprietary information in this segment of the proceeding. Timely written notification of the return or destruction of APO materials, or conversion to judicial protective order, is hereby requested. Failure to comply with the regulations and the terms of an APO is a sanctionable violation.
Notification to Interested Parties
We are issuing and publishing this notice in accordance with sections 751(a)(1) and 777(i)(1) of the Act, and
19 CFR 351.221(b)(5)
and
19 CFR 351.213(h)
.

AGENCY:

SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) is postponing the deadline for issuing the final determination in the less-than-fair-value (LTFV) investigation of Oil Country Tubular Goods (OCTG) from the United Arab Emirates (UAE) until March 15, 2027.
DATES:
Applicable November 16, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Alexander Rodriguez, AD/CVD Operations, Office IV, Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1401 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20230; telephone: (202) 482-0190.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
On April 22, 2026, Commerce initiated a LTFV investigation of imports of OCTG from the UAE.
[
1
]
The period of investigation (POI) is April 1, 2025, through March 31, 2026. On November 4, 2026, Commerce published its
Preliminary Determination
in this LTFV investigation of OCTG from the UAE.
[
2
]
Postponement of Final Determination
Section 735(a)(2) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act), and
19 CFR 351.210(b)(2)
provide that a final determination may be postponed until not later than 135 days after the date of the publication of the preliminary determination if, in the event of an affirmative preliminary determination, a request for such postponement is made by the exporters or producers who account for a significant proportion of exports of the subject merchandise, or in the event of a negative preliminary determination, a request for such postponement is made by the petitioners. Further,
19 CFR 351.210(e)(2)
requires that such postponement requests by exporters be accompanied by a request for extension of provisional measures from a four-month period to a period of not more than six months, in accordance with section 733(d) of the Act.
On November 4, 2026, Ajmal Steel Tubes and Pipes Industries, LLC., a mandatory respondent in this investigation, requested that Commerce postpone the deadline for the final determination until no later than 135 days from the publication of the
Preliminary Determination,
and extend the application of the provisional measures from a four-month period to a period of not more than six months.
[
3
]
In accordance with section 735(a)(2)(A) of the Act and
19 CFR 351.210(b)(2)(ii)
, because: (1) the
Preliminary Determination
was affirmative; (2) the request was made by the exporters and producers who account for a significant proportion of exports of the subject merchandise; and (3) no compelling reasons for denial exist, Commerce is postponing the final determination until no later than 135 days after the date of the publication of the
Preliminary Determination,
and extending the provisional measures from a four-month period to a period of not more than six months. Accordingly, Commerce will issue its final determination no later than March 15, 2027.
[
4
]
This notice is issued and published pursuant to
19 CFR 351.210(g)
.
Dated: November 10, 2026.
Kasey O'Connor,
Deputy General Counsel, performing the non-exclusive functions and duties of the Assistant Secretary for Enforcement and Compliance.

SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) determines that certain producers and exporters of sodium nitrite from India received countervailable subsidies during the period of review (POR) January 1, 2024, through December 31, 2024. In addition, Commerce is rescinding this review, in part, with respect to three companies.

Analysis of Comments Received
All issues raised by the interested parties in their case and rebuttal briefs are addressed in the Issues and Decision Memorandum. The topics discussed and the issues raised by parties to which we responded in the Issues and Decision Memorandum are listed in an appendix to this notice.
Methodology
Commerce is conducting this administrative review in accordance with section 751(a)(1)(A) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act). For each of the subsidy programs found countervailable, Commerce preliminarily determines that there is a subsidy,
i.e.,
a financial contribution by an “authority” that gives rise to a benefit to the recipient, and that the subsidy is specific.
[
10
]
For a full description of the methodology underlying our conclusions, including our reliance, in part, on facts otherwise available with adverse inferences pursuant to sections 776(a) and (b) of the Act,
see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.
Non-Selected Company Rate
The Act and Commerce's regulations do not address the establishment of a rate to apply to companies not selected for individual examination when Commerce limits its examination in an administrative review pursuant to section 777A(e)(2) of the Act. Generally, Commerce looks to section 705(c)(5) of the Act, which provides instructions for calculating the all-others rate in a CVD investigation. Section 777A(e)(2) of the Act provides that “the individual countervailable subsidy rates determined under subparagraph (A) shall be used to determine the all-others rate under section 705(c)(5) {of the Act}.” Under section 705(c)(5)(A)(i) of the Act, the all-others rate is normally an amount equal to the weighted average countervailable subsidy rates established for each of the companies individually investigated, excluding any rates that are zero,
de minimis
(
i.e.,
less than 0.5 percent), or determined entirely on the basis of facts available. Where the countervailable subsidy rates for each of the individually examined companies is zero,
de minimis,
or based entirely on facts available, section 705(c)(5)(A)(ii) of the Act provides that Commerce may use “any reasonable method to establish an all-others rate for exporters and producers not individually investigated, including averaging the weighted average countervailable subsidy rates determined for the exporters and producers individually investigated.”
For these final results, because the rate calculated for Kutch Chemical is based entirely on facts available, we are assigning to the company under review (
i.e.,
Kronox Lab Sciences Pvt Ltd.) that was not selected for individual examination a countervailable subsidy rate based on the rate calculated for DNL.

Assessment

19 CFR 351.212(b)(2)
, Commerce shall determine, and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) shall assess, countervailing duties on all appropriate entries covered by this review. Federal Register
. If a timely summons is filed at the U.S. Court of International Trade, the assessment instructions will direct CBP not to liquidate relevant entries until the time for parties to file a request for a statutory injunction has expired (
i.e.,
within 90 days of publication).
Cash Deposit Requirements
In accordance with section 751(a)(2)(C) of the Act, we also intend to instruct CBP to collect cash deposits of estimated countervailing duties in the amount shown for the companies listed above for shipments of subject merchandise entered, or withdrawn from warehouse, for consumption on or after the date of publication of the final results of this administrative review. For all non-reviewed firms, we will instruct CBP to continue to collect cash deposits of estimated countervailing duties at the all-others rate or the most recent company-specific rate applicable to the company, as appropriate. These cash deposit requirements, when imposed, shall remain in effect until further notice.
Administrative Protective Order
This notice also serves as a final reminder to parties subject to an administrative protective order (APO) of their responsibility concerning the disposition of proprietary information disclosed under APO in accordance with
19 CFR 351.305(a)(3)
. Timely
(
printed page 73564)
written notification of the return or destruction of APO materials or conversion to judicial protective order, is hereby requested. Failure to comply with the regulations and terms of an APO is a violation subject to sanction.

19 CFR 351.221(b)(5)

Background
On September 25, 2025, based on timely requests for review, in accordance with
19 CFR 351.221(c)(1)(i)
, we initiated an administrative review of the antidumping duty order on utility scale wind towers (wind towers) from Indonesia.
[
1
]
On December 12, 2025, Commerce identified PT. Kenertec Power System (Kenertec) as the mandatory respondent in this review.
[
2
]
Due to the lapse in appropriations and Federal Government shutdown, on November 14, 2025, Commerce tolled all deadlines in administrative proceedings by 47 days.
[
3
]
Additionally, due to a backlog of documents that were electronically filed via Enforcement and Compliance's Antidumping and Countervailing Duty Centralized Electronic Service System (ACCESS) during the Federal Government shutdown, on November 24, 2025, Commerce tolled all deadlines in administrative proceedings by an additional 21 days.
[
4
]
On June 23, 2026, we extended the preliminary results of this review to November 2, 2026.
[
5
]
On October 26, 2026 we fully extended the preliminary results of this review to no later than November 9, 2026.
[
6
]
For a complete description of the events that followed the initiation of this review,
see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.
[
7
]
A list of the topics discussed in the Preliminary Decision Memorandum is attached as Appendix I to this notice. The Preliminary Decision Memorandum is a public document and is on file electronically via ACCESS, which is available to registered users at
https://access.trade.gov
.
In addition, a complete version of the Preliminary Decision Memorandum can be accessed directly at
https://access.trade.gov/​frnotices
.
Scope of the Order
The merchandise subject to the
Order
are wind towers from Indonesia. For a complete description of the scope of the
Order, see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.
Rescission of Administrative Review, in Part
Pursuant to
19 CFR 351.213(d)(3)
, it is Commerce's practice to rescind an administrative review of an antidumping duty order where it concludes that there were no suspended entries of subject merchandise during the POR.
[
8
]
Normally, upon completion of an administrative review, the suspended entries are liquidated at the antidumping duty assessment rate for the review period.
[
9
]
Therefore, for an administrative review to be conducted, there must be a reviewable, suspended entry that Commerce can instruct U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to liquidate at the AD assessment rate calculated for the POR.
[
10
]
Commerce notified all interested parties of its intent to rescind the instant review regarding the companies listed in Appendix II because there were no reviewable, suspended entries of subject merchandise from these companies during the POR and invited interested parties to comment.
[
11
]
No party commented on this memorandum. In the absence of any suspended entries of subject merchandise from these companies during the POR, we are rescinding this administrative review for the companies listed in Appendix II, in accordance with
19 CFR 351.213(d)(3)
.
Methodology
Commerce is conducting this review in accordance with section 751(a) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act). Constructed export price is calculated in accordance with section 772 of the Act. NV is calculated in accordance with section 773 of the Act. For a full description of the methodology underlying our conclusions,

Case briefs or other written comments may be submitted to the Assistant Secretary for Enforcement and Compliance. Pursuant to

(

All briefs must be filed electronically using ACCESS. An electronically filed document must be received successfully in its entirety in ACCESS by 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time on the established deadline.
As provided under

and
(d)(2)(iii)

Note that Commerce has amended certain of its requirements pertaining to the service of documents in
19 CFR 351.303(f)
.
[
16
]
Pursuant to
19 CFR 351.310(c)
, interested parties who wish to request a hearing must submit a written request to the Assistant Secretary for Enforcement and Compliance, filed electronically via ACCESS by 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time within 30 days after the date of publication of this notice. Assessment Rates
Pursuant to section 751(a)(2)(A) of the Act and
19 CFR 351.212(b)(1)
, Commerce will determine, and CBP shall assess, antidumping duties on all appropriate entries of subject merchandise in accordance with the final results of this review. If Kenertec's weighted-average dumping margin is not zero or
de minimis
(
i.e.,
less than 0.50 percent) in the final results of this review, Commerce intends to calculate importer-specific assessment rates on the basis of the ratio of the total amount of dumping calculated for each importer's examined sales to the total entered value of those sales. Federal Register
. If a timely summons is filed at the U.S. Court of International Trade, the assessment instructions will direct CBP not to liquidate relevant entries until the time for parties to file a request for a statutory injunction has expired (

within 90 days of publication).

de minimis

Assessment Rates
Pursuant to section 751(a)(2)(C) of the Act and
19 CFR 351.212(b)(1)
, Commerce shall determine, and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) shall assess, antidumping duties on all appropriate entries covered by this review. Because the weighted-average dumping margin for Nishant has been determined to be zero percent, Commerce intends to instruct CBP to liquidate the appropriate entries without regard to antidumping duties, in accordance with
19 CFR 351.106(c)(2)
.
Because the weighted-average dumping margin for SLF/TEI is not zero or
de minimis
(
i.e.,
less than 0.5 percent), Commerce calculated importer-specific
ad valorem
assessment rates based on the ratio of the total amount of dumping calculated for each importer's examined sales to the total entered value of such sales.
[
6
]
Where an importer-specific
ad valorem
assessment rate is zero or
de minimis,
or a respondent's weighted-average dumping margin is zero or
de minimis,
Commerce will instruct CBP to liquidate appropriate entries without regard to antidumping duties.
[
7
]
In accordance with Commerce's “automatic assessment” practice, for entries of subject merchandise during the POR produced by Nishant or SLF/TEI for which these companies did not know that the merchandise was destined for the United States, we will instruct CBP to liquidate those entries at the all-others rate established in the original less-than-fair-value (LTFV) investigation if there is no rate for the intermediate company(ies) involved in the transaction.
[
8
]
For the companies that were not selected for individual review, Commerce assigned the assessment rate based on the review-specific average rate noted above.
Commerce intends to issue assessment instructions to CBP no earlier than 35 days after the publication date of the final results of this review in the
Federal Register
. If a timely summons is filed at the U.S. Court of International Trade, the assessment instructions will direct CBP not to liquidate relevant entries until the time for parties to file a request for a statutory injunction has expired (
i.e.,
within 90 days of publication).
Cash Deposit Requirements
The following cash deposit requirements will be effective for all shipments of the subject merchandise entered, or withdrawn from warehouse, for consumption on or after the publication date of the final results of this administrative review, as provided by section 751(a)(2)(C) of the Act: (1) the cash deposit rate for the companies listed in the final results of this review will be equal to the weighted-average dumping margin established in the final results of this administrative review; (2) for merchandise exported by producers or exporters not covered in this review but covered in a prior segment of the proceeding, the cash deposit rate will continue to be the company-specific rate published for the most recently-completed segment of this proceeding in which they were reviewed; (3) if the exporter is not a firm covered in this review, a prior review, or the original LTFV investigation, but the producer is, the cash deposit rate will be the rate established for the most recently completed segment of this proceeding for the producer of the subject merchandise; and (4) the cash deposit rate for all other manufacturers or exporters will continue to be 0.00 percent, the all-others rate established in the LTFV investigation.
[
9
]
These cash deposit requirements, when imposed, shall remain in effect until further notice.
Notification to Importers Regarding the Reimbursement of Duties
This notice serves as a final reminder to importers of their responsibility under
19 CFR 351.402(f)(2)
to file a certificate regarding the reimbursement of antidumping and/or countervailing duties prior to liquidation of the relevant entries during this review period. Failure to comply with this requirement could result in Commerce's presumption that reimbursement of antidumping and/or countervailing duties occurred and the subsequent assessment of double antidumping duties, and/or an increase in the amount of antidumping duties by the amount of the countervailing duties.
Administrative Protective Order (APO)
This notice also serves as a final reminder to parties subject to an APO of their responsibility concerning the return or destruction of proprietary information disclosed under APO in accordance with
19 CFR 351.305(a)(3)
, which continues to govern business proprietary information in this segment of the proceeding. Timely written notification of the return/destruction of APO materials, or conversion to judicial protective order, is hereby requested. Failure to comply with the regulations and the terms of an APO is a sanctionable violation.
Notification to Interested Parties
We are issuing and publishing this notice in accordance with sections 751(a)(1) and 777(i) of the Act.

AGENCY:
Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, Department of Commerce.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) preliminarily determines that countervailable subsidies were provided to Xingyi Metalworking Technology (Zhejiang) Co., Ltd. (XMT) for Certain Metal Lockers and Parts Thereof (Metal Lockers) from the People's Republic of China (China). The period of review (POR) is January 1, 2024, through December 31, 2024. In addition, Commerce is rescinding this review, in part, with respect to six companies. Interested parties are invited to comment on these preliminary results.
DATES:
Applicable November 16, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Frank Schmitt, AD/CVD Operations, Office III, Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1401 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20230; telephone: (202) 482- 4880.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
On September 25, 2025, based on timely requests for review, in accordance with
19 CFR 351.221(c)(1)(i)
, we initiated an administrative review of the countervailing duty order on metal lockers from China.
[
1
]
On February 19, 2026, Commerce selected XMT and Hangzhou Xline Machinery (Hangzhou Xline) as the mandatory respondents in this review.
[
2
]
On February 27, 2026, the petitioner timely withdrew its request for review.
[
3
]
Due to the lapse in appropriations and Federal Government shutdown, on November 14, 2025, Commerce tolled all deadlines in administrative proceedings by 47 days.
[
4
]
Additionally, due to a backlog of documents that were electronically filed via Enforcement and Compliance's Antidumping and Countervailing Duty Centralized Electronic Srvice System (ACCESS) during the Federal Government shutdown, on November 24, 2025, Commerce tolled all deadlines in administrative proceedings by an additional 21 days.
[
5
]
Between July 1, and October 27, 2026, we extended the deadline for the preliminary results of this review until November 9, 2026.
[
6
]
(
printed page 73568)
For a complete description of the events that followed the initiation of this review,
see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.
[
7
]
A list of topics included in the Preliminary Decision Memorandum is provided as an appendix to this notice. The Preliminary Decision Memorandum is a public document and is on file electronically via ACCESS which is available to registered users at
https://access.trade.gov
.
In addition, a complete version of the Preliminary Decision Memorandum can be accessed directly at
https://access.trade.gov/​frnotices
.
Scope of the Order
The product covered by the
Order
is metal lockers from China. For a complete description of the scope of the
Order, see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.
Rescission of Administrative Review, in Part
Pursuant to
19 CFR 351.213(d)(1)
, Commerce will rescind an administrative review, in whole or in part, if all parties that requested the review withdraw their requests within 90 days of the date of publication of the notice of initiation. As noted above, Commerce received timely-filed withdrawal requests with respect to the petitioner, and no other parties requested a review of: (1) Hangzhou Xline; (2) Hangzhou Evernew Machinery & Equipment Company, Ltd.; Zhejiang Yinghong Metalware Co., Ltd.;
[
8
]
(3) Kunshan Dongchu Precision Machinery Co., Ltd.; (4) Pinghu Chenda Storage Office Co., Ltd.; (5) Tianjin Jia Mei Metal Furniture Ltd.; and (6) Zhejiang Xingyi Metal Products Co., Ltd. Therefore, we are rescinding this administrative review with respect to these six companies, pursuant to
19 CFR 351.213(d)(1)
.
Methodology
Commerce is conducting this administrative review in accordance with 751(a)(1)(A) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act). For each of the subsidy programs found countervailable, Commerce preliminarily determines that there is a subsidy,
i.e.,
a financial contribution by an “authority” that gives rise to a benefit to the recipient, and that the subsidy is specific.
[
9
]
For a full description of the methodology underlying our conclusions, including our reliance, in part, on facts otherwise available with adverse inferences pursuant to sections 776(a) and (b) of the Act,
see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.

As a result of this review, we preliminarily determine the following net countervailable subsidy rate exists for the POR, January 1, 2024, through December 31, 2024:
Company
Subsidy rate
                             (percent
ad valorem
)
