AGENCY:
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), Department of Health and Human Services (HHS).
ACTION:
Notice of extension and modification of a temporary moratorium.
SUMMARY:
This notice announces the extension and modification of the nationwide temporary moratorium on the enrollment of new Medicare Home Health Agencies.
DATES:
The extension and modification of the moratorium is effective on November 12, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Frank Whelan, (410) 786-1302.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
A. CMS' Authority To Impose Temporary Enrollment Moratoria
1. Statutory and Regulatory Background
Under the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (
Pub. L. 111-148
), as amended by the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010 (
Pub. L. 111-152
) (collectively known as the Affordable Care Act), Congress provided the Secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services (the Secretary) with new tools and resources to combat fraud, waste, and abuse in Medicare, Medicaid, and the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP). One of these was section 6401(a) of the Affordable Care Act, which added a new section 1866(j)(7) to the Social Security Act (the Act). It provided the Secretary with authority to impose a temporary moratorium on the enrollment of new-fee-for-service (FFS) Medicare, Medicaid or CHIP providers and suppliers—including categories of providers and suppliers—if the Secretary determines that a moratorium is necessary to prevent or combat fraud, waste, or abuse under these programs.
Section 6401(b) of the Affordable Care Act added specific moratorium language applicable to Medicaid at section 1902(kk)(4) of the Act, requiring States to comply with any moratorium imposed by the Secretary unless the State determines that the imposition of such moratorium would adversely impact Medicaid beneficiaries' access to care. Section 6401(c) of the Affordable Care Act amended section 2107(e)(1) of the Act to provide that all the Medicaid provisions in sections 1902(a)(77) and 1902(kk) are also applicable to CHIP.
In February 2011, in accordance with the aforementioned authority, CMS published a final rule with comment period titled, “Medicare, Medicaid, and Children's Health Insurance Programs; Additional Screening Requirements, Application Fees, Temporary Enrollment Moratoria, Payment Suspensions and Compliance Plans for Providers and Suppliers” (
76 FR 5862
). This final rule implemented section 1866(j)(7) of the Act by establishing new regulations at
42 CFR 424.570
. Under § 424.570(a)(2)(i) and (iv), CMS—or CMS in consultation with the Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General (HHS-OIG) or the Department of Justice (DOJ) or both—may impose a temporary moratorium on newly enrolling Medicare providers and suppliers if CMS determines that there is a significant potential for fraud, waste, or abuse with respect to a particular provider or supplier type or particular geographic areas or both.
2. Particulars of a Moratorium as Outlined in § 424.570
a. Length
In accordance with § 424.570(b), a temporary enrollment moratorium imposed by CMS remains in effect for 6 months. If CMS deems it necessary, the moratorium may be extended in 6-month increments. CMS evaluates whether to extend or lift the moratorium before the end of the initial 6-month period and, if applicable, before the expiration of any subsequent moratorium periods. If the moratorium announced in this notice is extended, CMS will publish a document regarding such extension(s) in the
Federal Register
.
b. Cessation
As provided in § 424.570(d), CMS may lift a moratorium at any time if: (1) the President declares an area a disaster under the Robert T. Stafford Disaster Relief and Emergency Assistance Act; (2) circumstances warranting the imposition of a moratorium have abated or CMS has implemented program safeguards to address the program vulnerability; (3) the Secretary has declared a public health emergency; or (4) in the judgment of the Secretary, the moratorium is no longer needed. Once a moratorium is lifted, the provider or supplier types that were unable to enroll because of the moratorium will be assigned to the “high” screening level in accordance with §§ 424.518(c)(3)(iii) and 455.450(e)(2) if such provider or supplier applies for enrollment at any time within 6 months from the date the moratorium was lifted.
c. Circumstances Where Moratorium Is Inapplicable
Under current § 424.570(a)(1)(iii), a temporary moratorium does not apply to any of the following:
Changes in practice location (except if the location is changing from a location outside the moratorium area to a location inside the moratorium area).
Changes in provider or supplier information, such as phone number or address.
Changes in ownership (except changes in majority ownership (CIMOs) of home health agencies (HHAs), hospices, and suppliers of durable medical equipment, prosthetics, orthotics, and supplies (DMEPOS) that would require an initial enrollment).
Also, in accordance with § 424.570(a)(1)(iv), a temporary moratorium does not apply to any enrollment application that has been received by the Medicare contractor prior to the date the moratorium is imposed.
B. CMS' Previous Temporary Enrollment Moratoria
We first used our moratorium authority to prevent enrollment of new HHAs, subunits, and branch locations in Miami-Dade County, Florida and Cook County, Illinois, as well as surrounding counties, and Part B ambulance suppliers in Harris County, Texas and surrounding counties, in a notice issued on July 31, 2013 (
78 FR 46339
) in the
Federal Register
. We extended and expanded these moratoria several times, with the last in this series of moratoria expiring in 2019.
In the February 27, 2026,
Federal Register
(
91 FR 9855
), we published a notice announcing a 6-month nationwide enrollment moratorium on DMEPOS medical supply companies.
[
1
]
Said moratorium expired on August 27, 2026. It was not extended.
(
printed page 73604)
C. May 2026 HHA Moratorium
In weighing the need to establish an enrollment moratorium, CMS considers whether a significant risk of fraud, waste, or abuse exists. CMS also relies on its own and law enforcement's longstanding experience with ongoing and emerging fraud trends and activities gained through civil, criminal, and administrative investigations and prosecutions. Having analyzed this risk with respect to HHAs, we published a notice in the
Federal Register
on May 15, 2026, announcing a 6-month nationwide temporary moratorium on the Medicare enrollment of new HHAs and HHA branches (
91 FR 27954
).
[
2
]
The moratorium took effect on May 13, 2026.
We detailed in that notice our specific reasons for the HHA moratorium. We stated that HHA fraud, waste, and abuse has been a severe problem for over two decades as noted by the OIG in numerous past reports and studies. In fact, HHAs have long been among the highest-risk Medicare provider/supplier types in terms of program integrity. We outlined in the notice various steps that CMS has taken over the years to address HHA program integrity. Along with certain HHAs being part of the first enrollment moratorium imposed in July 2013, these steps included:
Capitalization
—Under § 489.28(a), newly enrolling HHAs must have available sufficient funds at the time of application submission and at all times during the enrollment process up to the expiration of the 3-month period following enrollment. The purpose is to ensure that the HHA is a viable and financially stable business, for an underfunded entity could skimp on patient care to save money or engage in fraud to improve its finances. HHAs remain the only Medicare provider/supplier type that have minimum capitalization requirements as a condition of enrollment; this underscores the uniquely serious fraud, waste, and abuse threat HHAs pose.
Screening Designation
—HHAs are one of only six provider/supplier types subject to the highest and strictest level of enrollment application screening under § 424.518.
[
3
]
In fact, they were one of only two types originally assigned to this level in our initial screening category assignments in 2011.
CIMOs
—Further underscoring the program integrity threat they pose, HHAs in 2009 became the first provider type (and, until 2022, were the only one) to be required under § 424.550(b) to enroll in Medicare as a new provider and undergo a State survey or accreditation following a change in majority ownership—the purpose being to ensure that the HHA under its new ownership is fully compliant with Medicare requirements.
Provisional Period of Enhanced Oversight (PPEO)
—Section 1866(j)(3) of the Act permits the Secretary to establish a PPEO of between 30 days and 1 year during which new providers or suppliers (including categories thereof) would be subject to enhanced oversight, such as prepayment review and payment caps. Consistent therewith, we implemented a PPEO in 2019 under which new HHAs would not receive upfront payments prior to the provision of services stemming from their requests for anticipated payments (RAPs).
[
4
]
As with our capitalization and CIMO provisions—and in light of the longstanding HHA payment safeguard threats—HHAs were the first provider type to be subject to a PPEO.
We also emphasized in the May 15, 2026, notice, though, that despite the foregoing HHA program integrity initiatives, HHA fraud, waste, and abuse remains a significant problem. We cited a number of criminal cases in recent years involving HHAs, and pointed out the deeply disconcerting matter of clusters, whereby large groups of the same provider type suddenly locate themselves within a certain geographic area as part of a potential fraud scheme. Two such situations we noted were the following:
The number of HHAs in Los Angeles County, California, between 2019 and 2023 rose more than 40 percent, and well over 1,000 new HHAs have enrolled in the county since 2019.
In Ohio, we found numerous HHAs operating out of a single, common practice location. There were at least nine cases in Ohio where at least five HHAs have the same practice location address; four of these nine situations involve at least 9 HHAs in one location, with one location having 18 HHAs.
Similar situations have been seen in Texas, Michigan, North Carolina, and Nevada. We explained that these situations occurring across various States—rather than being limited to one geographic region—highlighted the national nature of this problem, and that such clusters can pop up at any time and in any place.
Above all, we stressed that CMS must be aggressive in halting fraud before it begins; proactivity is a much better anti-fraud approach than a reactive, “pay-and-chase” model. We found our previous HHA moratoria beneficial in this regard, which is largely why we extended and expanded them over a 5-year period.
D. Continued Problems in the HHA Sphere and Consequent Need for Moratorium Extension
We believe there remains a significant potential for fraud, waste, and abuse in the HHA sphere. The payment safeguard threats from HHAs remain high, and the Department of Justice (DOJ) in an August 13, 2026, memorandum noted the DOJ's emphasis on halting home health misconduct. It stated in part that: “The [DOJ's] Fraud Division will use cutting-edge data analysis to target exploitative health care fraud schemes,” including with respect to home health.
[
5
]
Too, home health criminal and other cases continue to occur (including in Medicaid, which shows that the problem is wide-ranging), such as the following:
In May 2026, a Michigan nurse and home health care agency owner was convicted for operating a $1.6 million scheme to defraud Medicare. According to court documents and evidence presented at trial, the defendant:
++ Bribed a discharge nurse at a Detroit hospital to identify Medicare patients and fax their confidential records to the home health agency unbeknownst to the patients.
++ Developed the kickback relationship with the hospital discharge nurse at a home health company she had previously co-owned, but she offered the nurse an additional $100 per patient to induce her to refer patients to her new company, paying the discharge nurse over $130,000.
++ Used these stolen profiles to bill Medicare for home health services, exploiting the diagnostic and personal information of patients who were unaware their data had been compromised.
++ In billing claims for patients who were obtained through kickbacks, falsely represented to Medicare that a doctor had certified patients as meeting the Medicare requirements to receive home health services (including being homebound) when evidence proved no doctor had ever evaluated these patients for home health services.
++ In many instances, used the identities of real doctors to fabricate the
(
printed page 73605)
existence of these evaluations when, in reality, these doctors had never even met the patients and did not know that the defendant was using their information to fraudulently bill Medicare.
[
6
]
A Missouri woman pleaded guilty in March 2026 to one count of health care fraud. The defendant admitted submitting fraudulent documents to enroll her home health care company with Missouri Medicaid; the paperwork falsely claimed that someone else owned the company, concealing her ownership and role due to a 2012 criminal conviction. She also admitted submitting fraudulent claims to Missouri Medicaid seeking reimbursement for home healthcare services that were never provided. On numerous occasions, clients were in the hospital and could not have received any health care services at home; on other occasions, the defendant submitted claims when the company did not have any timesheet records or documentation of the services.
[
7
]
Two Florida home health providers in January 2026 agreed to pay over $700,000 to resolve allegations that they violated the Physician Self-Referral Law (commonly known as the Stark Law (section 1877 of the Act)) by making bonus payments to an employee based on the number of patient referrals made by the employee's spouse, a physician.
[
8
]
In July 2026, a California man was convicted of conspiracy to commit health care fraud. According to evidence presented at the trial:
++ The defendant conspired with his wife, the former CEO of a California home health agency, and two former agency employees to commit health care fraud. The defendant and his wife agreed to defraud Medicare by: (1) having unqualified medical professionals provide care for home health patients outside their authorized scope of practice; (2) billing Medicare for services never provided; (3) submitting false documents to California Department of Public Health inspectors to maintain the ability to bill Medicare; and (4) instructing former employees to lie to the FBI and Federal law enforcement to conceal their fraudulent activity.
++ The defendant took steps to thwart the law enforcement investigation into the home health agency. He and his wife met with one of the home health agency's former employees, who informed them that FBI agents had questioned her regarding the home health agency's billing practices and patient medical assessments. The defendant instructed the employee to lie to the FBI and falsely state that the employee had been trained and supervised by a registered nurse in the course of conducting patient assessments.
[
9
]
The United States Attorney stated that the defendant and his wife “defrauded Medicare by altering medical records and forging doctor signatures, and in the process stole millions from the hardworking American taxpayer.” The Special-Agent-in-Charge added: “[The defendant] and his conspirators orchestrated a deliberate scheme that put vulnerable patients at risk and stole from Medicare.”
[
10
]
A Missouri woman in February 2026 pleaded guilty to one count of wire fraud. She admitted that while owner of a home health care agency, she submitted hundreds of fraudulent reimbursement claims to the Missouri Medicaid Program and the Department of Veterans Affairs. She admitted submitting claims for services on dates when the veteran patients were in the hospital and could not possibly have received home healthcare services. She also submitted claims knowing both that the services were not provided and that she did not have any necessary documentation of the services.
[
11
]
The circumstances warranting the imposition of the HHA moratorium, in short, have not yet abated. CMS has accordingly determined that the moratorium on new HHA enrollments is still needed as we: (1) monitor the indicators; and (2) continue with administrative actions to combat fraud and abuse, such as payment suspensions and revocations of providers.
[
12
]
We note that we consulted with the HHS-OIG regarding the extension of this moratorium; OIG agreed there remains a significant potential for fraud, waste or abuse in the Medicare program with respect to HHAs. Based in part on said consultation, we believe our moratorium extension is justified.
We are, though, scaling back the moratorium's scope during the 6-month extension period. The moratorium extension will only apply to initially enrolling HHAs (including those initially enrolling pursuant to a non-exempt CIMO under § 424.550(b)). The extension will not apply to additions of HHA branches, and the moratorium on the addition of branches by currently enrolled HHAs will end as of the effective date of this notice. This modification is primarily due to our greater concern at this current time about new HHAs—with whom we may have no experience—than with HHAs that are already enrolled but are merely seeking to add a branch to their current enrollment (though the latter are still of concern to us).
2. Medicaid and CHIP
We stated in our May 15, 2026, notice that, in our view, it is in Medicaid and CHIP beneficiaries' best interests to allow each State to decide whether some form of HHA moratorium is appropriate for their respective Medicaid programs and CHIPs, and the scope of any such moratorium. Each State has greater expertise and experience with their pool of HHAs—including the requirements for each type of HHA—than CMS. Nevertheless, we encouraged each State to, as appropriate, implement an HHA moratorium tailored to the specifics of their beneficiary population as well as any geographic considerations (in accordance with
42 CFR 455.470(b)
). We also offered each State and territory the opportunity to consult with CMS on the prospect of implementing a Medicaid- or CHIP-based moratorium in their jurisdictions.
Two States—Ohio and Rhode Island—have implemented home health moratoria in response to our May 15, 2026, notice. Our extension notice is not intended to impact these existing moratoria. As we stated in the May 15, 2026, notice, the decision still lies with the State or territory.
3. Access to Care
We have not seen evidence that the May 15, 2026, HHA moratorium has materially reduced Medicare beneficiary access to HHA services on a nationwide or even a State level. In addition, States and territories have not indicated to CMS that the HHA moratorium has led to access to care problems for Medicaid or CHIP beneficiaries in their jurisdictions. Nonetheless, we will continue to monitor this important issue—particularly in rural areas—to
(
printed page 73606)
ensure that such problems do not arise with our moratorium extension.
III. No Judicial Review of CMS's Decision To Impose an Enrollment Moratorium
In accordance with section 1866(j)(7)(B) of the Act, there is no judicial review under sections 1869 and 1878 of the Act, or otherwise, of the decision to impose a temporary enrollment moratorium. Under §§ 424.530(a)(10) and 424.570(c), CMS denies the enrollment application of a provider or supplier if the provider or supplier is subject to a moratorium. In addition, § 424.514(d)(2)(v)(C) states that if the provider or supplier was required to pay an application fee, the application fee will be refunded if the application was denied because of the imposition of a temporary moratorium.
A provider or supplier that is impacted by a moratorium may use the existing appeal procedures at
42 CFR part 498
to administratively appeal a denial of billing privileges based on the imposition of a temporary moratorium. The scope of any such appeal, though, would be limited solely to assessing whether the temporary moratorium applies to the provider or supplier appealing the denial (see
42 CFR 498.5(l)(4)
).
IV. Collection of Information Requirements
This document does not impose information collection requirements, that is, reporting, recordkeeping or third-party disclosure requirements. Consequently, there is no need for review by the Office of Management and Budget under the authority of the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (
44 U.S.C. 3501
et seq.
).
V. Regulatory Impact Statement
A. Statement of Need
This extension notice is necessary to help reduce the prevalence of Medicare fraud, waste, and abuse among HHAs.
B. Overall Impact
We have examined the impacts of this notice as required by
Executive Order 12866
, “Regulatory Planning and Review”;
Executive Order 13132
, “Federalism”;
Executive Order 13563
, “Improving Regulation and Regulatory Review”;
Executive Order 14192
, “Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation”; the Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) (
5 U.S.C. 601
through
612
); section 1102(b) of the Social Security Act; and section 202 of the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995.
Executive Orders 12866 and 13563 direct agencies to assess all costs and benefits of available regulatory alternatives and, if regulation is necessary, to select those regulatory approaches that maximize net benefits (including potential economic, environmental, public health and safety, and other advantages; and distributive impacts). Section 3(f) of
Executive Order 12866
defines a “significant regulatory action” as any regulatory action that is likely to result in a rule that may: (1) have an annual effect on the economy of $100 million or more or adversely affect in a material way the economy, a sector of the economy, productivity, competition, jobs, the environment, public health or safety, or State, local, or tribal governments or communities; (2) create a serious inconsistency or otherwise interfere with an action taken or planned by another agency; (3) materially alter the budgetary impact of entitlements, grants, user fees, or loan programs or the rights and obligations of recipients thereof; or (4) raise novel legal or policy issues arising out of legal mandates, the President's priorities, or the Executive Order itself.
An RIA must be prepared for a regulatory action that is significant under section 3(f)(1) of
Executive Order 12866
. Based on our analysis, the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) has determined that this notice is not significant pursuant to section 3(f)(1) of
Executive Order 12866
. Accordingly, we have not prepared a regulatory impact analysis. In accordance with Subtitle E of the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act of 1996 (also known as the Congressional Review Act), OIRA has also determined that this notice does not meet the criteria for a major rule as defined in
5 U.S.C. 804(2)
.
In addition, section 1102(b) of the Act requires us to prepare an RIA if a rule may have a significant impact on the operations of a substantial number of small rural hospitals. This analysis must conform to the RFA provisions at
5 U.S.C. 604
. For purposes of section 1102(b) of the Act, we define a small rural hospital as a hospital that is located outside of a metropolitan statistical area and has fewer than 100 beds. This notice is primarily applicable to HHAs, not rural hospitals. Therefore, the Secretary has certified that this notice will not have a significant economic impact on the operations of small rural hospitals.
We continue to expect savings for the Medicare program from the reduction in the number of newly enrolling HHAs. However, we do not yet have data upon which to base an estimate of the amount of savings.
C. Regulatory Flexibility Analysis (RFA)
1. Small Business Impact
The RFA requires agencies to analyze options for regulatory relief of small businesses. For purposes of the RFA, small entities include small businesses, nonprofit organizations, and small governmental jurisdictions. Most entities and most other providers and suppliers are small entities, either by nonprofit status or by having revenues less than $19 million to $41 million in any 1 year. Individuals and States are not included in the definition of a small entity. For reasons stated in the May 15, 2026, notice, we do not believe that our HHA moratorium has a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small businesses. Even conceding the impact on newly enrolling HHA, we believe that the risk that HHA fraud, waste, and abuse poses to the Trust Funds, Medicare beneficiaries, and the taxpayers far exceeds this and thus justifies our measure.
2. Alternatives Considered
There are two principal alternatives we considered in preparing this notice. First, we contemplated allowing the May 15, 2026, moratorium to expire without extension. Yet as already mentioned, fraud schemes remain a significant problem. We believe that permitting new HHAs—some of which may, after enrollment, engage in fraud, waste, or abuse—to begin enrolling again without limitation would only exacerbate the dilemma. Second, we contemplated extending the moratorium but limiting it to southern California, which is a recognized area of HHA fraud, waste, and abuse. We believe, though, that the problems the moratorium seeks to address are nationwide, rather than restricted to particular geographic areas.
D. Unfunded Mandates Reform Act (UMRA)
Section 202 of the UMRA of 1995 also requires that agencies assess anticipated costs and benefits before issuing any rule whose mandates require spending in any 1 year of $100 million in 1995 dollars, updated annually for inflation. In 2026, that threshold is approximately $193 million. This notice will not impose a mandate that will result in the expenditure by State, local, and Tribal governments, in the aggregate, or by the private sector, of more than $193 million in any 1 year. UMRA only applies in situations where an agency
(
printed page 73607)
engages in notice-and-comment rulemaking. It does not apply to this notice.
E. State and Local Costs
Executive Order 13132
establishes certain requirements that an agency must meet when it promulgates a proposed regulatory action (and subsequent final action) that imposes substantial direct requirement costs on State and local governments, preempts State law, or otherwise has Federalism implications. Since this notice does not impose any costs on State or local governments, the requirements of
Executive Order 13132
are not applicable.
In accordance with the provisions of
Executive Order 12866
, this notice was reviewed by the Office of Management and Budget.
The Administrator of the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), Dr. Mehmet Oz, having reviewed and approved this document, authorizes Vanessa Garcia, who is the Federal Register Liaison, to electronically sign this document for purposes of publication in the
Federal Register
.
Vanessa Garcia,
Federal Register Liaison, Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services.

AGENCY:
National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), Department of Transportation (DOT).
ACTION:
Extension of comment period.
SUMMARY:
In response to requests from the Alliance for Automotive Innovation (the Alliance), Society of Automotive Engineers (SAE) International, and Gatik AI Inc. (Gatik), NHTSA is announcing a 15-day extension of the public comment period for the notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) published on October 26, 2026 proposing to amend Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard (FMVSS) No. 108, “Lamps, reflective devices, and associated equipment.” The proposed modifications would distinguish how regulations apply to vehicles with and without manually operated driving controls. The comment period for the notice was originally scheduled to end on November 25, 2026. It will now end on December 10, 2026.
DATES:
The comment period for the proposed rule published at
91 FR 67243
on October 26, 2026 is extended to December 10, 2026.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
On October 26, 2026, NHTSA published an NPRM proposing to amend FMVSS No. 108.
[
1
]
The proposed updates to the standard are intended to remove unnecessary requirements and to provide design flexibility without impact on vehicle safety. The first two proposed changes would amend the test voltage specification for integral beam headlamps and remove requirements that apply to vertical headlamp arrangements. Further proposed changes address vehicles equipped with Automated Driving Systems (ADS) that do not have manually operated driving controls. Those modifications would limit the application of certain requirements for manually operated turn signal, hazard warning signal, and beam switching controls to vehicles with manually operated driving controls. The changes are intended to address regulatory burdens and costs associated with equipment that does not fulfill the same purpose or provide safety benefits in an ADS-equipped vehicle without manually operated driving controls as in a vehicle with such controls. The changes would also narrow certain requirements for telltales to vehicles with manually operated driving controls and incorporate the term “telltale” where appropriate throughout the standard. Finally, a proposed addition to the standard would allow cyan-colored ADS marker lamps as optional motor vehicle lighting equipment in ADS-equipped vehicles. The notice provided a 30-day comment period which closes on November 25, 2026.
NHTSA received a request from the Alliance on October 26, 2026 for a 15-day extension of the comment period.
[
2
]
The Alliance stated that the NPRM's 30-day comment period is insufficient given the technical and legal complexity of the proposed lighting requirements, their application to ADS-specific designs, and their potential effects on both ADS-equipped and traditional vehicles. The requested 15-day extension, the Alliance indicated, would support more substantive public feedback without materially delaying final rulemaking activity. NHTSA received similar requests from Gatik and SAE International. While Gatik also requested a 15-day extension, SAE International requested a 20-day extension. SAE International also asked if an extension is not granted, that NHTSA consider a partial submission within the time window with a subsequent filing after the closing date.
NHTSA is granting the request to extend the comment period by 15 days. NHTSA has determined that the requestors have shown good cause for an extension and that the extension is consistent with the public interest. A 15-day extension appropriately balances NHTSA's interest in providing the public with sufficient time to comment on the notice with its interest in obtaining specific feedback from stakeholders in a timely manner. In addition, to the extent possible NHTSA will also consider comments that Docket Management receives after the closing date. If Docket Management receives a comment too late for us to consider in developing the final rule, NHTSA will consider that comment as an informal suggestion for future rulemaking action. Accordingly, NHTSA is extending the comment period until December 10, 2026.

3
]

AGENCY:
National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), Department of Transportation (DOT).
ACTION:
Notice and request for comments on a request for approval of a new information collection.
SUMMARY:
NHTSA invites public comments about our intention to request approval from the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for a new information collection. Before a Federal agency can collect certain information from the public, it must receive
(
printed page 73635)
approval from OMB. Under procedures established by the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995, before seeking OMB approval, Federal agencies must solicit public comment on proposed collections of information, including extensions and reinstatement of previously approved collections. This document describes a collection of information for which NHTSA intends to seek OMB approval titled “
49 CFR part 555
, Temporary Exemption from Motor Vehicle Safety and Bumper Standards.”
DATES:
Comments must be submitted on or before January 15, 2027.
ADDRESSES:
You may submit comments identified by Docket No. NHTSA-2026-1453 through any of the following methods:
Electronic submissions:
Go to the Federal eRulemaking Portal at
http://www.regulations.gov
.
Follow the online instructions for submitting comments.
Fax:
(202) 493-2251.
Mail or Hand Delivery:
Docket Management, U.S. Department of Transportation, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, West Building, Room W58-213, Washington, DC 20590, between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m., Monday through Friday, except on Federal holidays. To be sure someone is there to help you, please call (202) 366-9826 or (202) 366-9317 before coming.
Instructions:
All submissions must include the agency name and docket number for this notice. Note that all comments received will be posted without change to
http://www.regulations.gov
,
including any personal information provided. Please see the Privacy Act heading below.
Privacy Act:
Anyone is able to search the electronic form of all comments received into any of our dockets by the name of the individual submitting the comment (or signing the comment, if submitted on behalf of an association, business, labor union, etc.). You may review DOT's complete Privacy Act Statement in the
Federal Register
published on April 11, 2000 (
65 FR 19477-78
) or you may visit
https://www.transportation.gov/​privacy
.
Docket:
For access to the docket to read background documents or comments received, go to
http://www.regulations.gov
or the street address listed above. Follow the online instructions for accessing the dockets via internet.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Andrew Magaletti, National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590; email
Andrew.Magaletti@dot.gov
;
telephone (202) 366-1810.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Under the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (
44 U.S.C. 3501
et seq.
), before an agency submits a proposed collection of information to OMB for approval, it must first publish a document in the
Federal Register
providing a 60-day comment period and otherwise consult with members of the public and affected agencies concerning each proposed collection of information. The OMB has promulgated regulations describing what must be included in such a document. Under OMB's regulation (at
5 CFR 1320.8(d)
), an agency must ask for public comment on the following: (a) whether the proposed collection of information is necessary for the proper performance of the functions of the agency, including whether the information will have practical utility; (b) the accuracy of the agency's estimate of the burden of the proposed collection of information, including the validity of the methodology and assumptions used; (c) how to enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected; and (d) how to minimize the burden of the collection of information on those who are to respond, including the use of appropriate automated, electronic, mechanical, or other technological collection techniques or other forms of information technology,
e.g.,
permitting electronic submission of responses. In compliance with these requirements, NHTSA asks for public comments on the following proposed collection of information for which the agency is seeking approval from OMB.
Title:
49 CFR part 555
, Temporary Exemption from Motor Vehicle Safety and Bumper Standards.
OMB Control Number:
New.
Form Number(s):
N/A.
Type of Request:
New Information Collection.
Type of Review Requested:
Regular.
Requested Expiration Date of Approval:
3 years from date of approval.
Summary of the Collection of Information
Under
49 CFR part 555
, a manufacturer of motor vehicles or passenger motor vehicles may apply to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration for a temporary exemption from any Federal motor vehicle safety or bumper standard, or for a renewal of any exemption. Each application filed for an exemption or its renewal must be written in the English language and be submitted electronically to the Administrator. The application must state the full name and address of the applicant, the nature of its organization, and the name of the State or country under the laws of which it is organized. It must also state the number and title, and the text or substance of the standard or portion thereof from which the temporary exemption is sought, and the length of time desired for such exemption. The applicant must set forth the reasons why granting the exemption would be in the public interest, and, as applicable, consistent with the objectives of
49 U.S.C. Chapter 301
or Chapter 325.
Furthermore, the applicant must set forth the basis for the application and the information required for that specific basis. If the basis of the application is that compliance with the standard would cause substantial economic hardship to a manufacturer that has tried to comply with the standard in good faith, the applicant must provide engineering and financial information demonstrating in detail how compliance or failure to obtain an exemption would cause substantial economic hardship. This includes a list or description of each item of motor vehicle equipment that would have to be modified in order to achieve compliance, as well as the itemized estimated cost to modify each such item as soon as possible, and at the end of a 1-year, 2-year, and 3-year exemption period. The application must include the estimated price increase per vehicle to balance the total costs incurred, corporate balance sheets and income statements for the three fiscal years immediately preceding the filing of the application, a projected balance sheet and income statement for the fiscal year following a denial of the application, and a discussion of any other hardships. The applicant must also provide a description of its efforts to comply with the standards, including a chronological analysis of such efforts, a discussion of alternate means of compliance considered and the reasons for rejection of each, a description of the steps to be taken while the exemption is in effect, and the total number of motor vehicles produced by or on behalf of the petitioner in the 12-month period prior to filing the petition.
If the basis of the application is that the exemption would make easier the development or field evaluation of a new motor vehicle safety or impact protection features providing a safety or impact protection level at least equal to that of the standard, the applicant must provide a description of the safety or impact protection features, and research, development, and testing documentation establishing the innovational nature of such features. The applicant must provide an analysis establishing that the level of safety or impact protection of the feature is
(
printed page 73636)
equivalent to or exceeds the level of safety or impact protection established in the standard, along with substantiation that a temporary exemption would facilitate the development or field evaluation of the vehicle. The applicant must also include a statement whether, at the end of the exemption period, it intends to conform to the standard, apply for a further exemption, or petition for rulemaking to amend the standard to incorporate the safety or impact protection features.
If the basis of the application is that the exemption would make the development or field evaluation of a low-emission vehicle easier and would not unreasonably lower the safety or impact protection level of that vehicle, the applicant must provide substantiation that the vehicle is a low-emission vehicle, alongside research, development, and testing documentation establishing that a temporary exemption would not unreasonably degrade the safety or impact protection of the vehicle. This documentation must include a detailed description of how the motor vehicle equipped with the low-emission engine would differ from one that complies with the standard, the results of any tests conducted on the vehicle that demonstrate its failure to meet the standard expressed as comparative performance levels, and reasons why the failure to meet the standard does not unreasonably degrade the safety or impact protection of the vehicle. The applicant must also provide substantiation that a temporary exemption would facilitate the development or field evaluation of the vehicle, and a statement whether, at the end of the exemption period, the manufacturer intends to conform with the standard.
If the basis of the application is that the applicant is otherwise unable to sell a vehicle whose overall level of safety or impact protection is at least equal to that of a nonexempted vehicle, the applicant must provide a detailed analysis of how the vehicle provides the overall level of safety or impact protection at least equal to that of nonexempted vehicles. This analysis must include a detailed description of how the motor vehicle, if exempted, differs from one that conforms to the standard, a detailed description of any safety or impact protection features that the vehicle offers as standard equipment that are not required by the Federal standards, and the results of any tests conducted on the vehicle demonstrating that its overall level of safety or impact protection exceeds that which is achieved by conformity to the standards. The applicant must also provide substantiation that compliance would prevent the sale of the vehicle, and a statement whether, at the end of the exemption period, the manufacturer intends to comply with the standard.
For applications based on the development of new safety features, the development of low-emission vehicles, or an equal or greater overall safety level, the applicant must provide a statement that not more than 2,500 exempted vehicles will be sold in the United States in any 12-month period for which an exemption may be granted.
Once an exemption is granted, a manufacturer of an exempted vehicle shall submit to the Administrator, within 30 days after receiving notification of the grant of an exemption, a sample of the certification label and affix securely to the windshield or side window of each exempted vehicle a label in the English language.
If necessary, NHTSA may establish conditions for more direct and continuous oversight over exempt vehicles. Under this framework, NHTSA issues an initial operational authorization at the time that the grant notice is published in the
Federal Register
that would contain initial operational terms and conditions. The manufacturer would be able to begin manufacturing and commercially deploying vehicles immediately consistent with the terms and conditions of the initial authorization. The operational permissions could later be modified via additional operational authorizations, such as after a manufacturer requests a change. This approach gives NHTSA flexibility to change operational terms quickly and is particularly useful for vehicles equipped with advanced vehicle technologies, like automated driving systems (ADS), which may require expanding the scope of the operational permission as the ADS continues to develop. This allows the exemption to mirror real-world ADS development, which often starts with smaller, more limited operations, before expanding over time. Requests for modifications would include sufficient technical information about the vehicle technology and proposed operations to allow NHTSA to make a determination on whether to grant the modification request in whole or in part.
Description of the Need for the Information and Proposed Use of the Information:
Under
49 U.S.C. 30113
and
32502
, the Secretary of Transportation is authorized to exempt, on a temporary basis, motor vehicles from a Federal motor vehicle safety standard or passenger motor vehicles from a bumper standard. This statutory authority has been delegated to NHTSA. To implement these provisions, NHTSA promulgated
49 CFR part 555
, which establishes the requirements for temporary exemptions. The information collections described in this document are necessary to administer the part 555 General Exemptions program.
NHTSA relies on the collected information to assess the merits of exemption applications submitted by motor vehicle manufacturers, alterers, and intermediate or final-stage manufacturers. Specifically, the agency uses the submitted documentation to determine whether granting a requested exemption is in the public interest, is consistent with the objectives of the National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act, and whether an applicant satisfies at least one of the four statutory bases for an exemption.
[
1
]
Furthermore, as authorized by
49 U.S.C. 30113
, NHTSA may establish appropriate terms and conditions for any granted exemption. The agency uses the submitted technical and operational information to tailor these terms on a case-by-case basis, ensuring the exemption is consistent with the public interest and meets its statutory basis. While this flexible approach to operational terms helps address the complexity of novel technologies like Automated Driving Systems (ADS), NHTSA applies it to any part 555 application as appropriate. Ultimately, this information collection is necessary for the agency to process applications, grant or deny petitions, apply safety conditions, and fulfill its statutory obligation to regulate motor vehicle safety.
Affected Public:
The respondents are manufacturers of motor vehicles seeking temporary exemptions from Federal motor vehicle safety standards or bumper standards. This also includes alterers, incomplete vehicle manufacturers, intermediate manufacturers, and final-stage manufacturers seeking exemptions for vehicles built in two or more stages.
Estimated Number of Respondents:
NHTSA estimates that, on average, approximately 13 manufacturers will apply for part 555 exemptions, 13 manufacturers will submit required labeling text, and 5 manufacturers will submit requests to modify operational authorizations annually.
Frequency:
Applications for exemptions are submitted on an occasional, as-needed basis. However,
(
printed page 73637)
exemptions may not be granted for longer than two or three years and manufacturers. Manufacturers may seek renewals of their exemptions. Requests for modification of operational authorizations are also submitted on occasional, as-needed basis. The submission of language for labeling is a one-time collection for each exemption granted.
Estimated Number of Responses:
NHTSA estimates that it will receive, on average, approximately 13 part 555 applications, 13 submissions of requiring labeling language, and 5 requests to modify operational authorizations each year.
Estimated Total Annual Burden Hours:
1,453.
NHTSA estimates that the average time to prepare a part 555 application ranges from several dozen hours up to 80 hours depending on the complexity of the application. NHTSA estimates that the burden for applications submitted by low-volume manufacturers on the basis of economic hardship will take less time, while more complex applications involving vehicles with new and emerging technology, such highly complex Automated Driving Systems will take more. Conservatively, for an average of 13 manufacturers filing annually, NHTSA estimates the annual burden for compiling and submitting part 555 applications to be 1,040 hours. In addition, 13 manufacturers are estimated to spend an average annual total of 13 burden hours for submission of labeling language, and 5 manufacturers are expected to spend a total of 400 hours annually submitting requests to modify operational authorizations. As a result, the total estimated burden for this information collection is 1,453 annual burden hours.
To calculate the labor cost associated with submitting applications for temporary exemptions under
49 CFR part 555
, submitted required labeling language, and submitting requests to modify operational authorizations, NHTSA looked at wage estimates for the type of personnel involved with compiling and submitting the documents. NHTSA estimates the total labor costs associated with these burden hours by looking at the average wage for technical, management, and legal personnel. The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) estimates that the average hourly wage for Automotive Engineers/Technical Writers (BLS Occupation codes 17-2141/27-3042) is $48.47, for Architectural and Engineering Managers (BLS Occupation code 11-9041) is $78.38, and for Lawyers (BLS Occupation code 23-1011) is $89.38 in the Motor Vehicle Manufacturing Industry (NAICS 336100).
[
2
]
Across the allocated 80 hours per application (60 technical hours, 12 engineering management hours, and 8 legal review hours), the weighted average base hourly wage is $57.05.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics estimates that private industry workers' wages represent 70.4% of total labor compensation costs.
[
3
]
Therefore, NHTSA estimates the total loaded hourly labor cost to be $81.03 ($57.05 ÷ 0.704) for combined technical, engineering management, and legal staff. Assuming 13 annual respondents submitting 1 response each, NHTSA estimates the total annual burden to be 1,040 hours (13 × 80 hours) and the total annual labor cost to be $84,274.72 ($6,482.67 per submission × 13). You are asked to comment on any aspects of this information collection, including (a) whether the proposed collection of information is necessary for the proper performance of the functions of the Department, including whether the information will have practical utility; (b) the accuracy of the Department's estimate of the burden of the proposed information collection; (c) ways to enhance the quality, utility and clarity of the information to be collected; and (d) ways to minimize the burden of the collection of information on respondents, including the use of automated collection techniques or other forms of information technology.

AGENCY:
The Department of Health and Human Services, Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services.
ACTION:
Notice of a new matching program.
SUMMARY:
In accordance with subsection (e)(12) of the Privacy Act of 1974, as amended, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), is providing notice of a new matching program between CMS and the U.S. Department of Education (ED), Federal Student Aid. The matching program supports eligibility determinations for enrollment in applicable State health subsidy programs under the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (PPACA), including Qualified Health Plans (QHPs), Medicaid, the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP), and Basic Health Programs (BHPs). The matching program also supports implementation of statutory requirements concerning Medicaid community engagement and the prevention of concurrent Medicaid
(
printed page 73602)
enrollment in more than one State through the Multi-State Enrollment Prevention (MSEP) system.
DATES:
The deadline for comments on this notice is December 16, 2026. The new matching program will commence not sooner than 30 days after publication of this notice, provided no comments are received that warrant a change to this notice and the advance reporting requirements applicable to the matching program have been satisfied. The matching program will be conducted for an initial term of 18 months and, within 3 months prior to expiration, may be renewed for a period not to exceed one year if the parties certify that the matching program will be conducted without change and has been conducted in compliance with the matching agreement.
ADDRESSES:
Interested parties may submit written comments on this notice to the CMS Privacy Act Officer by mail at: Division of Security, Privacy Policy and Governance, Information Security and Privacy Group, Office of Information Technology, Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, Location: N1-14-56, 7500 Security Boulevard, Baltimore, MD 21244-1849, or by email at
Barbara.Demopulos@cms.hhs.gov
.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
If you have questions about the matching program, you may contact Terence Kane, Director, Division of Automated Verifications and SEP Policy, Marketplace Eligibility and Enrollment Group, Center for Consumer Information & Insurance Oversight, Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, at (301) 492-4449, by email at
Terence.Kane@cms.hhs.gov
,
or by mail at 7501 Wisconsin Avenue, Bethesda, MD 20814.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The Privacy Act of 1974, as amended (
5 U.S.C. 552a
), provides certain protections for individuals applying for and receiving federal benefits. The law governs the use of computer matching by federal agencies when records in a system of records (meaning, federal agency records about individuals retrieved by name or other personal identifier) are matched with records of other federal or non-federal agencies. The Privacy Act requires agencies involved in a matching program to:
1. Enter into a written agreement, which must be prepared in accordance with the Privacy Act, approved by the Data Integrity Board of each source and recipient federal agency, provided to Congress and the Office of Management and Budget (OMB), and made available to the public, as required by
5 U.S.C. 552a(o)
, (u)(3)(A), and (u)(4).
2. Notify the individuals whose information will be used in the matching program that the information they provide is subject to verification through matching, as required by
5 U.S.C. 552a(o)(1)(D)
.
3. Verify match findings before suspending, terminating, reducing, or making a final denial of an individual's benefits or payments or taking other adverse action against the individual, as required by
5 U.S.C. 552a(p)
.
4. Report the matching program to Congress and the OMB, in advance and annually, as required by
5 U.S.C. 552a(o)(2)(A)(i)
, (r), and (u)(3)(D).
5. Publish advance notice of the matching program in the
Federal Register
as required by
5 U.S.C. 552a(e)(12)
.
This matching program meets these requirements and establishes a new matching program through which ED will provide student enrollment match results to CMS for eligibility verification purposes described below.
Barbara Demopulos,
CMS Privacy Act Officer, Division of Security, Privacy Policy and Governance, Information Security and Privacy Group, Office of Information Technology, Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services.
Participating Agencies:
The agencies participating in the matching program are the Department of Health and Human Services, Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), and the U.S. Department of Education (ED), Federal Student Aid.
Authority for Conducting the Matching Program:
Authorities governing the eligibility determinations and uses of data under the matching agreement include section 1902(xx) of the Social Security Act, as added by section 71119 of
Public Law 119-21
; sections 1331, 1401, 1402, 1411, and 1412 of the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act, as applicable;
26 U.S.C. 36B
and
5000A(f)
; and implementing regulations, including
45 CFR 155.302
and
155.305
. Section 1902(xx) requires applicable individuals to demonstrate community engagement as a condition of Medicaid eligibility and requires States to use reliable information available to determine whether individuals have fulfilled community engagement requirements.
Purpose(s):
The purpose of the matching program is to assist CMS and State-based Administering Entities (AEs) in determining eligibility for Insurance Affordability Programs, specifically Medicaid, by verifying whether an applicant or enrollee is enrolled in a postsecondary educational institution. CMS and State AEs will use ED match results to verify educational enrollment for purposes of determining Medicaid eligibility based on satisfaction of community engagement requirements, if applicable. CMS may make ED match results available to State-based AEs through the CMS Federal Data Services Hub or a similar platform.
Categories of Individuals:
The individuals whose information will be used in the matching program are individuals who apply for eligibility determinations for Medicaid or another Insurance Affordability Program for whom CMS or a State-based AE needs to verify enrollment in a postsecondary educational institution.
Categories of Records:
The categories of records that will be used in the matching program are identifying records which includes: Social Security number (required); first name (required); middle name or initial, if provided; surname/last name (required); date of birth (required); and transaction ID (required).
When ED is authorized to disclose information and a matching request is made, ED will provide a response to the Hub containing current and historical enrollment data for the two years prior to the request date, including: OPEID; school name; enrollment status (including, but not limited to, full-time, half-time, less than half-time, graduated, and withdrawn); enrollment start date; enrollment end date; certification date; anticipated graduation date; and transaction ID. An error or coded response will be returned when there is no match on the student or no enrollment record for the relevant period.
System(s) of Records:
The records used in this matching program will be disclosed from the following systems of records, as authorized by routine uses published in the System of Records Notices (SORNs) cited below:
A. System of Records Maintained by CMS
The Health Insurance Exchanges (HIX) Program, System No. 09-70-0560, last published in full at
78 FR 63211
(Oct. 23, 2013), and partially amended at
83 FR 6591
(Feb. 14, 2018).
B. System of Records Maintained by ED
The National Student Loan Data System (NSLDS), System No. 18-11-06, last fully published at
91 FR 21480
(Apr. 22, 2026).

AGENCY:
The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).
ACTION:
Proposed rule.
SUMMARY:
The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is proposing to approve a request from Alaska to revise the boundary designation of the existing Fairbanks North Star Borough nonattainment area for the 2006 primary 24-hour fine particulate matter (PM
2.5
) National Ambient Air Quality Standard (NAAQS). The EPA is proposing to split the existing nonattainment area into two distinct nonattainment areas, an area covering Fairbanks and the Goldstream Valley, and an area covering North Pole. The proposed new areas cover the same geographic area as the existing area. The EPA is also proposing to issue a clean data determination (CDD), for the proposed Fairbanks and Goldstream Valley area (“proposed Fairbanks nonattainment area”) based on a determination that the area is attaining the 2006 PM
2.5
NAAQS. If the EPA finalizes this CDD, certain Clean Air Act (CAA) requirements that apply to the proposed Fairbanks nonattainment area will be suspended for so long as the area continues to meet the 2006 24-hour PM
2.5
NAAQS. The EPA is taking this action pursuant to Clean Air Act sections 107, 110, 172, and 189.

Throughout this document, the use of “we,” “us,” or “our” is intended to refer to the EPA. We use multiple abbreviations and terms in this proposed rule. While this list may not be exhaustive, for ease of reading and for reference purposes, the EPA defines the following terms and acronyms here:
Alaska DEC Alaska Department of Environmental Conservation

Table of Contents
I. Executive Summary
A. What action is the EPA taking?
B. What is the legal authority and what are the requirements?
