I. Executive Summary
A. What action is the EPA taking?
The EPA is proposing to approve a request from Alaska to revise the boundary designation of the Fairbanks North Star Borough nonattainment area for the 2006 primary 24-hour PM
2.5
NAAQS.
[
1
]
The Agency is proposing to split the existing nonattainment area into two distinct nonattainment areas, a Fairbanks and Goldstream Valley area (“Fairbanks nonattainment area”) and a North Pole area (“North Pole nonattainment area'), that cover the same geographic area as the existing nonattainment area. The EPA is also proposing to issue a CDD for the proposed Fairbanks nonattainment area for the 2006 24-hour PM
2.5
NAAQS.
B. What is the legal authority and what are the requirements?
The EPA is proposing to revise the existing nonattainment area boundary pursuant to CAA section 107. CAA section 107(d)(3)(D) authorizes the Governor of any State to submit to the Administrator a revised designation of any area or portion thereof within the State. The Agency must approve or deny such proposed redesignation within 18 months. Under CAA section 107(d)(1)(A), any area that does not meet (or that contributes to ambient air quality in a nearby area that does not meet) the NAAQS must be designated as a nonattainment area.
The EPA is proposing the CDD pursuant to CAA sections 172 and 189 and 40 Code of
Federal Register
(CFR) 51.1015 for the proposed Fairbanks nonattainment area. These statutory and regulatory provisions authorize the Agency to suspend certain nonattainment planning obligations if a PM
2.5
nonattainment area has attained the PM
2.5
NAAQS. If finalized, the CDD would relieve the State from the
(
printed page 73501)
requirements to submit an attainment demonstration, reasonable further progress plan, quantitative milestones and quantitative milestone reports, and contingency measures until the proposed Fairbanks nonattainment area is redesignated to attainment, after which such requirements are permanently discharged; or the EPA determines that the area has re-violated the PM
2.5
NAAQS, at which time the State shall submit such attainment plan elements for the Serious nonattainment area by a future date to be determined by the Agency and announced through publication in the
Federal Register
at the time the EPA determines the area is violating the PM
2.5
NAAQS.
[
2
]
II. Background
Under CAA section 109, the EPA has established primary and secondary NAAQS for certain air pollutants (referred to as “criteria pollutants”) and conducts periodic reviews of the NAAQS to determine whether they should be revised or whether new NAAQS should be established. The primary NAAQS represent ambient air quality standards which the Agency has determined are necessary to protect the public health with an adequate margin of safety. The secondary NAAQS represent ambient air quality standards which the EPA has determined are requisite to protect the public welfare from any known or anticipated adverse effects associated with the presence of such air pollutant in the ambient air. PM
2.5
is one such NAAQS.
Following promulgation of a new or revised NAAQS, the EPA is required by CAA section 107(d)(1) to designate areas throughout the United States as attainment, nonattainment, or unclassifiable for the NAAQS. Effective December 18, 2006, the EPA revised the primary and secondary 24-hour PM
2.5
NAAQS to 35 µg/m
[
3
]
.
[
3
]
On November 13, 2009, the EPA designated a portion of the Fairbanks North Star Borough as nonattainment for the 2006 24-hour PM
2.5
NAAQS (hereafter referred to as the “existing Fairbanks nonattainment area”) upon evaluation of monitored air quality data for 2006-2008.
[
4
]
Based on the 43 μg/m
[
3
]
2006-2008 design value at the State Office Building monitoring site,
[
5
]
the Alaska Department of Environmental Conservation (Alaska DEC) and the EPA determined that a portion of the Fairbanks North Star Borough was violating the NAAQS or contained sources contributing to a violation of the NAAQS. Alaska DEC noted that exceedances of the standard occur during cold and stagnant weather patterns in the winter season and in the summer months as the result of wildfires which Alaska DEC flagged as “exceptional events” in accordance with the EPA's Exceptional Events Rule at
40 CFR 50.14
.
The ambient air monitoring network has continued to evolve since initial designation, with a focus on monitoring areas of expected maximum PM
2.5
concentrations throughout the existing Fairbanks nonattainment area.
[
6
]
In November of 2009, Alaska DEC established a multipollutant monitoring station at 907 Terminal Street in downtown Fairbanks, Alaska. This station eventually became the Fairbanks National Core multipollutant monitoring station (NCore), with an Air Quality System (AQS) site identification of 02-090-0034.
[
7
]
On March 1, 2012, Alaska DEC established a special purpose monitor near the North Pole Fire Station on Hurst Road (AQS ID: 02-090-0035).
[
8
]
Originally, this monitoring station only operated during the winter. However, measured PM
2.5
concentrations from this station indicated it was located in the area of maximum PM
2.5
concentration in the nonattainment area.
[
9
]
Therefore, on January 1, 2015, the EPA and Alaska DEC converted this monitor from a special purpose monitor to a state or local air monitoring station (SLAMS) year-round monitor. SLAMS are required by the Agency network design regulations and are used for comparison to the NAAQS.
[
10
]
In 2019, Alaska DEC established a new SLAMS PM
2.5
monitoring station to characterize expected maximum concentration in the Fairbanks and Goldstream Valley portion of the nonattainment area at the A Street location
[
11
]
(AQS ID: 02-090-0040).
[
12
]
Regarding the nonattainment planning requirements, on September 8, 2017, the EPA approved the nonattainment plan for the existing Fairbanks nonattainment area as meeting the Moderate area plan requirements under CAA section 189(a).
[
13
]
However, the area failed to attain the NAAQS by the Moderate area attainment date, so the nonattainment area was classified as a Serious nonattainment area on May 10, 2017.
[
14
]
Subsequently, on September 2, 2020, the EPA determined that the area failed to attain by the Serious area attainment date and denied the State's Serious area attainment date extension request.
[
15
]
As a result, Alaska was required to submit a revised SIP submission to meet both the Serious area attainment plan requirements and the additional requirements set forth in CAA section 189(d) by December 31, 2020.
[
16
]
Alaska submitted the revised plan on December 15, 2020 (Fairbanks 189(d) Plan). The Fairbanks 189(d) Plan updated a number of chapters of the narrative portion of the State Air Quality Control Plan, adopted and incorporated by reference into State law at 18 AAC 50.030(a).
On September 24, 2021, the EPA approved the 2013 base year emissions inventory and the PM
2.5
precursor demonstration elements of the Fairbanks Serious Plan as meeting the Serious area planning requirements.
[
17
]
In the same action, the Agency approved other plan components as SIP strengthening, including: (1) the updated Fairbanks Emergency Episode Plan
[
18
]
that the State adopted on November 18, 2020, and submitted on December 15, 2020; and (2) the regulatory control measures included in the SIP submissions on October 25, 2018, and November 28, 2018 (in addition to the December 13, 2019, submission).
[
19
]
The EPA did not determine as part of the September 24,
(
printed page 73502)
2021, approval whether these SIP strengthening components met specific nonattainment plan requirements, including control strategy requirements in CAA section 189 and
40 CFR 51.1010
or the contingency measure requirements in CAA section 172(c)(9) and
40 CFR 51.1014
.
On December 5, 2023, the EPA acted on the remaining elements required for a Serious nonattainment area that failed to attain by the Serious area attainment date, approving in part and disapproving in part the Fairbanks Serious Plan and Fairbanks 189(d) Plan.
[
20
]
On December 4, 2024, Alaska made a SIP submission (Fairbanks Revised 189(d) Plan) intended to address the nonattainment requirements that were disapproved as part of the EPA's December 5, 2023, final rule. On November 18, 2025, the EPA fully approved the nonattainment plan for the existing Fairbanks nonattainment area as meeting Serious area requirements under CAA section 189(b) and the requirements for failing to attain as a Serious area under CAA section 189(d).
[
21
]
The current applicable attainment date for the existing Fairbanks nonattainment area is December 31, 2027.
III. Summary of Alaska's Redesignation Request
On May 18, 2025, the Governor of Alaska submitted a request and accompanying supporting analysis for the EPA to revise the boundary designation of the existing Fairbanks nonattainment area.
[
22
]
Alaska requested, under CAA section 107(d)(3)(D), to revise the boundary for the existing Fairbanks nonattainment area by splitting it into two distinct nonattainment areas: a Fairbanks and Goldstream Valley area and a North Pole area.
[
23
]
The boundaries of the two areas follow the existing air quality control zone boundaries. In 2016, Alaska DEC established three air quality control zones for the purposes of implementing burn bans: a Goldstream zone located on the northwestern portion of the nonattainment area, a Fairbanks zone principally consisting of downtown Fairbanks and surrounding residential and commercial areas, and a North Pole zone principally consisting of the city of North Pole and surrounding residential areas.
[
24
]
The proposed Fairbanks nonattainment area combines the Goldstream zone and Fairbanks zone. The proposed North Pole nonattainment area consists of the North Pole zone.
The regulatory air quality monitors in the proposed Fairbanks nonattainment area demonstrate a decrease of PM
2.5
levels since 2014. The design values at the NCore and A Street monitors in the Fairbanks portion of the nonattainment area are well below the 2006 NAAQS for the 2022-2024 and 2023-2025 monitoring periods (particularly when excluding state-flagged exceedances likely due to summer wildfires). Alaska DEC has also demonstrated that the proposed Fairbanks nonattainment area does not contribute to a violation of the 2006 PM
2.5
NAAQS in the proposed North Pole nonattainment area, based on consideration of air quality data, emissions and emissions-related data, meteorology, geography/topography, and jurisdictional boundaries.
The EPA is using the technical information contained in Alaska DEC's May 18, 2026, submittal and the most recent complete, quality-assured, and certified air quality data for the 2023-2025 monitoring period to support this proposed action.
IV. Proposed Action
The Agency is proposing to take two actions. Under the authority of CAA section 107(d)(3)(D), the Agency is proposing to approve Alaska's requested revisions to the existing Fairbanks nonattainment area boundary designation to create two separate nonattainment areas that together cover the same geographic area as the existing nonattainment area. Second, pursuant to
40 CFR 51.1015
, the EPA is proposing to make a CDD for the proposed Fairbanks nonattainment area for the 2006 PM
2.5
NAAQS.
A. Revisions to the Existing Fairbanks Nonattainment Area Boundary
In determining whether to approve or deny a State's request for a revision to the designation of an area under CAA section 107(d)(3)(D), the EPA considers the same factors when the Agency initiates a revision to a designation of an area on its own motion under CAA section 107(d)(3)(A). These CAA section 107(d)(3)(A) factors include “air quality data, planning and control considerations, or any other air quality related considerations the Administrator deems appropriate.” Using CAA section 107(d)(3)(A) as a framework, the EPA considers five factors when evaluating requests under CAA section 107(d)(3)(D): air quality data, emissions and emissions-related data, meteorology, geography/topography, and jurisdictional boundaries.
If the EPA finalizes this action as proposed, the existing Fairbanks nonattainment area would be split into two distinct nonattainment areas that together cover the same geographic area as the existing area. One of the proposed separate areas, to be called the “Fairbanks nonattainment area,” would consist of the Fairbanks and Goldstream zones of the current area. The other proposed separate area, to be called the “North Pole nonattainment area,” would consist of the North Pole zone. All areas would continue to be designated nonattainment and classified as Serious for the 2006 PM
2.5
NAAQS.
CAA section 107(d)(1)(A)(i) defines “nonattainment” as “any area that does not meet (or that contributes to ambient air quality in a nearby area that does not meet)” the NAAQS. Therefore, consistent with the statute, the EPA will not redraw the boundaries of nonattainment areas where one portion of the area, though monitoring clean data, contributes to the nonattainment of another portion of the area.
1. Proposed Fairbanks Nonattainment Area for the 2006 PM
2.5
NAAQS
Based on a consideration of the information submitted by Alaska and other available information discussed in the EPA's technical support document (TSD) included in the docket for this action, the Agency is proposing to find that the air quality data, emissions and emissions-related data, meteorology, geography/topography, jurisdictional boundaries, other air quality related considerations, as well as planning and control considerations, support the State's request to revise the existing Fairbanks nonattainment area boundary.
Alaska's May 18, 2026, submittal requested that the EPA split the Fairbanks nonattainment area for the 2006 PM
2.5
NAAQS and create a distinct nonattainment area for the Fairbanks and Goldstream portion of the existing nonattainment area.
[
25
]
In this action, the Agency is proposing to revise the existing nonattainment area boundary and create two separate nonattainment areas, acknowledging the differences in the factors contributing to PM
2.5
levels
(
printed page 73503)
in the separate areas, and thus providing Alaska DEC with additional flexibility in meeting the CAA's nonattainment area planning and emissions control requirements. This includes the ability to account for differences in air quality in the separate areas in the event that one of the new, separate areas attains the PM
2.5
standards faster than the other.
The EPA proposes in this action that, based on consideration of the five CAA section 107(d)(3)(A) factors, the proposed Fairbanks nonattainment area does not contribute to a violation of the 2006 PM
2.5
NAAQS in the proposed North Pole nonattainment area, and thus it is appropriate that the two areas be considered separate for implementation and planning purposes. An analysis of the five factors and a weight-of-evidence approach supports this conclusion. The air quality data in the proposed Fairbanks nonattainment area indicate that the 2022-2024 and 2023-2025 design values are below the 2006 PM
2.5
NAAQS.
[
26
]
An analysis of emissions data, considering meteorological and geographical/topographical factors, support the conclusion that the emissions from this area are not contributing to the violations in the proposed North Pole nonattainment area. A detailed analysis supporting this demonstration may be found in the TSD in the docket for this action.
Because this action also proposes to find that the proposed Fairbanks nonattainment area is attaining the 2006 PM
2.5
NAAQS, it is not necessary to consider whether the proposed North Pole nonattainment area contributes to a violation of the 2006 PM
2.5
NAAQS in the proposed Fairbanks nonattainment area, as no such violation exists.
2. Proposed North Pole Nonattainment Area for the 2006 PM
2.5
NAAQS
The Agency is proposing to approve Alaska's request to create a distinct nonattainment area for the North Pole portion of the current nonattainment area based on air quality data, emissions and emissions-related data, meteorology, geography/topography, jurisdictional boundaries, other air quality related considerations, as well as planning and control considerations.
The air quality data in the proposed North Pole nonattainment area remains above the 2006 PM
2.5
NAAQS. However, the proposed North Pole nonattainment area does not contribute to a violation of the 2006 PM
2.5
NAAQS in the proposed Fairbanks nonattainment area. Likewise, based on consideration of the five CAA section 107(d)(3)(A) factors, the proposed Fairbanks nonattainment area does not contribute to a violation of the 2006 PM
2.5
NAAQS in the proposed North Pole nonattainment area. Thus, it is appropriate that the two areas be considered separate for implementation and planning purposes. An analysis of the five recommended factors and a weight-of-evidence approach supports this conclusion.
B. Clean Data Determination for the Proposed Fairbanks Nonattainment Area
As determined in accordance with
40 CFR 50.18
and Appendix N to 40 CFR part 50, an area is attaining the 2006 PM
2.5
NAAQS if it meets the 2006 PM
2.5
NAAQS, based on three complete, consecutive calendar years of quality-assured air quality data for all monitoring sites in the area. To attain the 2006 24-hour PM
2.5
NAAQS, the three-year average of the annual 98th percentile of the daily 24-hour average PM
2.5
concentrations (PM
2.5
design values) at each site must not exceed 35 µg/m
[
3
]
.
[
27
]
The air quality data must be collected and quality-assured in accordance with
40 CFR part 58
and recorded in the EPA's Air Quality System (AQS.)
[
28
]
Ambient air quality monitoring data for the three-year period must also meet data completeness requirements.
[
29
]
A 24-hour PM
2.5
design value is valid if quarterly data capture rates for all four quarters in each year of the three-year period are at least 75 percent.
[
30
]
However, years shall be considered valid, notwithstanding quarters with less than complete data (even quarters with less than 11 creditable samples, but at least one creditable sample must be present for the year), if the resulting annual 98th percentile value or resulting 24-hour NAAQS design value (rounded according to the conventions of section 4.3 of Appendix N) is greater than the level of the standard. Furthermore, where the explicit 75 percent quarterly data capture requirement is not met, the 24-hour PM
2.5
NAAQS design value shall still be considered valid if it passes the maximum quarterly value data substitution test.
[
31
]
According to the EPA's AQS air quality monitor data in the proposed Fairbanks nonattainment area, the 2023-2025 design value at the A Street monitor is 35 µg/m
[
3
]
and the NCore monitor is 34 µg/m
[
3
]
.
[
32
]
These design values include all air quality data and do not include potential data that could be approved by the EPA for treatment as Exceptional Events (in this case, monitoring data influenced by summer wildfires). The design value from the prior 3-year period, 2022-2024, at the A Street monitor was 26 µg/m
[
3
]
and the NCore monitor was 24 µg/m
[
3
]
, when removing all monitor data that the State determined were influenced by summer wildland fires.
[
33
]
The 2023-2025 design values at the A Street monitor is 25 µg/m
3
and NCore monitor is 24 µg/m
3
, after excluding state-flagged data that is influenced by summer wildfires. Therefore, based on recent year 3-year design values below the 35 µg/m
3
24-hour PM
2.5
NAAQS, the EPA proposes to find that the proposed Fairbanks nonattainment area will have attained the 2006 24-hour PM
2.5
NAAQS, and proposes to issue a CDD based on the most recent air quality data at monitors located in the proposed Fairbanks nonattainment area. This proposed action is consistent with the Agency's clean data requirements for PM
2.5
Serious nonattainment areas established in
40 CFR 51.1015
. If finalized, this CDD would relieve the requirements for the State to submit an attainment demonstration, reasonable further progress plan, quantitative milestones and quantitative milestone reports, and contingency measures for the proposed Fairbanks nonattainment area, in accordance with
40 CFR 51.1015(b)
.
C. Summary
This action proposes to revise the boundary of an existing PM
2.5
nonattainment area by splitting it into two separate nonattainment areas that together cover the same geographic area as the existing nonattainment area. This action also proposes to make a CDD for the 2006 24-hour PM
2.5
NAAQS based on air quality data for one of those proposed areas—the proposed Fairbanks nonattainment area. If the EPA finalizes the boundary revision for the Fairbanks nonattainment area and finalizes the
(
printed page 73504)
proposed CDD for that area, then the EPA will suspend requirements to submit certain plan requirements to attain the 2006 24-hour PM
2.5
NAAQS, so long as the area continues to attain the standard. These actions do not impose additional requirements.
V. Transportation Conformity Implementation
Transportation conformity is required under CAA section 176(c) to ensure that federally funded or approved highway and transit activities are consistent with (“conform to”) the purpose of the SIP.
[
34
]
The EPA notes for informational purposes that, if this proposal is finalized, when Alaska submits a PM
2.5
control strategy SIP or maintenance plan that addresses either of the two proposed, separate areas, such a SIP would need to include separate motor vehicle emissions budget(s) that apply to the new geographic boundaries for use in transportation conformity. The EPA intends to work with the State and the Fairbanks metropolitan planning organization to provide additional technical assistance for transportation conformity purposes prior to adequate or approved budgets being available for the proposed new, separate nonattainment area boundaries. The EPA notes that the Agency is providing this information to provide additional background for this rulemaking; the Agency is not proposing changes to the transportation conformity regulation in this rulemaking.
VI. Statutory and Executive Order Reviews
This action proposes to revise the boundary of an existing PM
2.5
nonattainment area by splitting it into two separate nonattainment areas that together cover the same geographic area as the existing nonattainment area. It also proposes to make a CDD for the proposed Fairbanks nonattainment area, which if finalized would suspend the requirement to submit certain attainment plan requirements for the 2006 24-hour PM
2.5
NAAQS. This proposed action does not impose additional requirements. For that reason, this action:
Is not a significant regulatory action subject to review by the Office of Management and Budget under
Executive Order 12866
(
58 FR 51735
, October 4, 1993);
Is not subject to
Executive Order 14192
(
90 FR 9065
, February 6, 2025) because SIP actions are exempt from review under
Executive Order 12866
;
Does not impose an information collection burden under the provisions of the Paperwork Reduction Act (
44 U.S.C. 3501
et seq.
);
Is certified as not having a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities under the Regulatory Flexibility Act (
5 U.S.C. 601

Assessment
Pursuant to section 751(a)(2)(C) of the Act and
19 CFR 351.212(b)

For entries of subject merchandise during the POR produced by GARMCO for which GARMCO did not know that the merchandise was destined to the United States, we will instruct CBP to liquidate those entries at the all-others rate in the
Final Determination

. If a timely summons is filed at the U.S. Court of International Trade, the assessment instructions will direct CBP not to liquidate relevant entries until the time for parties to file a request for a statutory injunction has expired,
i.e.,

Cash Deposit Requirements
The following cash deposit requirements will be effective for all shipments of the subject merchandise entered, or withdrawn from warehouse, for consumption on or after the publication date of the final results of
(
printed page 73558)
this administrative review, as provided by section 751(a)(2)(C) of the Act: (1) the cash deposit rate for GARMCO will be equal to the company-specific weighted-average dumping margin established in the final results of the review; (2) for merchandise exported by companies not covered in this review but covered in a prior segment of this proceeding, the cash deposit rate will continue to be the company-specific rate published in the completed segment for the most recent period; (3) if the exporter is not a firm covered in this review or a prior segment of the proceeding (
e.g.,
the LTFV investigation) but the producer is, then the cash deposit rate will be the rate established in the completed segment for the most recent period for the producer of the merchandise; and (4) the cash deposit rate for all other producers and exporters will continue to be 4.83 percent, the all-others rate established in the LTFV investigation.

Failure to comply with this requirement could result in Commerce's presumption that reimbursement of antidumping and/or countervailing duties occurred and the subsequent assessment of double antidumping duties, and/or an increase in the amount of antidumping duties by the amount of the countervailing duties.

This notice also serves as a final reminder to parties subject to the APO of their responsibility concerning the return or destruction of proprietary information disclosed under APO in accordance with
19 CFR 351.305(a)(3)

Notification to Interested Parties

Take notice that on October 30, 2026, Delfin LNG LLC (Delfin) requested that the Commission grant an extension of time, until September 28, 2030, to construct and place into service certain onshore metering, compression, and piping facilities located in Cameron Parish, Louisiana (Onshore Facilities or Project)
[
1
]
that will be used solely to transport natural gas to Delfin's planned Deepwater Port as authorized in the Order Issuing Certificate, Granting Abandonment, and on Clarification (Order).
[
2
]
The Order required Delfin to complete construction of the Project and make it available for service within two years of the date of the Order, or by September 28, 2019. The Commission has subsequently granted five extensions of time, making the current date for the Project facilities to be constructed and placed into service September 28, 2027.
[
3
]
In 2025, the Maritime Administration issued the final Deepwater Port Act license authorizing Delfin's deepwater port and the Department of Energy granted two extensions of time for Delfin to commence LNG exports, resulting in a current requirement to do so by June 1, 2031. On June 3, 2026, Delfin reached a $5 billion Final Investment Decision for the first floating LNG vessel that will be moored at the deepwater port and executed an agreement with Samsung Heavy Industries for the liquefaction technology. Because that floating LNG vessel will not be in-place at Delfin's deepwater port until 2030, Delfin requests an additional three-year extension of the time for its Onshore Facilities to be constructed and placed in service by September 28, 2030.
This notice establishes a 15-calendar day intervention and comment period deadline. Any person wishing to comment on Delfin's request for an extension of time may do so. No reply comments or answers will be considered. If you wish to obtain legal status by becoming a party to the proceedings for this request, you should, on or before the comment date stated below, file a motion to intervene in accordance with the requirements of the Commission's Rules of Practice and Procedure (
18 CFR 385.214
or
385.211
) and the Regulations under the Natural Gas Act (NGA) (
18 CFR 157.10
).
As a matter of practice, the Commission itself generally acts on requests for extensions of time to complete construction for NGA facilities when such requests are contested before order issuance. For those extension requests that are contested,
[
4
]
the Commission will aim to issue an order acting on the request within 45 days.
[
5
]
The Commission will address all arguments relating to whether the applicant has demonstrated there is good cause to grant the extension.
[
6
]
The Commission will not consider arguments that re-litigate the issuance of the certificate order, including whether the Commission properly found the project to be in the public convenience and necessity and whether the Commission's environmental analysis for the certificate complied with the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA).
[
7
]
At the time a pipeline requests an extension of time, orders on certificates of public convenience and necessity are final and the Commission will not re-litigate their issuance.
[
8
]
The Director of the Office of Energy Projects, or his or her designee, will act on all of those extension requests that are uncontested.

On September 10, 2026, Great River Hydro, LLC filed an application for a temporary variance from minimum flows under Article 401 for the Fifteen Mile Falls Hydroelectric Project No. 2077. The project is located on the Connecticut River in Grafton County, New Hampshire, and Caledonia County, Vermont. The project does not occupy federal lands.
Due to unusually low precipitation and river flow, Great River Hydro, LLC plans to reduce minimum flows from the Comerford Development, beginning on the date when the Moore reservoir drops two feet below its historic minimum operating level and upstream flow forecasts are below the required minimum flow, and ending on December 31, 2026. A variance in the minimum flows required by Article 401 is necessary to preserve the depleted storage capacity of its upstream Moore reservoir. The variance will allow the licensee to decrease the seasonal minimum flows of 818 cubic feet per second (cfs) from June 1 to September 30, and 1,145 cfs from October 1 to March 31, to 600 cfs. On September 17, 2026, the Commission issued a public notice, soliciting for comments, motions to intervene, and protests. On October 19, 2026, Vermont Department of Environmental Conservation filed a motion to intervene.
This notice identifies Commission staff's intention to prepare an environmental assessment (EA) under the National Environmental Policy Act (
42 U.S.C. 4321
et seq.

Commission staff plans to issue an EA by December 30, 2026. Revisions to the schedule may be made as appropriate. The EA will be issued for a 30-day comment period. All comments filed on the EA will be reviewed by staff and considered in the Commission's final decision on the proceeding.

SUMMARY:
The Coast Guard will enforce a special local regulation to provide for the safety of life on navigable waterways during the Seminole Hard Rock Winterfest Holiday Boat Parade. Our regulation for marine events within the Captain of the Port Miami identifies the regulated area for this event in Fort Lauderdale, FL. All non-participant persons and vessels are prohibited from entering, transiting, anchoring, or remaining within the regulated area during the enforcement period unless authorized by the Captain of the Port Miami or a designated representative. The operator of any vessel in the regulated area must comply with directions from the Coast Guard or designated representative.
DATES:

33 CFR 100.702
will be enforced for the location identified in Item 11 of Table 1 to § 100.702 on December 12, 2026, from 1:30 p.m. through 11:30 p.m.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
If you have questions about this notification of enforcement, call or email MST2 Elliot Cortes, Sector Miami Waterways Management Division, U.S. Coast Guard; Telephone: 786-295-9051, Email:
SectorMiamiWaterways@uscg.mil
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The Coast Guard will enforce a special local regulation published in
33 CFR 100.702
, Item 11 of Table 1 to § 100.702, for the Seminole Hard Rock Winterfest Holiday Boat Parade on December 12, 2026, from 1:30 p.m. to 11:30 p.m. This action is being taken to provide for the safety and security of certain navigable waters within the New River and Atlantic Intracoastal Waterway during this one-day event. Our regulation for marine events within the Seventh Coast Guard District, Item 11 of Table 1 to § 100.702, specifies the location of the regulated area for the Seminole Hard Rock Winterfest Holiday Boat Parade which includes a moving buffer zone of 50 yards around the parade as it travels along the New River and Intracoastal Waterway in Fort Lauderdale, FL. Only event sponsor designated participants and official patrol vessels may enter the regulated area. Spectator vessels may contact the Coast Guard Patrol Commander to request permission to pass through the regulated area. In addition to this notification of enforcement in the

, the Coast Guard plans to provide notification of this enforcement period via the Local Notice to Mariners and marine information broadcasts at least 24 hours in advance of the enforcement of the special local regulation.

SUMMARY:

Background
EASA, which is the Technical Agent for the Member States of the European Union, has issued EASA AD 2026-0002, dated January 12, 2026 (EASA AD 2026-0002) (also referred to as the MCAI), to correct an unsafe condition for all Dassault Aviation Model FALCON 6X airplanes. Airplanes with an original airworthiness certificate or original export certificate of airworthiness issued after November 17, 2025, must comply with the airworthiness limitations specified as part of the approved type design and referenced on the type certificate data sheet; this proposed AD therefore does not include those airplanes in the applicability. The MCAI states that new or more restrictive airworthiness limitations have been developed.
The FAA is proposing this AD to address reduced structural integrity and reduced control of the airplane due to the failure of system components. You may examine the MCAI in the AD docket at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2026-13815.
Material Incorporated by Reference Under
1 CFR Part 51
EASA AD 2026-0002 specifies new or more restrictive airworthiness limitations for airplane structures and safe life limits.
This material is reasonably available because the interested parties have access to it through their normal course of business or by the means identified in the
ADDRESSES
section.
FAA's Determination
These products have been approved by the civil aviation authority of another country and are approved for operation in the United States. Pursuant to the FAA's bilateral agreement with this State of Design Authority, that authority has notified the FAA of the unsafe condition described in the MCAI referenced above. The FAA is issuing this NPRM after determining that the unsafe condition described previously is likely to exist or develop in other products of the same type design.
Proposed AD Requirements in This NPRM
This proposed AD would require revising the existing maintenance or inspection program, as applicable, to incorporate new or more restrictive airworthiness limitations, which are specified in EASA AD 2026-0002 described previously, as incorporated by reference. Any differences with EASA AD 2026-0002 are identified as exceptions in the regulatory text of this proposed AD.
This proposed AD would require revisions to certain operator maintenance documents to include new actions (
e.g.,
inspections) and Critical Design Configuration Control Limitations (CDCCLs). Compliance with these actions and CDCCLs is required by
14 CFR 91.403(c)
. For airplanes that have been previously modified, altered, or repaired in the areas addressed by this proposed AD, the operator may not be able to accomplish the actions described in the revisions. In this situation, to comply with
14 CFR 91.403(c)
, the operator must request approval for an alternative method of compliance (AMOC) according to paragraph (j)(1) of this proposed AD.
Explanation of Required Compliance Information
In the FAA's ongoing efforts to improve the efficiency of the AD process, the FAA developed a process to use some civil aviation authority (CAA) ADs as the primary source of information for compliance with requirements for corresponding FAA ADs. The FAA has been coordinating this process with manufacturers and CAAs. As a result, the FAA proposes to incorporate EASA AD 2026-0002 by reference in the FAA final rule. This proposed AD would, therefore, require compliance with EASA AD 2026-0002 in its entirety through that incorporation, except for any differences identified as exceptions in the regulatory text of this proposed AD. Using common terms that are the same as the heading of a particular section in EASA AD 2026-0002 does not mean that operators need comply only with that section. For example, where the AD requirement refers to “all required actions and compliance times,” compliance with this AD requirement is not limited to the section titled “Required Action(s) and Compliance Time(s)” in EASA AD 2026-0002. Material required by EASA AD 2026-0002 for compliance will be available at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2026-13815 after the FAA final rule is published.
(
printed page 73485)
Airworthiness Limitation ADs Using the New Process
The FAA's process of incorporating by reference MCAI ADs as the primary source of information for compliance with corresponding FAA ADs has been limited to certain MCAI ADs (primarily those with service bulletins as the primary source of information for accomplishing the actions required by the FAA AD). However, the FAA is now expanding the process to include MCAI ADs that require a change to airworthiness limitation documents, such as airworthiness limitation sections.
For these ADs that incorporate by reference an MCAI AD that changes airworthiness limitations, the FAA requirements are unchanged. Operators must revise the existing maintenance or inspection program, as applicable, to incorporate the information specified in the new airworthiness limitation document. The airworthiness limitations must be followed according to
14 CFR 91.403(c)
and
91.409(e)
.
The previous format of the airworthiness limitation ADs included a paragraph that specified that no alternative actions (
e.g.,
inspections), intervals, or CDCCLs may be used unless the actions, intervals, and CDCCLs are approved as an AMOC in accordance with the procedures specified in the AMOC paragraph under “Additional AD Provisions.” This new format includes a “Provisions for Alternative Actions, Intervals, and CDCCLs” paragraph that does not specifically refer to AMOCs, but operators may still request an AMOC to use an alternative action, interval, or CDCCL.
Costs of Compliance
The FAA estimates that this AD, if adopted as proposed, would affect 5 airplanes of U.S. registry. The FAA estimates the following costs to comply with this proposed AD:
The FAA has determined that revising the existing maintenance or inspection program takes an average of 90 work-hours per operator, although the agency recognizes that this number may vary from operator to operator. Since operators incorporate maintenance or inspection program changes for their affected fleet(s), the FAA has determined that a per-operator estimate is more accurate than a per-airplane estimate. Therefore, the FAA estimates the average total cost per operator to be $7,650 (90 work-hours × $85 per work-hour).
Authority for This Rulemaking
Title 49 of the United States Code specifies the FAA's authority to issue rules on aviation safety. Subtitle I, section 106, describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII: Aviation Programs, describes in more detail the scope of the Agency's authority.
The FAA is issuing this rulemaking under the authority described in Subtitle VII, Part A, Subpart III, Section 44701: General requirements. Under that section, Congress charges the FAA with promoting safe flight of civil aircraft in air commerce by prescribing regulations for practices, methods, and procedures the Administrator finds necessary for safety in air commerce. This regulation is within the scope of that authority because it addresses an unsafe condition that is likely to exist or develop on products identified in this rulemaking action.
Regulatory Findings
The FAA has determined that this proposed AD would not have federalism implications under
Executive Order 13132
. This proposed AD would not have a substantial direct effect on the States, on the relationship between the national government and the States, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government.
For the reasons discussed above, I certify this proposed regulation:
(1) Is not a “significant regulatory action” under
Executive Order 12866
,
(2) Would not affect intrastate aviation in Alaska, and
(3) Would not have a significant economic impact, positive or negative, on a substantial number of small entities under the criteria of the Regulatory Flexibility Act.

SUMMARY:
The National Park Service (NPS) proposes to promulgate special regulations to allow hunting in Castle Mountains National Monument and Craters of the Moon National Monument. The regulations would recognize the authority of the States to manage wildlife while also allowing for appropriate management of hunting by the NPS to protect public health and safety, objects of historic and scientific interest that the Monuments were established to protect, and endangered or threatened species. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
Castle Mountains National Monument
On February 16, 2016, President Obama exercised authority provided in
54 U.S.C. 320301
(known as the “Antiquities Act”) to establish Castle Mountains National Monument (CAMO) for the purpose of protecting the historic and scientific objects in the Castle Mountains area, as further described in Proclamation 9394. CAMO consists of 20,920 acres and is located in the eastern Mojave Desert in northeastern San Bernardino County, California, along the Nevada state line. CAMO is bounded on three sides by Mojave National Preserve, which also is administered by the NPS. The Castle Mountains area provides a critical linkage for plants, animals, and water between two mountain ranges within the Preserve, the New York Mountains to the northwest and the Piute Mountains to the southeast. The area's high-quality desert habitat includes some of the finest Joshua tree forest in the Mojave Desert, as well as pinyon pine and juniper forest at the upper elevations. The area's native desert grassland is a hotspot of botanical diversity. The relatively intact and undisturbed habitat within CAMO connects water flow and wildlife corridors of the Preserve and its habitat is important to the long-term survival of significant wildlife populations, including a herd of desert bighorn sheep that lives on the steep, rocky slopes of the Castle Mountains. They and other wildlife traverse the area between the Piute Mountains and the New York Mountains. Numerous bat species live in rock crevices and mine remnants in the area. Wildlife species of special concern include the Townsend's big-eared bat, California leaf-nosed bat, Swainson's hawk, golden eagle, desert tortoise, Bendire's thrasher, and gray vireo. CAMO contains cultural resources that reflect a long history of prehistoric and historic human use, including prehistoric rock art and archeological sites. Within the external boundaries of CAMO is an area referred to as the “Castle Mountain Mine Area,” which contains a commercial mining operation. This area is administered by the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) and mining activities are governed by a plan of operations issued by BLM.
Hunting is currently prohibited within CAMO by NPS regulations in
36 CFR 2.2
, which prohibit hunting in units of the National Park System except where specifically mandated or authorized by Federal statutory law, which does not exist for CAMO.
Craters of the Moon National Monument
President Calvin Coolidge exercised authority provided by the Antiquities Act to establish Craters of the Moon National Monument (CRMO) on May 2, 1924, for the purpose of protecting the unusual landscapes of the Craters of the Moon Lava Field, as further described in Proclamation 1694. CRMO is located in south central Idaho in Blaine and Butte counties. As further described in Proclamation 1694, the “lunar” landscape within CRMO was thought to resemble that of the moon and was described in the presidential proclamation as “a weird and scenic landscape peculiar to itself.” Presidential Proclamations issued in 1928 (Proclamation 1843), 1930 (Proclamation 1916), 1941 (Proclamation 2499), and 1962 (Proclamation 3506) made minor boundary adjustments, as did Section 205 of the Omnibus Parks and Public Lands Management Act of 1996 (
Public Law 104-333
). On November 9, 2000, President Clinton issued Proclamation 7373 which expanded CRMO from roughly 54,000 acres to approximately 753,000 acres to ensure protection of the Great Rift volcanic rift zone and its associated features. The expanded monument includes almost all the features of basaltic volcanism, including the craters, cones, lava flows, caves, and fissures of the 65-mile-long Great Rift, a geological feature that is comparable to the great rift zones of Iceland and Hawaii. It comprises the most diverse and geologically recent part of the lava terrain that covers the southern Snake River Plain, a broad lava plain made up of innumerable basalt lava flows that erupted during the past 5 million years. Isolated islands of older terrain surrounded by new lava are known as “kipukas.” These areas represent some of the last nearly pristine and undisturbed vegetation in the Snake River Plain.
Proclamation 7373 placed lands within the expanded CRMO under the administration of both the NPS and BLM, with each agency having primary management authority over separate portions. The NPS was given primary management authority over the portion of CRMO that includes the exposed lava flows, with BLM given primary management authority over the remaining portion. On August 21, 2002,
Public Law 107-213
designated the NPS-administered portion of the monument expansion area as a National Preserve. The area within the CRMO as it existed before the 2000 expansion is referred to in this rule as the “Original CRMO.”
Public Law 107-213
requires the NPS to allow hunting within the NPS-administered National Preserve in accordance with Federal and State law, except that the NPS, in consultation with the State of Idaho, may designate zones where, and establish periods when, no hunting may be permitted for reasons of public safety, protection of resources, administration, or public use and enjoyment. Hunting also is allowed in the BLM-administered portion of CRMO pursuant to authorities applicable to BLM-administered lands. Hunting is currently prohibited within Original CRMO by NPS regulations in
36 CFR 2.2
, which prohibits hunting in units of the National Park System except where specifically mandated or authorized by Federal statutory law, which does not exist for Original CRMO.
Reinvigorating America's Hunting Heritage
On September 17, 2026, President Trump issued
Executive Order 14429
, “Reinvigorating America's Hunting Heritage,” which announced that it is a policy of the Administration to reinvigorate, protect, and expand America's hunting heritage to benefit our people and our land.
E.O. 14429
recognizes that American hunters, anglers, and landowners are the greatest conservationists the world has ever known, and that hunting promotes healthy and robust animal populations, conserves our beautiful wildlife for future generations, and ensures that every American can enjoy our rugged, diverse, and untamed frontier areas.
E.O. 14429
directs Federal agencies to institute various reforms to pull back on the Federal Government's regulatory overreach that has led to a decline in hunting opportunities, confusing and
(
printed page 73490)
inconsistent access policies, and heavy-handed restrictions on hunter education and recruitment efforts.
E.O. 14429
reverses this overreach by applying a presumption of accessibility to federally managed lands so that the next generation of Americans shall once again have the opportunity to share in our Nation's rich sporting heritage. Consistent with these policies, Section 2(a) of
E.O. 14429
states that within 90 days the Secretary of the Interior is directed to allow for hunting of species that are not subject to
16 U.S.C. 1533
(the Endangered Species Act) within CAMO and Original CRMO.
E.O. 14429
states that President Trump has determined that appropriately managed hunting would not put the objects of historic and scientific interest that these monuments protect at risk.
Proposed Rule
This rule would implement the directive in Section 2(a) of
E.O. 14429
by allowing hunting within CAMO and Original CRMO. The proposed regulations for each System unit recognize the primary role of the States in managing fish and wildlife, while at the same time allowing the NPS to appropriately manage hunting, consistent with
E.O. 14429
, to meet its statutory mandates to protect resources and visitors within park areas. The NPS believes the regulations in this proposed rule would promote cooperative federalism as directed in Section 1 of
E.O. 14429
. The NPS has developed these rules in coordination with the California Department of Fish & Wildlife (CDFW) for CAMO and the Idaho Department of Fish and Game (IDFG) for Original CRMO.
Elements Common to Both Monuments
This proposed rule would establish special regulations for CAMO and Original CRMO that relax the general NPS regulatory prohibition on hunting that applies in these Monuments.
[
1
]
Special regulations for CAMO would be codified in a new § 7.98 and special regulations for Original CRMO would be codified in a new § 7.101. This rule proposes several regulatory provisions that are common to the special regulations for each Monument. Paragraph (a) would state that notwithstanding any other provision contained in this chapter, hunting shall be allowed in each Monument. This would establish that the special regulations preempt the otherwise applicable prohibition in
36 CFR 2.2
and allow hunting in each Monument. Paragraph (b) would state that where hunting is authorized, such activities shall be conducted in accordance with Federal law and the laws of the State, with the effect that State law would govern hunting in each Monument unless specifically preempted by Federal law, including NPS regulations and closures and restrictions deemed necessary by the Superintendent. Paragraph (c) would prohibit the hunting of species subject to
16 U.S.C. 1533
, notwithstanding any provision in State law. This provision implements part of the directive in Section 2(a) of
E.O. 14429
and ensures that endangered or threatened species receive the protections provided by Federal law. Paragraph (d) would allow the superintendent to establish closures, restrictions, and conditions on hunting that are the minimum necessary to prevent a significant impact to public health and safety, objects of historic and scientific interest that the Monument was established to protect, or endangered or threatened species. Except in emergencies, the Superintendent would be required to consult with appropriate State agencies, such as CDFW and IDFG, before taking those actions, and to notify the public of any such closures, restrictions or conditions through appropriate methods listed in
36 CFR 1.7
, including publication in the Superintendent's Compendium (or written compilation) of discretionary actions referred to in paragraph (b) of § 1.7. Providing the superintendents with this authority is consistent with the Federal statutory authority provided to the NPS for the administration of Mojave National Preserve, which allows the NPS, after consultation with the State except in emergencies, to designate areas where, and establish periods when no hunting, fishing, or trapping will be permitted for reasons of public safety, administration, or compliance with provisions of applicable law.
16 U.S.C. 410aaa-46
. It also is consistent with the Federal statutory authority provided to the NPS in
Public Law 107-213
for the NPS-administered Craters of the Moon National Preserve, which allows the NPS, after consultation with the State except in emergencies, to designate zones where, and establish periods when, no hunting may be permitted for reasons of public safety, protection of resources, administration, or public use and enjoyment. The similar authorities in the rule for both Monuments would allow the superintendents to respond to unforeseen circumstances that require mitigation in order to protect resources and visitors. These authorities also would help ensure that hunting in either Monument does not jeopardize the President's determination in
E.O. 14429
that hunting will not put the objects of historic and scientific interest that the Monuments protect at risk.
Mitigations Specific to Castle Mountains National Monument
In addition to regulatory provisions described above that would apply to both Monuments, this proposed rule would establish specific mitigation measures for hunting in Original CRMO that are the minimum necessary to protect resources and visitors. These mitigations were developed in coordination with CDFW.
First, the rule would prohibit hunting within 200 yards of a wildlife watering place within CAMO. “Wildlife watering place” would be defined, consistent with State law, as a waterhole, spring, seep, or a man-made watering device for wildlife such as a guzzler (a self-filling, in-the-ground water storage tank), horizontal well, or small impoundment of less than one surface acre in size. See CCR Title 14 § 730. Wildlife watering places within CAMO include natural watering holes and artificial water sources used by wildlife. This prohibition is necessary to prevent human disturbance that cuts off wildlife from scarce, life-sustaining water. Water in arid desert biomes is extremely limited. Game and non-game species—such as desert bighorn sheep, mule deer, and desert tortoises—frequently rely on isolated springs, seeps, or man-made guzzlers set up for wildlife watering. Human presence within 200 yards spooks animals away, forcing them to avoid drinking, which can cause dehydration or death. Concentrated human activities, such as hunting, within immediate riparian and waterhole zones trample fragile soil crusts, destroy native vegetative shelter, and cause contamination to limited pools of water. Finally, ambushing thirsty animals concentrated around artificial or natural watering holes is considered unsporting. Enforcing a 200-yard buffer prevents hunters from executing easy ambushes on distressed wildlife using vital watering holes. The second mitigation in the rule would prohibit hunting within one mile of the Castle Mountain Mine. This prohibition is necessary to protect the safety of employees of the mine. The rule would state that these mitigations do not prevent an individual from retrieving lawfully taken wildlife from within the restricted areas, provided the wildlife
(
printed page 73491)
was not otherwise hunted within those areas. Penalizing this conduct would not further the policy purpose of the restrictions, which is to protect wildlife while using those places for survival.
Mitigations Specific to Craters of the Moon National Monument
In addition to regulatory provisions described above that would apply to both Monuments, this rule would establish specific mitigation measures for hunting in Original CRMO that are the minimum necessary to protect resources and visitors. These mitigations were developed in coordination with IDFG.
First, the rule would prohibit the use of weapons other than short range weapons, which would be defined consistent with State law as (1) any shotgun using any slug or double-aught (#00) or larger buckshot; (2) any muzzleloader that is at least forty-five (0.45) caliber for deer, pronghorn, mountain lion, or gray wolf, or at least fifty (0.50) caliber for elk, moose, bighorn sheep, mountain goat, or black bear; (3) any bow having a peak draw weight of not less than forty (40) pounds up to or at a draw of twenty-eight (28) inches; (4) any crossbow having a peak draw weight of not less than one hundred fifty (150) pounds; (5) any handgun using straight wall centerfire cartridges not originally developed for rifles; (6) any airgun using pre-charged pneumatic power to propel a projectile (excluding shot and arrows) with unignited compressed air or gas and projectiles at least thirty-five (0.35) caliber for deer and pronghorn antelope or at least forty-five (0.45) caliber for elk and moose. See IAC 13.01.08.407. Other weapons, such as modern centerfire rifles, have effective ranges of hundreds of yards, and projectiles can travel considerably farther. The open nature of the Original CRMO landscape provides relatively few natural backstops or other obstructions to reduce the risk posed by errant rounds. Because the definition is codified in State law, the NPS believes this restriction will be relatively straightforward to communicate to hunters. Prohibiting centerfire rifles and other long-range weapons would substantially reduce concerns about the safety of visitors and NPS employees and volunteers.
Second, the rule would prohibit hunting in NPS-administered areas in the Original CRMO located north and northwest of Highway 20/93. This area is currently restricted to administrative use and contains two developed areas, the Yurt Campground and Administrative Campground, both of which receive substantial use by NPS personnel, partners, and cooperators throughout the year, including during the fall hunting season. The area also contains critical park infrastructure, including the park's entire potable water system and associated wellheads, electrical distribution infrastructure, a photovoltaic solar array, a pumphouse, and a chlorinator building. Additionally, the area contains numerous sensitive archeological sites and a historic trail listed on the National Register. The area's relatively narrow, linear configuration, combined with the concentration of developed facilities, critical infrastructure, sensitive cultural resources, and ongoing administrative activities, presents significant challenges and risks to safely accommodate recreational hunting. At approximately 5,000 acres, this area represents less than 10% of the total acreage that would otherwise be available to hunting under the proposed rule. Accordingly, the prohibition would provide substantial protection for park operations and resources while imposing a relatively modest limitation on the overall hunting opportunities that would be authorized elsewhere within the Monument.
Compliance With Other Laws, Executive Orders, and Department Policy
Regulatory Planning and Review (Executive Orders 12866 and 14192)
This rule has been determined to be significant for purposes of
Executive Order 12866
. This proposed rule is expected to have minor economic effects. It would generate benefits for current and potential hunters by authorizing hunting in two NPS-administered Monuments for the first time, subject to appropriate management. However, these Monuments represent a relatively small portion of the lands currently available for hunting in the surrounding areas. Hunting is already authorized on hundreds of thousands of acres of adjacent BLM- and NPS-administered lands surrounding Craters of the Moon National Monument and on more than one million acres of NPS-administered lands surrounding Castle Mountains National Monument. Further, no changes to State hunting seasons or tag quotas for specific species are anticipated. As a result, this action is expected to have minimal effects on overall hunter-days in the areas, but may increase the value of the hunting experience by providing hunters with additional locations in which to hunt.
This proposed rule could impose costs on some current non-hunting visitors due to noise or other adverse effects associated with allowing this new use. However, these costs are expected to be minimal due to mitigations such as restrictions on types of weapons and distance restrictions from populated areas. The NPS may experience a small increase in costs associated with implementation and enforcement.
This rule is a “one-time” enabling regulation that would expand consumption options for the American public by increasing opportunities for access and recreation at each Monument. As a result, this rule qualifies as an
E.O. 14192
deregulatory action pursuant to M-25-20, “Guidance Implementing Section 3 of
Executive Order 14192
, Titled `Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation' ” issued by the Office of Management and Budget, Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs, on March 26, 2025.
Regulatory Flexibility Act
This proposed rule would not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities under the Regulatory Flexibility Act (
5 U.S.C. 601
et seq.
). No small entities would be directly regulated by this rule, which would authorize hunting by the general public within each Monument, subject to appropriate management. This action is expected to have minimal effects on visitation and is not expected to adversely affect local businesses or other small entities. For these reasons, the NPS certifies that this rule would not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities; therefore, a regulatory flexibility analysis is not required.
Congressional Review Act
This proposed rule, if finalized, is not expected to be a major rule under
5 U.S.C. 804(2)
. This proposed rule:
(a) Would not have an annual effect on the economy of $100 million or more.
(b) Would not cause a major increase in costs or prices for consumers, individual industries, Federal, State, or local government agencies, or geographic regions.
(c) Would not have significant adverse effects on competition, employment, investment, productivity, innovation, or the ability of U.S.-based enterprises to compete with foreign-based enterprises.
Unfunded Mandates Reform Act
Section 202 of the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (
2 U.S.C. 1531
) requires that agencies assess whether a rule would impose a Federal mandate that may result in the
(
printed page 73492)
expenditure by State, local, and Tribal governments in the aggregate, or by the private sector of $100,000,000 or more (adjusted annually for inflation) in any 1 year. As of 2025, that threshold is approximately $206 million (2024 dollars). This rule would not result in expenditures by State, local, or Tribal governments, in the aggregate, or by the private sector, in excess of the threshold. Thus, no written assessment of unfunded mandates is required.”
Takings (
Executive Order 12630
)
This proposed rule would not effect a taking of private property or otherwise have takings implications under
Executive Order 12630
. A takings implication assessment is not required.
Federalism (
Executive Order 13132
)
Under the criteria in section 1 of
Executive Order 13132
, this proposed rule would not have sufficient federalism implications to warrant the preparation of a federalism summary impact statement. This rule would only affect use of federally administered lands and waters. It would have no direct effects on other areas. A federalism summary impact statement is not required.
Civil Justice Reform (
Executive Order 12988
)
This proposed rule complies with the requirements of
Executive Order 12988
. This proposed rule:
(a) Meets the criteria of section 3(a) requiring that all regulations be reviewed to eliminate errors and ambiguity and be written to minimize litigation; and
(b) Meets the criteria of section 3(b)(2) requiring that all regulations be written in clear language and contain clear legal standards.
Consultation With Indian Tribes (
Executive Order 13175
and Department Policy)
The Department of the Interior strives to strengthen its government-to-government relationship with Indian Tribes through a commitment to consultation with Indian Tribes and recognition of their right to self-governance and Tribal sovereignty. The NPS has evaluated this proposed rule under the criteria in
Executive Order 13175
and under the Department's consultation policy and has concluded that this rule would not have substantial direct effects on Indian Tribes. Cultural resources staff at CRMO have provided
Executive Order 14429
to the Shoshone-Bannock Tribes of Fort Hall and the Shoshone-Paiute Tribes of the Duck Valley Reservation for their awareness. Staff will also send formal consultation letters to consulting tribes, which consist of the two aforementioned tribes and the Northwestern Band of the Shoshone Nation, to initiate consultation pursuant to Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act. The Superintendent of CRMO has met with the Shoshone-Bannock Tribes of Fort Hall's Section 106 representative to discuss any concerns the Tribe may have regarding treaty rights under the Fort Bridger Treaty of 1868. The tribal liaison for CAMO will meet with the Fort Mojave and Chemehuevi tribes to inform them of this proposed rule and the opportunity for comment.
Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (
44 U.S.C. 3501
et seq.
)
This proposed rule contains no new information collections. All information collections require approval under the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (PRA;
44 U.S.C. 3501
et seq.
). The NPS may not conduct or sponsor, and you are not required to respond to a collection of information unless it displays a currently valid OMB control number.
National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (NEPA;
42 U.S.C. 4321
et seq.
)
The NPS does not expect a detailed statement under the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (NEPA) would be required because the NPS anticipates that the rule would be covered by a categorical exclusion and will not involve any of the extraordinary circumstances listed in
43 CFR 46.215
that would require further analysis under NEPA. The NPS will document the application of a categorical exclusion to this rule if applicable.
Effects on the Energy Supply (
Executive Order 13211
)
This proposed rule is not a significant energy action under the definition in
Executive Order 13211
; this proposed rule is not likely to have a significant adverse effect on the supply, distribution, or use of energy, and this proposed rule has not otherwise been designated by the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs as a significant energy action. A Statement of Energy Effects in not required.
Public Comment Period
Department of the Interior policy states that the bureaus should allow at least 60 calendar days for public comments on proposed rules but that shorter periods may be used in special cases requiring more timely action. 318 DM HB Section 5.4. The NPS has determined that the direction in Section 2(a) of
E.O. 14429
that the NPS allow hunting in the Monuments within 90 days of the date of the order is a special case that requires more timely action.
E.O. 14429
was issued on September 17, 2026. A 60-day comment period would leave only 15 days to develop and complete internal review and approval of the proposed and final rules, including public comment analysis, and publish each in the
Federal Register
. This would be an insufficient amount of time. As a result, the NPS has shortened the public comment period to 30 days in order to complete the rulemaking process in a sufficient and timely manner.

§ 7.98
Castle Mountains National Monument.

Hunting.

State law.

(1) Hunting species subject to

(3) Hunting within one mile of the Castle Mountain Mine.

Craters of the Moon National Monument.

State law.

16 U.S.C. 1533
is prohibited.
(2) The use of a weapon other than a short-range weapon is prohibited. For purposes of this § 7.101, a short-range weapon is:
(i) Any shotgun using any slug or double-aught (#00) or larger buckshot.
(ii) Any muzzleloader that is at least forty-five (0.45) caliber for deer, pronghorn, mountain lion, or gray wolf, or at least fifty (0.50) caliber for elk, moose, bighorn sheep, mountain goat, or black bear.

AGENCY:
U.S. Small Business Administration.
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
This final rule makes several changes to the U.S. Small Business Administration (SBA) Surety Bond Guarantee (SBG) program regulations. The rule reduces the burden on participating surety companies for submission and retention of documents. The rule also corrects conflicting provisions, as well as revising the obsolete Preferred Surety admissions requirements and the Quarterly Contract Completion Report.
DATES:
This rule is effective January 15, 2027.
