SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background Information
SBA is amending several regulations applicable to its Surety Bond Guarantee (SBG) program. SBA guarantees bid, payment, and performance bonds for small and emerging contractors who cannot obtain surety bonds through regular commercial channels. SBA's guarantee, authorized pursuant to part B of title IV of the Small Business Investment Act of 1958,
15 U.S.C. 694a
et seq.,
gives Sureties an incentive to provide bonding for small businesses and thereby assists small businesses in obtaining greater access to contracting opportunities. SBA's guarantee is an agreement between a Surety and SBA that SBA will assume a certain percentage of the Surety's loss should a contractor default on the underlying contract.
As part of its ongoing responsibility to ensure that the rules it issues align with surety industry practices and do not have an adverse economic impact on those affected by those rules, SBA held a series of listening sessions with Surety professionals for input about their experiences using the SBG program. Findings of the listening sessions and additional impact studies resulted in the decision to change and clarify several procedures and regulations to improve customer experience and better enable modernization efforts within the SBG program. SBA published a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking in the
Federal Register
on November 19, 2024 (
89 FR 91284
).
II. Summary of Comments Received
On January 21, 2025, the notice of proposed rulemaking comment period ended. SBA received 18 comments to the notice of proposed rulemaking, of which 2 were beyond the scope of the notice for proposed rulemaking (NPRM) and 1 strictly addressed a grammatical concern. Of the 15 unique comments received, 2 were national trade associations, 3 were surety companies and agencies, 5 were individual surety professionals, and 5 were anonymous individuals. The 2 comments beyond the scope of the NPRM were from anonymous individuals, as well as the 1 grammatical comment.
Public comments received regarding the proposed changes will be addressed in the Section-by-Section Analysis. Of the 15 comments received in direct response to the proposals, 12 entirely supported, 2 partially supported, and 1 opposed the changes set forth in the notice of proposed rulemaking. In addition to comments on these regulations, there were also comments requesting that SBA implement policies and procedures on the guarantee percentage to women-owned small businesses (WOSBs), expansion of the Quick Bond application, support for concessionaire bonds, and expansion of SBA's role in the surety's underwriting of applications to improve opportunity and efficiencies across the Surety Bond Guarantee program.
III. Section-by-Section Analysis and Response to Comments
A. Prior Approval Agreement: § 115.11, § 115.30(b) and (d)
Sections 115.11, 115.30(b), and 115.30(d) address application submission parameters and signature requirements in the Prior Approval program. Current SBA regulation
13 CFR 115.11
requires prospective Surety Partners to submit partnership applications by mail. Current SBA regulation
13 CFR 115.30(b)
requires signature on the approval of all Prior Approval program applications. Current SBA regulation
13 CFR 115.30(d)
outlines requirements for application submission to SBA in the Prior Approval program.
This final rule adds the option to email Surety Partner application packages. Additionally, the rule adds a requirement for a Prior Approval Agreement between SBA and the Prior Approval Surety Partner that will contain a master certification for all the applications to follow and changes language from “signed” documents to “executed” documents. The agreement's certification effectively removes the need for each application to be individually signed and certified by both parties. SBA estimates the new agreements will reduce application annual time burden on program participants and SBA by 692 hours, or $32,773 according to fiscal year 2024 program activity. These changes will modernize program regulations to align with current business practices and improve the customer experience of the program in alignment with agency priority goals.
In a survey, all Prior Approval participants surveyed agreed that having
(
printed page 73437)
a Surety Partner participation agreement for the Prior Approval program would greatly benefit program participants by removing SBA's requirement to individually sign and certify every application submission. Four commenters on the proposed rule expressed support for this change. One of the supporting commenters expressed concern about whether the change will impact SBA's responsibility of first-time applicant review and underwriting to establish bonding parameters. To clarify, the rule change does not change the responsibility of the Surety to review and underwrite all small business bond needs prior to SBG program submission. It also does not remove responsibility of the Surety to verify information submitted by the Principal is true, correct, and complete to the best of their knowledge. The rule change does not change SBA's review and underwriting of Prior Approval applications for eligibility and suitability in the program; however, SBA does not currently, and will not, set the Surety's bonding parameters for the small business. Sureties participating in the Prior Approval program currently, and will continue to, certify that an applicant's information is true, correct, and complete to the best of their knowledge, and that the applicant appears to have the financial management and technical abilities to successfully complete the subject contract but falls below normal underwriting standards of the Surety. All applications in the program must be submitted after the Surety's bond approval conditioned on SBA's support. No other commenters expressed concern or opposition.
B. Streamline Fee Collection Process: § 115.19(g), § 115.32(b) and (d), § 115.66, § 115.67, and § 115.14(a)(5)
Sections 115.19(g), 115.32(b), 115.32(d), 115.66 and 115.67 address fee collection requirements, while section 115.14(a)(5) addresses the consequence to the Principal if their fee is not paid. Current SBA regulation
13 CFR 115.19(g)
establishes SBA's right to deny liability when a Surety does not remit the Principal's fee payment or Surety's fee payment within the timeliness requirements set by SBA. Current SBA regulation
13 CFR 115.32(b)
requires the Principal's fee payment be submitted with the application, establishing that the fee must be received by SBA prior to SBA's final approval of the application. Current SBA regulation
13 CFR 115.32(d)
requires a Prior Approval Surety remit payment of the Principal's guarantee fee at the time of submission for an increase to an existing SBA guaranteed bond when it meets both SBA's increase threshold of 25% or $500,000 (whichever is less) and SBA's fee threshold ($250) for fee remittance. Current SBA regulation
13 CFR 115.66
requires the Principal's fee payment be submitted with the application, establishing that the fee must be received by SBA at the time of the Surety's guarantee submission to SBA. Current SBA regulation
13 CFR 115.67
requires a PSB Surety remit payment of the Principal's guarantee fee at the time of submission for an increase to an existing SBA guaranteed bond when it meets both SBA's increase threshold of 25% or $500,000 (whichever is less) and SBA's fee threshold ($250) for fee remittance. Lastly, current SBA regulation
13 CFR 115.14(a)(5)
addresses the failure of the Principal to pay their required fee and the loss of eligibility for further SBA bond guarantees.
This final rule changes the timeliness requirement of all fees to 60 calendar days, in alignment with current surety fee collection timeliness requirements. The final rule also simplifies regulatory language to clarify the current responsibility of Sureties to ensure all fees payments, including Principal fee payments, are successfully received by SBA. By making these changes, SBA better streamlines the final bond application approval process by not stalling approvals for fee payments. Additionally, the changes enable SBA to accept bulk payments of Principal fees from Sureties. The changes allow Sureties to develop their own fee collection and remittance procedures, reducing burden and better integrating program workflows with their non-SBA processes. SBA estimates the new agreements will reduce application annual time burden on program participants and SBA by 993 hours, or $39,012 according to fiscal year 2024 program activity.
In a survey, several surety professional participants stated SBA's contractor fee collection process is incongruent with surety industry practice for premium (industry fee) collection. Instead of small businesses directly paying surety bond companies for each individual premium due, surety bond companies typically bill premiums (fees) due to surety bond agencies (intermediaries) representing applicant businesses via monthly billing statements. Collection is directly from these agencies, net their commission. The agencies independently manage premium collection from applicant businesses and are responsible for payment to surety bond companies. The industry almost always issues bonds before receiving premium. Prior Approval survey participants all stated SBA's current contractor fee collection requirements delay the bonding process since payment cannot be made prior to an initial intent-to-approve from SBA and the surety bond cannot be issued until payment is made by the small business. Two participants noted a small business can sometimes take days to pay SBA's fee, which further delays the bonding process.
Seven commenters on the proposed rule expressed support for this change. Six of these commenters stated the change will save the industry time and money through reduced procedural burdens. One of these commenters stated having the option to provide subsequent SBA fee billing aligns the program with industry standards. One commenter stated the change allows small businesses to receive bond costs reimbursement from project owners prior to payment of the fee, reducing cash reserve impacts to the small business. Three commenters on the proposed rule expressed opposition to this change. All three commenters opposed the change on the basis that SBA requiring Sureties to collect fees instead of SBA could adversely impact the program by increasing the program's bad debt, confusing small businesses on who ultimately receives the payment, and reducing program participation by the surety industry due to concern for responsibility of the fees. SBA acknowledges these concerns and corrected language to reflect that this change is not requiring Sureties to directly collect the Principal's fee. The rule revisions only change the timeliness requirement of Principal fees from at the time of SBA submission to within 60 calendar days from approval in SBA's online system and clarify existing responsibility language in the regulations. The responsibility of Sureties to the federal government to ensure the timely remittance of Principal fee payments is a current requirement of participation in the SBG program. Per the current Section 115.19(g) mentioned above, failure of Principal fee remittance by the Surety is already grounds for denial of liability by SBA. Methods of ensuring successful Principal fee remittance currently used by Sureties partnered with the SBG program include direct oversight of successful payment by the small business, direct payment by the Surety, and indirect oversight (by surety agencies) of successful payment by the small business. However, the current responsibility of ensuring fee payment
(
printed page 73438)
ultimately remains with the Surety. Language simplifications on this subject do not make any changes to the current responsibility of Sureties participating in the program. The change to timeliness requirements of fee remittance enables Sureties greater flexibility in management of this responsibility. In enabling SBA to allow bulk payments in addition to the current method of individual payments through U.S. Treasury's
pay.gov
website, Sureties participating in the program will have expanded options for compliance with fee remittance requirements. SBA is not requiring direct Principal fee collection by Sureties. A Surety's procedure for compliance with ensuring successful Principal fee remittance is a program management concern outside SBA and is not restricted by this rule change beyond remittance timeliness. One commenter provided a neutral response, identifying a grammatical error in the proposed rule. The grammatical error was accepted and is corrected in this final rule.
C. Quarterly Contract Completion Report: § 115.22
Section 115.22 requires Sureties with active SBA bond guarantees to submit a quarterly contract completion report (QCCR) detailing all contracts for guaranteed bonds that were completed during the most recently completed quarter. Current SBA regulation
13 CFR 115.22
requires the QCCR report be submitted within 45 calendar days of each fiscal year quarter's end and outlines the information to be provided in the report. This final rule moves the reporting parameters and timing from regulation to a standard operating procedure (SOP). SBA managing procedures for reporting in an SOP will provide greater flexibility for bond guarantee closeout management in the program and procedural streamlining. SBA estimates the new agreements will reduce program management annual time burden on program participants and SBA by 26 hours, or $2,463 according to fiscal year 2024 program activity.
At the time the QCCR was originally implemented, the surety industry commented on the proposed rule that the report creates an administrative burden on Surety Partners. During SBA's recent survey, participants stated the industry typically considers contracts up to $250,000 complete upon the estimated completion date on file without verification. In fiscal year 2024, nearly 45% of guaranteed bonds for awarded contracts were within this range. Surety Partners for the program have stated reporting details, such as the contract completion date, can require additional work when contracts are within this range. Two commenters on the proposed rule expressed support for this change. None expressed opposition or concern.
D. Surety Bonding Line: § 115.19(f)(1)(i), § 115.33(b)(1)
Sections 115.19(f)(1)(i) and 115.33(b)(1) address SBA bond guarantees in relation to bond execution and bonding line parameters. Current SBA regulation
13 CFR 115.33(b)(1)
allows Sureties participating in SBA's Prior Approval program to submit applications up to 15 days after bond execution under an SBA-approved bonding line. However, current SBA regulation
13 CFR 115.19(f)(1)(i)
requires bonds be approved by SBA prior to execution.
This final rule reconciles the conflicting language between these two regulations to allow SBA acceptance of executed bonds under an SBA bonding line. The rule also clarifies that a bonding line expires at the end of the fiscal year in which it was approved. These changes will resolve conflicts in regulatory language and clarify that SBA bonding lines cannot extend past the originated fiscal year per allocated funding restrictions of the program. Two commenters on the proposed rule expressed support for this change. None expressed opposition or concern.
E. Revisions To Underwriting and the Preferred Surety Bond (PSB) Program: § 115.11, § 115.60, § 115.65(b)
Sections 115.11, 115.60, and 115.65(b) address requirements to participate in SBA's PSB program. Current SBA regulation
13 CFR 115.60
requires PSB-partnered Sureties maintain an underwriting limitation of $6.5 million with the U.S. Treasury Department's Circular 570 list, its premium income from federally-guaranteed contract bonds not exceed one quarter of its total contract bond premium income, and its underwriting authority of SBA-guaranteed bonds only be vested in its employees. Current SBA regulation
13 CFR 115.65(b)
requires PSB-partnered Sureties handle SBA guaranteed bonds in the same manner and with the same staff as the Surety's activity outside the PSB program.
This final rule revises SBA's selection and admission regulations for Sureties participating in the PSB program by moving the regulatory requirements for a minimum underwriting limit on U.S. Treasury's 570 Circular and the initial participation limits to an SOP. It also removes the premium income limitation of the program and expands vesting of underwriting for SBA-guaranteed bonds to a Surety's employees, its affiliates, or its PSB-authorized agencies. These changes enable SBA to approve participation in the PSB program for the size-limited Affiliates of larger Sureties and small regional Sureties, and exercise more flexibility when assessing the portfolio management structure of Sureties applying to the program. Some surety bond companies utilize Affiliates with low T-listing limits to support small specialty before moving them to surety Affiliates with higher T-listing amounts. Overall, SBA expects this to increase the number of surety partners and bond opportunities for small businesses.
Seven commenters on the proposed rule expressed support for this change. Five of these commenters stated the change will streamline program participation and decrease program burden by allowing PSB-authorized agencies to underwrite SBA-guaranteed bonds in the PSB program. No commenters expressed concern or opposition. During listening sessions, meetings, and other engagements with the surety bond industry, SBA found it is common practice in the industry to delegate bond writing authority to staff of an affiliated surety and vetted surety bond agencies. The agents in vetted surety bond agencies are vetted for their underwriting knowledge and performance in the industry in relation to their portfolio with the surety bond company delegating such authority. Agencies with this authority are referred to as “Managing General Agencies” (MGAs) and “Managing General Underwriters” (MGUs). With this authority, these entities act on behalf of the surety by performing the underwriting of a bond application and issuing the surety bond. Oftentimes, MGAs and MGUs handle large portfolios of business that normal underwriting practices make too cumbersome or time-consuming for surety bond companies to manage.
The Prior Approval program does not have staff restrictions on underwriting by participating surety bond companies. In FY2024, a comparative review of program performance for fiscal years 2014-2021 by known MGAs and MGUs in the Prior Approval program showed performance by these entities has been on par with the rest of the program during the same period. SBA will refer to MGAs and MGUs delegated by SBA-partnered surety bond companies as PSB-authorized agencies.

F. Revisions to the Quick Bond Agreement: § 115.30(d)(2)
Section 115.30(d)(2) outlines requirements for SBA's Quick Bond agreement (Quick Bond). Current SBA regulation
13 CFR 115.30(d)(2)
limits contract size to no more than $500,000 on Quick Bonds and excludes applications with previous contract defaults, commencement of work, contract duration over 12 months, liquidated damages over $2,500 per day, work scope involving several types of work, and bonds that can be issued under a bonding line. This final rule moves these requirements to an SOP. The change enables SBA to more dynamically support small business through Quick Bonds and more flexibility to align with industry fast-track program practices and better support small businesses.
Nine commenters on the proposed rule expressed support for this change. Seven of these commenters stated SBA should increase the limit on contract size. Two of these commenters stated SBA should increase the limit on liquidated damages. While SBA acknowledges these recommendations and is taking them into consideration in review of current Quick Bond parameters, the comments are out of scope of the proposed rule changes. The final rule change improves SBA's ability to reduce its historical lag behind changes to industry standards for programs similar to Quick Bonds, but the final rule does not change the specific requirements. Upon the effective date of this final rule, any change to requirements by SBA will be issued to the public in the form of a Policy Notice by SBA. One of these commenters stated the program should support concessionaire bonds for airport contracts. While SBA acknowledges the recommendation, the comment is out of scope of the proposed rule changes. No commenters expressed concern or opposition.

As described above, this final rule could affect small entities that participate as sureties in SBA's Surety Bond Guarantee program and small entities seeking assistance through the program. SBA's final rule will reduce time in two significant ways.
First, all Prior Approval participants surveyed agreed that having a Surety Partner participation agreement for the Prior Approval program would greatly benefit program participants by removing SBA's requirement to individually certify every application submission. SBA proposes changes to
13 CFR 115.30(d)
to require a new Prior Approval Agreement between SBA and the Prior Approval Surety Partner which will contain a master certification for all the applications to follow. This removes the need for each application to be individually certified. SBA estimates the new agreements would reduce application time burden on program participants by 557 hours, or $15,818 according to fiscal year 2023 program activity.
The final rule change is estimated to save each impacted program participant an average of 3 minutes per response, or a total of 557 total burden hours for all small businesses. To quantify the value of time saved, the SBA relies on BLS
(
printed page 73441)
wage data and assumes that the representative impacted occupation would be “insurance sales agents”. The median wage from 2023 for this occupation was $28.40. Using the program data from FY2023, the estimated total burden hours saved for program participants per year is approximately 557. The total annual savings that the SBA estimates for program participants as a result of the changes is $15,818 ($28.40 * 557), on average.
Second, SBA is extending the timeliness requirement for Surety Partners to successfully remit SBA's contractor fee payment from before the approval of a Surety Bond Guarantee to 60 calendar days after the approval of a Surety Bond Guarantee. This enables the industry flexibility to align SBA contractor fee collection procedures with industry fee collection practices and reduce the amount of uncollectible fees owed by small businesses. Surety Partners can still independently require applicant contractors to pay the fee prior to issuance of the SBA guaranteed surety bond. This change affords greater flexibility by permitting a Surety Partner to obtain SBA's approval before completing remittance of the contractor fee. As explained above, SBA estimates the change would reduce application time burden on program participants and small businesses by 568 hours, or $14,495 according to fiscal year 2023 program activity.

deregulatory action with an annualized net savings total of approximately $146,300 at a seven percent discount rate, discounted relative to 2024, over a perpetual time horizon.
This rule streamlines application procedures, modernizes forms execution, increases workflow flexibility, enables automation, and reduces regulatory burdens. It replaces the requirement for a separate Surety certification for each Prior Approval guarantee application with a single Surety participation certification, removes applicant guarantee fee payment and verification as a barrier for approval of a bond guarantee, permits electronic submission of Surety Partner participation applications, and reduces paperwork reporting burdens for Surety participants.
This rule also removes obsolete and conflicting provisions and gives SBA greater flexibility to align certain program requirements with surety industry practices and small business needs, including requirements governing Quick Bond applications and Preferred Surety Bond delegated authority.
There are currently 141 Surety participants in the program. Fiscal year 2024 experienced 6,920 submissions requiring Surety participant signatures on SBA forms. Of those submissions, 3,971 required verifications of applicant fee payments prior to application approval finalization. Of the 141 Surety participants, 44 were required to submit a total of 176 quarterly contract completion reports. Removal of signature requirements reduces time costs by 692 hours for Surety participants and SBA staff with an initial cost of 14 hours have all Surety participants complete Surety participation certifications. Removal of manual fee payment requirements and verifications prior to the approval of a surety bond guarantee reduces time costs by 662 hours with no additional costs due to automation enhancements. Reporting burden reductions from regulatory removal of the quarterly contract completion report reduces time costs by 30 hours for Surety participants and SBA staff with no additional costs. These cost savings are valued at $39.19 per hour—the mean hourly wage for Insurance Sales Agents 2024 Bureau of Labor Statistics (“BLS”) data, and at $64.28—the mean hourly wage for SBA staff based on the 2024 Office of Personnel Management (“OPM”) data. These calculations include 100 percent more for benefits and overhead adjustment. This produces an estimated total savings per year of approximately 1,384 hours, or $146,300.

The Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA), as amended by the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act of 1996, requires an agency issuing a rulemaking to prepare a final regulatory flexibility analysis that describes the impact of the final rule on small entities. (
5 U.S.C. 604(a)
). Section 605 of the RFA allows an agency, in lieu of preparing an analysis, to certify that the rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities.
This is expected to be a time saving rule making so it is not anticipated to have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities. As of fiscal year end 2023, the Program had 9,265 surety bond guarantees to 32 active surety companies (which may or may not be small businesses) that would be impacted by this rulemaking. Accordingly, the Administrator of the SBA hereby certifies that this rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Information Collection Request Title:
Rural Maternity and Obstetrics Management Strategies Program Data Collection, OMB No. 0915-0394—Revision.
Abstract:
HRSA administers the Rural Maternity and Obstetrics Management Strategies (RMOMS) Program, which is authorized by section 330A-2(d) of the Public Health Service Act. The RMOMS Program grants support networks that improve access to, and continuity of, maternal and obstetrics care in rural communities. The goals of the RMOMS Program are to: (1) improve maternal and neonatal outcomes within a rural region; (2) develop a sustainable network approach to increase the delivery and access of preconception, prenatal, pregnancy, labor and delivery, and postpartum services; (3) develop a safe delivery environment with the support and access to specialty care for perinatal patients and infants; and (4) develop sustainable financing models for the provision of maternal and obstetrics care in rural hospitals and communities. HRSA currently collects information about RMOMS grants using an OMB-approved set of performance measures and seeks to revise that approved collection. The proposed changes are a result of keeping this instrument relevant, responsive to the RMOMS Program needs, and to improve clarity of reporting for respondents.
A 60-day notice published in the
Federal Register
on August 19, 2026, vol. 91, No. 159; pp. 53622-53623. There were no public comments.
Need and Proposed Use of the Information:
The purpose of the revised data collection is to assess RMOMS awardees' progress in meeting the program goals and how well each awardee meets their community needs. Additionally, HRSA will be able to monitor and assess the impact of the RMOMS Program and ensure that funds are effectively used to provide services that meet the target population's needs.
The proposed changes to this data collection include:
Changing the frequency of data reporting from an annual basis to a biannual basis (twice a year).

SUMMARY:
This document provides the public with notice that, on November 1, 2026, the Northern Indiana Commuter Transportation District (NICD) submitted a request for amendment (RFA) to its FRA-certified positive train control (PTC) system. NICD intends to replace several Cisco Networking devices as part of a PTC hardware replacement project. This will involve three of NICD's trains, Trains 35, 432, and 601, operating without PTC technology for approximately three hours from 11:00 p.m. to 2:20 a.m. on one date that is to be determined following FRA's review and approval. FRA is publishing this notice and inviting public comment on NICD's RFA to its PTC system.

https://www.regulations.gov

All submissions must include the agency name and the applicable docket number. The relevant PTC docket number for this host railroad is Docket No. FRA-2010-0043. For convenience, all active PTC dockets are hyperlinked on FRA's website at
https://railroads.dot.gov/​research-development/​program-areas/​train-control/​ptc/​railroads-ptc-dockets
.
All comments received will be posted without change to

AGENCY:
Department of Veterans Affairs.
ACTION:
Proposed rule.
SUMMARY:
The Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) is proposing regulations to implement the Dole State and Tribal Outreach Grant Program (DSTOGP), as authorized under the Senator Elizabeth Dole 21st Century Veterans Healthcare and Benefits Improvement Act. This program aids veterans and their families by awarding funding to eligible organizations to carry out programs to improve covered outreach and assistance to ensure that veterans and their families are fully informed about, and assisted in applying for, any veterans and veterans-related benefits and programs (including veterans programs of a State or Indian Tribe) for which they may be eligible.
DATES:
Comments must be received on or before December 16, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
You may submit comments through
www.regulations.gov
under RIN 2900-AS68. That website includes a plain-language summary of this rulemaking. Comments will be posted for viewing by the public on
www.regulations.gov
,
including any personally identifiable information (
e.g.,
a social security number or address) within a comment and its supporting materials. However, VA retains discretion to redact personal or sensitive information, including but not limited to personal or sensitive information pertaining to third parties. Additionally, VA will not post public comments that make threats to individuals or institutions or suggest that the commenter will take actions to harm an individual. Instructions for accessing agency documents, submitting comments, and viewing the rulemaking docket, are available on
www.regulations.gov
under “FAQ.” Any public comment received after the comment period's closing date is considered late and will not be considered in the final rulemaking.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Stacy Valenti, Veterans Benefits Administration (VBA), 504-460-9138 or
VBACOM2CRPostSepn@va.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The Senator Elizabeth Dole 21st Century Veterans Healthcare and Benefits Improvement Act (the Act), Public Law (Pub. L.) 118-210, was enacted on January 2, 2025. Section 302 of the Act, codified at title 38 United States Code (U.S.C.) 6307, authorizes the Secretary of Veterans Affairs to establish the DSTOGP to provide assistance to States and Indian Tribes to carry out programs that improve covered outreach and assistance to veterans and their spouses, children, and parents; to ensure that such individuals are fully informed about, and assisted in applying for, any veterans and veterans-related benefits and programs (including veterans programs of a State or Indian Tribe) for which they may be eligible; and to
(
printed page 73494)
facilitate opportunities for such individuals to receive competent, qualified services in the preparation, presentation, and prosecution of veterans benefits claims. The Secretary delegated implementation authority to the Office of Military to Civilian Readiness (M2CR) within VBA. VA proposes to amend its regulations by adding a new part 85 to
title 38, Code of Federal Regulations
(CFR) to establish the requirements and procedures needed to administer this grant program in accordance with
38 U.S.C. 6307
.
Purpose of the DSTOGP
As part of the implementation of section 302 of the Act, the DSTOGP would provide funding to States and Indian Tribes to improve proactive outreach, benefits education, and claims assistance for veterans and their families. Pursuant to the Act, this could include but not limited to using funds to:
Reach out to recently separated or long-discharged veterans—and their spouses, children, and parents—to identify those who may be unaware of VA, State, or Tribal benefits.
Explain veterans benefits by delivering clear briefings on compensation, education, housing, and other entitlements, and by tailoring information to each family's circumstances.
Develop and advance VA, State, and Tribal claims by pairing veterans and family members with accredited or other representatives, as appropriate, who can compile evidence, complete applications, and represent claimants through every stage of the decision-making process.
Increase the number of county or Tribal veterans service officers (VSO) serving in the State by hiring new, additional such officers.
To apply applicants must submit a proposal to VA. Part of that proposal must demonstrate a documented need in their target communities and explain how their proposed project would track and achieve certain outcome measures established by VA. (for example, these could include metrics such as outreach contacts, benefit enrollments, and claim outcomes). Proposals that devote the bulk of the requested resources to informing, guiding, and advocating for veterans and their families fall within the Act's primary intent. Complementary services (such as, coordinated transportation to VA medical centers and onsite legal aid clinics for discharge upgrades) could also be considered. VA would further prioritize proposals that serve areas with a critical shortage of county or Tribal VSOs, or areas with high rates of suicide among veterans or referrals to the Veterans Crisis Line. See
38 U.S.C. 6307(f)
.
Applications for DSTOGP funding must present a clear, evidence-based narrative that shows how the applicant will locate hard-to-reach veterans and family members, inform them of every benefit for which they may be eligible, and guide them through the full lifecycle of a VA or similar claim. A strong proposal describes step-by-step outreach channels (such as, Tribal radio spots, faith community briefings, and social media geo-targeting), intake and needs assessment tools, accredited claims prep support, and follow-up contacts that confirm benefits enrollment or payment. Applicants must also detail any wraparound supports (such as, translation, transportation, and legal aid for discharge upgrades) that remove barriers to successful claims completion.
Proposals must include a detailed, cost-justified budget tied to these proposed activities. The budgets must show costs associated with staff time, travel, technology, and evaluation costs, while demonstrating how resources are tied to outreach, benefits education, and claims development for the targeted veteran population and their families. Applicants may include participant flow chart, Gantt chart, or similar graphic may illustrate the sequence from initial outreach to claim decision and post-award check-ins. Examples of proven outreach activities include mobile “benefits buses,” community benefits fairs cohosted with State and Tribal agencies, virtual claims workshops, and embedded VSOs in rural county offices.
Grantees would be required to carry out proactive outreach, intake, and needs assessments to identify veterans and family members who may not be receiving the benefits they have earned. They must deliver individualized benefits counseling and claims assistance, guiding participants through each stage of the claims process, including the initial application, evidence gathering, and appeals processes. Grantees are expected to track and confirm benefit awards, then address any economic, benefits, or healthcare gaps that remain. To ensure participants can fully leverage their benefits, programs should also provide, or coordinate, wraparound supports such as employability skills workshops, financial literacy coaching, or referrals to medical services.
Part 85 of Title 38, Code of Federal Regulations
VA proposes to establish and implement, in new
38 CFR part 85
, the DSTOGP authorized by section 302 of the Act. Establishment of this new part ensures organization and clarity for implementation of this new grant program. Consistent with the Act, VA proposes to title part 85 the “Dole State and Tribal Outreach Grant Program.”
85.1 Purpose and Scope
Proposed § 85.1 would set forth the purpose and scope of DSTOGP. Paragraph (a) would state that this part implements the DSTOGP with the purpose of improving covered outreach and assistance to veterans and their families to ensure such individuals are fully informed of, and assisted in applying for, any veteran and veterans-related benefits and programs (including veterans' programs of a State or Indian Tribe). This is consistent with the purpose noted in
38 U.S.C. 6307(a)
. Paragraph (b) would outline the scope of VA's authority, consistent with § 6307(b). Specifically, it would make clear that VA may provide grants to eligible organizations to provide outreach services and intensive client-centered case management services tailored to the unique needs of veterans and their families and that these services may include, but are not limited to, benefits assistance, claims navigation, local resource referrals, and engagement activities that improve access to services and support.
85.2 Definitions
As this is a new VA authority, VA proposes to define terms in § 85.2 that would be referenced in the new part. First, VA proposes to define the terms “applicant,” “grantee,” “Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO),” and “grant agreement” in a manner consistent with other VBA regulations for outreach assistance grant programs. See,
e.g.,
38 CFR 80.2
.
Section 6307(b) authorizes VA to award grants to States and Indian Tribes. Thus, VA proposes to define the term “eligible recipient (organization)” to mean: a “State government,” which would be defined as any of the fifty States of the United States, the District of Columbia, Commonwealths, territories, or possessions of the United States, or any agency or instrumentality of a State government; or a “Tribal organization” or an organization with the meaning given in section 4(l) of the Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act (
25 U.S.C. 5304
).
(
printed page 73495)
VA's proposed definition of State government is consistent with how VA has previously defined State entities eligible for outreach assistance grant programs. See,
e.g.,
38 CFR 80.2
. As for VA's proposed definition of “Tribal organization,” VA believes specifying a “Tribal organization” (as defined at
25 U.S.C. 5304
) as an eligible organization is consistent with
38 U.S.C. 6307(n)(3)
, which defines “Indian tribe” to have the meaning given such term in section 4 of the Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act (
25 U.S.C. 5304(e)
).
VA also proposes to define the term “veterans-related benefits and programs” to clarify the scope of services supported under this authority. For purposes of this part, “veterans-related benefits and programs” would mean benefits, services, and assistance administered by VA under the authority of the Under Secretary for Benefits, as well as comparable benefits, services, and assistance provided by State and Tribal governments that support veterans, their dependents, and beneficiaries. This definition aligns with VA's statutory authority while allowing flexibility for State and Tribal partners to deliver similar outreach, benefits, and services within their respective jurisdictions.
Finally, VA proposes to define the term “participant” as a veteran, or a spouse, child, or parent of a veteran, who receives services for which a DSTOGP grant is awarded. The purpose of the DSTOGP is to improve outreach to veterans and their spouses, children, and parents; therefore, VA proposes to use a definition that captures additional family members within the expanded scope of the DSTOGP, compared to the term “participant” as used in another veteran grant program (see
38 CFR 80.2(n)
).
85.3 Grants—General
In § 85.3, VA proposes to provide general information about DSTOGP grants. Paragraph (a) would state that VA would award DSTOGP grants to applicants selected in accordance with this part. Paragraph (b) would state that the maximum amount to be awarded to each grantee and the total maximum amount for all grants would be specified in the NOFO. Paragraph (c) would specify that the number of grants VA would award would depend on the total amount of grant funding available at VA's discretion and the funding amount awarded to each grantee, which is based on each grantee's proposal.
Paragraph (d) would clarify that VA would award only one DSTOGP grant in any one location, as specified in the NOFO. This limitation ensures VA compliance with section 6307(d), requiring the Secretary to equitably distribute grants among States and Indian Tribes with varying levels of urbanization. Paragraph (e) would provide that DSTOGP grant awards last for a maximum period of 2 years, beginning on the date of the award. Awards will not be extended; however, this limitation would not preclude an entity from subsequent award grants under a separate NOFO. Paragraph (f) would specify that a grant under this part should not exceed the amount required by the organization to provide the services described in § 85.1. Finally, paragraph (g) would prohibit a grantee from charging fees to a participant or requiring participation in other activities sponsored by the grantee as a condition of receiving services under the DSTOGP grant.
85.4 Notice of Funding Opportunity
VA will notify the public, through a NOFO, when funds for this grant program are available. Proposed § 85.4 would explain that when funds are available for DSTOGP grants, VA would publish a NOFO on
Grants.gov
website. It would include the location for obtaining grant applications; submission deadlines; any preferences for priority population(s); the estimated amount of funding available, in total and per grantee; the minimum number of total points and points per category that an applicant must receive to be considered for a DSTOGP grant; any timeframes and manner for grant payments; a description of eligible organizations; and any other information necessary for the application process, as determined by VA. This could include, but is not limited to, a description of the program, including the program goals and objectives, a reference to the relevant Assistance Listings (“detailed public descriptions of Federal programs that provide grants, loans, scholarships, insurance, and other types of assistance awards,” per
SAM.gov
), and a description of how the award will contribute to the achievement of the program's goals and objectives. These components are consistent with the requirements and recommendations within
2 CFR part 200
regarding notices of funding opportunity (see
2 CFR 200.204
).
Additionally, proposed § 85.4 would state that the NOFO would include a description of outcome measures developed by the Secretary that would be used to assess grantee performance. In addition to requirements under
2 CFR part 200
to establish and include performance goals in any Federal award (see
2 CFR 200.211
), section 6307(j) directs the Secretary to develop and provide to grantees outcome measures for the DSTOGP that consider specific goals outlined in the statute. Applicants must describe how their proposal would meet such outcome measures, as required under section 6307(c)(2)(B). Thus, VA would need to identify these measures in the NOFO.
85.5 Applications
VA proposes to describe in § 85.5 that, to apply for a DSTOGP grant, an applicant must submit a complete application package to VA, as described in the NOFO posted at
Grants.gov.
VA intends to define a complete application in the NOFO as including those application items expressly required under section 6307(c)(2) and any other information the Secretary may need to make in selecting grantees. See
38 U.S.C. 6307(c)(1)
. This information would likely include a well-articulated project narrative that describes program design (including outreach), recruitment and engagement plans, assessment process, identification of local area network providers, and the applicant's ability and capacity to administer the grant.
85.6 Additional Factors for Selecting Applications
In addition to the scoring criteria published in the NOFO, VA proposes to outline, in § 85.6, additional factors VA may consider when selecting grantees. These factors would include evaluation of certain financial factors, such as performance on previous Federal grants, ability to demonstrate standards of fiscal integrity, per
2 CFR 200.206
, and financial capability and internal controls. VA would also specify in proposed § 85.6 that priority would be given to projects that would serve areas with a critical shortage of county or Tribal VSOs or areas with high rates of suicide among veterans or referrals to the Veterans Crisis Line. Finally, VA would include in proposed paragraph (e) a requirement that at least five percent of any total amount of grants awarded under a NOFO must be made to Tribal organizations, as required under
38 U.S.C. 6307(e)
.
85.7 Scoring and Selection
Under proposed § 85.7, VA would evaluate each DSTOGP application, submitted on time and in full compliance with the NOFO, against clear, benefit-centric scoring criteria specified in the NOFO. The NOFO announcement would specify the relative weight (point value) for each scoring criterion. Point totals would
(
printed page 73496)
emphasize an applicant's capacity to perform targeted outreach, deliver accurate benefits education, and provide claims preparation and follow-through. VA would rank applications by score, in order of highest to lowest total score, then weigh additional factors outlined in proposed § 85.6 to ensure each grantee can responsibly expand veterans' access to earned benefits.
85.8 Disposition of Applications
Proposed § 85.8 states that VA would assign one of three dispositions to an application reviewed under § 85.7 and notify applicants via a written notice of the decision. The first potential disposition would be to approve the application, in whole or in part. The second would be to disapprove an application because, while minimally acceptable, it does not rank high enough in relation to other applications based on the level of funding available, or for another reason as provided in the decision document. Finally, VA could disapprove an application because it was not complete. As noted under proposed § 85.18, VA application decisions would be discretionary and not subject to appeal.
85.9 Withdrawal of Grant Application
VA proposes to include a withdrawal provision in § 85.9. Applicants would be able to request to withdraw their application from consideration by writing to the VA point of contact specified in the published NOFO. While not required, VA recommends that applicants provide a rationale for the withdrawal request.
85.10 Grant Agreement
For grant awards, VA proposes in § 85.10 that VA would memorialize awards in an agreement to be drafted by VA and executed by VA and the grantee. Grantees and subrecipients would be required to agree to operate the project in accordance with proposed
38 CFR part 85
,
2 CFR part 200
, and any terms outlined in the grant agreement. Part 200 offers uniform guidance and conditions for the management and administration of Federal grants. VA also proposes to require grantees and subrecipients to comply with such other terms and conditions as VA may establish for purposes of carrying out DSTOGP, including those concerning recordkeeping and reports for program monitoring and evaluation purposes, in an effective and efficient manner; and provide any necessary additional information requested by VA in the manner and timeframe specified by VA. These proposed requirements are consistent with other VA grant programs. Finally, VA proposes to include a paragraph stating that VA will include in the grant agreement any outcome measures, consistent with the NOFO, that must be met in order to qualify for subsequent DSTOGP grants.
85.11 Payments Under the Grant
Proposed § 85.11 would specify that payments would follow the schedule described in the NOFO and that grantees would not be reimbursed for costs resulting from obligations incurred before the effective date of the award.
85.12 Grantee Reporting Requirements
Under proposed § 85.12(a), grantees would be required to submit to VA quarterly reports no later than 30 days after the quarter ends. Such reports would be required to include information outlined in the grant agreement, including but not limited to outreach activity, participant numbers, expenditures, and outcomes. Proposed paragraph (b) would require grantees, within 120 days after the last day of the grant period, to submit a final report to VA complying with the NOFO requirements. Finally, proposed paragraph (c) would specify that additional reports may be required for accountability, program evaluation, and compliance with the Foundations for Evidence-Based Policymaking Act of 2018 (Evidence Act),
Public Law 115-435
. The Evidence Act requires agencies to “advance program evaluation as an essential component of Federal evidence building.” Program evaluation is defined as “an assessment using systematic data collection and analysis of one or more programs, policies, and organizations intended to assess their effectiveness and efficiency.” While specific program evaluations are required in various applicable laws and Congressional reports, VA may also evaluate major acquisition programs, other programs, and policies that in the judgment of VA leaders are significant and are likely to benefit from such evaluation.
85.13 Remediation Plan; Subsequent Grants
Section 6307(m) prohibits VA from awarding a subsequent grant under the DSTOGP to any grantee who fails to meet the outcome measures developed by the Secretary, unless the Secretary approves a remediation plan submitted by the grantee. As discussed above, VA would announce such outcome measures in the NOFO, providing applicants an opportunity to describe how their proposal would accomplish such measures. VA would then incorporate such measures into the DSTOGP agreement, consistent with the Act and the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) guidance under
2 CFR part 200
. Proposed § 85.13 would inform grantees that, in the event the grantee does not meet the outcome measures developed by the Secretary, the grantee would not be eligible for a subsequent DSTOGP grant unless the grantee submits and VA approves a remediation plan describing how and when the grantee plans to meet such outcome measures.
85.14 Withholding, Suspension, Deobligation, Termination, and Recovery of Funds by VA
Upon execution of the grant agreement, VA would obligate grant funds to the extent authorized by VA in the NOFO or the grant agreement or subsequently authorized by VA in writing. Proposed § 85.14(a) explains that VA would enforce part 85 through such actions as may be appropriate. Appropriate actions would include withholding, suspension, deobligation, termination, recovery of funds by VA, and actions in accordance with
2 CFR part 200
. VA also proposes to define withholding to mean that payment of DSTOGP grant funds would not be paid until such time as VA determines that the grantee provides sufficiently adequate documentation or takes actions to correct a deficiency.
The specific sections of
2 CFR part 200
on withholding, suspension, deobligation, termination, and recovery of funds are
2 CFR 200.208
,
200.305
, and
200.339
through
200.343
, and
200.346
. VA would refer to
2 CFR part 200
rather than include those requirements in this section as those requirements in
2 CFR part 200
may change. Referring to
2 CFR part 200
provides VA the ability to implement those changes without having to conduct further rulemaking.
VA acknowledges that when certain actions (such as suspension and termination) are taken against grantees pursuant to this section and
2 CFR part 200
, a disruption in services to participants may occur. While VA would not be regulating responsibilities for grantees to continue to provide services or to coordinate the transfer of participants to other sources of support, VA would include such requirements and responsibilities in the grant agreement entered into by VA and the grantee pursuant to this part. This arrangement would ensure that the disruption and impact upon participants is minimized as much as possible.
(
printed page 73497)
85.15 Compliance Review Requirements
VA would further ensure fiscal responsibility by proposing in § 85.15 to conduct site visits and inspections to review grantee accomplishments, management systems, and records. All visits would be performed with minimal disruption to the grantee to the extent practicable.
85.16 Financial Management
Proposed § 85.16 would ensure compliance with Federal grant regulations (that is,
2 CFR part 200
) by requiring all grantees and subgrantees to comply with the Single Audit Act Amendments of 1996 and to use financial management systems based on OMB cost principles outlined at
2 CFR 200.400
through
200.475
.
85.17 Recordkeeping
Proposed § 85.17 would state that grantees must maintain records per
2 CFR 200.334-200.338
and produce them upon VA's request.
85.18 Non-Appealability of Grant Award Decisions
Grant decisions under this part do not award benefits and are at the discretion of the Secretary. As such, proposed § 85.18 would specify that any decisions under this part are final and not subject to appeal.
Executive Orders 12866, 13175, 13563, and 14192
VA examined the impact of this rulemaking as required by Executive Orders 12866 (Sept. 30, 1993) and 13563 (Jan. 18, 2011), which direct agencies to assess all costs and benefits of available regulatory alternatives and, if regulation is necessary, to select regulatory approaches that maximize net benefits. The Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs has determined that this rulemaking is a significant regulatory action under
Executive Order 12866
, as supplemented by
Executive Order 13563
. This proposed rule is expected to be neither a regulatory nor deregulatory action under
Executive Order 14192
due to costs being no more than
de minimis.
The regulatory impact analysis associated with this rulemaking can be found as a supporting document at
www.regulations.gov
.
Executive Order 12866
directs agencies to “in most cases . . . include a comment period of not less than 60 days.” This rulemaking proposes to establish regulations that govern the newly authorized DSTOGP with funds appropriated in fiscal years 2026 and 2027. However, OMB has issued government-wide guidance regarding Federal grant assistance outlined at
2 CFR part 200
, with agencies required to issue implementing regulations for specific grant programs that are consistent with that part. As such, VA generally receives few, if any, substantive comments regarding its program-specific grant assistance regulations. Thus, we believe there is nothing in this proposed rule that would be unfamiliar to the public and that providing 30 days would still be sufficient for the public to meaningfully comment on this rule. For these reasons, the Secretary issues this rule with a 30-day public comment period. VA will consider and address comments that are received within 30 days of the date this proposed rule is published in the
Federal Register
.
Executive Order 13175
provides that Federal agencies may not issue a regulation that has Tribal implications, that imposes substantial direct compliance costs on Tribal governments, and that is not required by statute, unless the Federal government provides the funds necessary to pay the direct compliance costs incurred by the Tribal Organizations or the Federal agency consults with Tribal officials early in the process of developing the proposed regulation and develops a Tribal summary impact statement. VA's DSTOGP is required by statute, but participation is voluntary and 100 percent of the costs for an approved project may be provided by VA. Thus,
Executive Order 13175
requirements are not applicable.
However, in the spirit of the Executive Order, VA has communicated with the Tribal Organizations regarding the implementation of this grant program. Senior VA officials and representatives continue to meet with and communicate with Tribal Organizations that are interested in the grant program. VA has not received any written comments regarding the subject of this proposed regulation from Tribal Organizations, but welcomes their input during the 30-day comment period following publication of the proposed rule.
Regulatory Flexibility Act
The Secretary hereby certifies that this proposed rule would not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities as defined by the Regulatory Flexibility Act (
5 U.S.C. 601-612
). The Secretary acknowledges that this proposed rule may affect some Tribal governments that may be considered small entities; however, VA does not believe it would impact a substantial number of small entities. Further, even if a substantial number of small entities were affected, the economic impact of this rule is not significant. This proposed rule would not impose any mandatory requirements or costs on small entities as a whole and will only affect those that choose to participate in the DSTOGP. To the extent this proposed rule would have any impact on small entities, the impact of this amendment is both minimal and entirely beneficial. Therefore, under
5 U.S.C. 605(b)
, the initial and final regulatory flexibility analysis requirements of
5 U.S.C. 603
and
604
do not apply.
Unfunded Mandates
This proposed rule would not result in the expenditure by State, local, and Tribal governments, in the aggregate, or by the private sector, of $100 million or more (adjusted annually for inflation) in any one year.
Paperwork Reduction Act
This proposed rule includes provisions constituting a new collection of information under the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (PRA) (
44 U.S.C. 3501-3521
). Under the PRA, Federal agencies must obtain approval from OMB for each collection of information they conduct or sponsor.
Comments on this new collection of information should be submitted through
www.regulations.gov
during the public comment period for this rulemaking. VA invites comments on: (1) whether the proposed collection of information is necessary for the proper performance of VA's functions, including whether the information will have practical utility; (2) the accuracy of VA's estimate of the burden of the proposed collection of information; (3) ways to enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected; and (4) ways to minimize the burden of the collection of information on respondents, including through the use of automated collection techniques or the use of other forms of information technology.

PART 85—DOLE STATE AND TRIBAL OUTREACH GRANT PROGRAM

85.2

Authority:
38 U.S.C. 501
,
512
,
6307
.
§ 85.1
Purpose and scope.
(a)
Purpose.
This part implements the Dole State and Tribal Outreach Grant Program (DSTOGP) with the purpose of improving covered outreach and assistance to veterans and their families to ensure such individuals are fully informed about, and assisted in applying for, any veterans and veterans-related benefits and programs (including veterans programs of a State or Indian Tribe).
(b)
Scope.
Under this program, VA may provide grants to eligible organizations to provide outreach services and intensive client-centered case management services tailored to the unique needs of veterans and their families. These services may include, but are not limited to, benefits assistance, claims navigation, local resource referrals, and engagement activities that improve access to services and support.
§ 85.2
Definitions.
For purposes of this part and any Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO) issued pursuant to this part:
(a)
Applicant
means an organization that submits an application for a DSTOGP grant as announced in a NOFO.
(b)
Eligible recipient (organization)
means one of the following:
(1) State government; or
(2) Tribal organization.
(c)
State government
means any of the fifty States of the United States, the District of Columbia, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, any territory or possession of the United States, or any agency or instrumentality of a State government.
(d)
Tribal organization
has the same meaning given in section 4(l) of the Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act (
25 U.S.C. 5304
)).
(e)
Grantee
means an applicant that is awarded a grant under this part.
(f)
Participant
means a veteran or a spouse, child, or parent of a veteran who receives services for which a DSTOGP grant is awarded.
(g)
Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO)
means a Notice of Funding Opportunity published at
Grants.gov
in accordance with § 85.4.
(h)
Grant agreement
means a legal instrument of financial assistance between a Federal awarding agency or pass-through entity and a non-Federal entity that is consistent with
31 U.S.C. 6302
and
6304
.
(i)
Veterans-related benefits and programs benefits
means services and assistance administered by VA under the authority of the Under Secretary for Benefits, as well as comparable benefits, services, and assistance provided by State and Tribal governments that support veterans, their dependents, and beneficiaries.
§ 85.3
Grants—general.
(a)
Grants.
VA will award DSTOGP grants to applicants selected in accordance with this part.
(b)
Maximum amounts.
The maximum amount to be awarded to each grantee and the total maximum amount for all grants will be specified in the NOFO.
(c)
Number of grants awarded.
The number of grants VA will award will depend on the total amount of grant funding available at VA's discretion and the funding amount awarded to each grantee, which is based on each grantee's proposal.
(d)
Grant award limitation.
Only one DSTOGP grant will be awarded in any one location, as specified in the NOFO.
(e)
Period of performance.
DSTOGP grants will be awarded for a maximum period of 2 years, beginning on the date on which the DSTOGP grants are awarded. They will not be extended. This does not preclude an entity from subsequent award grants under a separate NOFO.
(
printed page 73499)
(f)
Amount of grant.
A grant under this part shall not exceed the amount required by the organization to provide the services described in § 85.1.
(g)
No participant charges.
A grantee may not charge any participants a fee for services provided by the grantee or require participation in other activities sponsored by the grantee as a condition of receiving services under the DSTOGP grant.
§ 85.4
Notice of Funding Opportunity (NOFO).
When funds are available for DSTOGP grants, VA will publish a NOFO at
Grants.gov
(
https://www.grants.gov
). The NOFO will include:
(a) The location for obtaining DSTOGP grant applications, including the specific forms required;
(b) The date, time, and place for submitting completed DSTOGP grant applications;
(c) Priority population categories;
(d) The estimated total amount of funds available and the maximum funds available to a single grantee;
(e) The minimum number of total points and points per category that an applicant must receive to be considered for a grant and information regarding the scoring process;
(f) Any timeframes and manner for payments under the DSTOGP grant;
(g) A description of eligible organizations or other eligibility requirements;
(h) A description of outcome measures developed by the Secretary that will be used to assess grantee performance; and
(i) Other information necessary for the DSTOGP grant application process, as determined by VA.
§ 85.5
Applications.
To apply for a grant, an applicant must submit a complete application package to VA, as described in the NOFO. Applications will be accepted only through
www.grants.gov
.
(Approved by the Office of Management and Budget under control number 2900-NEW)
§ 85.6
Additional factors for selecting applications.
(a)
Applicant's performance on prior award.
VA may consider the applicant's noncompliance with requirements applicable to prior VA or other agency awards.
(b)
Applicant's fiscal integrity.
Applicants must meet and maintain standards of fiscal integrity, per
2 CFR 200.206
.
(c)
Priority preference.
Priority will be given to applicants whose proposals will serve:
(1) Areas with a critical shortage of county or Tribal veterans service officers; or
(2) Areas with high rates of—
(A) suicide among veterans; or
(B) referrals to the Veterans Crisis Line.
(d)
Risk assessment evaluation.
VA will evaluate the applicant's financial capability and internal controls.
(e)
Set-aside.
VA must ensure that at least five percent of any total amount of grants awarded under a NOFO is made to Tribal organizations.
§ 85.7
Scoring and selection.
(a)
Scoring.
VA will only score complete applications received from eligible applicants by the deadline established in the NOFO. The applications must meet the minimum criteria set forth in the NOFO and will be scored as specified in the NOFO.
(b)
Selection.
Applications will be ranked by score and selected accordingly, also considering factors in § 85.6.
§ 85.8
Disposition of applications.
(a) Based on application review and funding availability, VA will:
(1) Approve the application for funding, in whole or in part;
(2) Determine the application is acceptable but not fund the proposed program because it does not rank sufficiently high in relation to other applications to qualify for an award based on the level of funding available, or for another reason as provided in the decision document; or
(3) Determine the application was not complete and therefore VA did not evaluate the application pursuant to § 85.7.
(b) Applicants will receive written notice of the decision.
§ 85.9
Withdrawal of grant application.
Applicants may withdraw a DSTOGP application submitted via
Grants.gov
by writing to the VA contact specified in the NOFO.
§ 85.10
Grant agreement.
(a) VA will draft a DSTOGP grant agreement to be executed by VA and the grantee.
(b) The DSTOGP grant agreement will provide that the grantee agrees to, and will ensure that each subgrantee (if applicable) agrees to:
(1) Operate the project in accordance with this part,
2 CFR part 200
, and the terms of the grant agreement.
(2) Comply with such other terms and conditions as VA may establish for purposes of carrying out DSTOGP, including those concerning recordkeeping and reports for program monitoring and evaluation purposes, in an effective and efficient manner; and
(3) Provide any necessary additional information requested by VA in the manner and timeframe specified by VA.
(c) VA will include in the grant agreement any outcome measures, consistent with the NOFO, that must be met in order to qualify for subsequent DSTOGP grants.
§ 85.11
Payments under the grant.
(a) Payments will follow the schedule described in the NOFO.
(b) Grantees will not be reimbursed for costs resulting from obligations incurred before the effective date of the award.
§ 85.12
Grantee reporting requirements.
(a) Quarterly reports are due 30 days after the quarter ends and must include information outlined in the grant agreement, including but not limited to outreach activity, participant numbers, expenditures, and outcomes.
(b) Final reports are due 120 days after the end of the grant period.
(c) Additional reports may be required for accountability, program evaluation, and compliance with the Foundations for Evidence-Based Policymaking Act of 2018.
(Approved by the Office of Management and Budget under control number 2900-NEW)
§ 85.13
Remediation plan; subsequent grants.
In the event a grantee does not meet the outcome measures outlined in the DSTOGP grant agreement, VA will not approve a subsequent DSTOGP grant unless the grantee submits and VA approves a remediation plan describing how and when the grantee plans to meet such outcome measures.
§ 85.14
Withholding, suspension, deobligation, termination, and recovery of funds by VA.
VA will enforce this part through such actions as may be appropriate. Appropriate actions include withholding, suspension, deobligation, termination, recovery of funds by VA, and actions in accordance with
2 CFR part 200
. For purposes of this section, withholding means that payment of DSTOGP grant funds will not be paid until such time as VA determines that the grantee provides sufficiently adequate documentation or takes actions to correct a deficiency for the grant.
§ 85.15
Compliance review requirements.
(a) VA may conduct site visits, as needed, to review grantee
(
printed page 73500)
accomplishments and management control systems.
(b) VA may inspect grantee records to determine compliance with the provisions of this part.
§ 85.16
Financial management.
(a) All grantees (and subgrantees) must comply with the applicable requirements of the Single Audit Act Amendments of 1996, as implemented by
2 CFR part 200
.
(b) Grantees must use financial management systems that comply with
2 CFR 200.400-200.475
.
§ 85.17
Recordkeeping.
Grantees must maintain records per
2 CFR 200.334-200.338
and produce them upon VA request.
(Approved by the Office of Management and Budget under control number 2900-NEW)
§ 85.18
Non-appealability of grant award decisions.
VA grant award decisions under this part are final and not subject to appeal.

B. What is the legal authority and what are the requirements?
CAA section 110(a)(2)(C) requires that SIPs include a program to regulate the construction and modification of any stationary source as necessary to assure that the National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) are achieved. CAA section 110(a)(2)(C) is the statutory foundation for the regulatory requirements in the portion of the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) at
40 CFR 51.160-51.164
, which apply to all new minor sources and modifications under a State's minor NSR program in accordance with
40 CFR 51.160
, which sets forth requirements for “legally enforceable procedures” applicable to minor NSR programs. The implementing regulations at
40 CFR 51.160-51.164
serve primarily as the basis for the EPA's evaluation of minor NSR programs, and States have discretion to define the scope of their minor NSR programs within the bounds of CAA section 110 and
40 CFR 51.160-51.164
.
(
printed page 73450)
Under CAA section 110(k)(3), the EPA has a statutory obligation to approve SIP submittals that meet all applicable CAA requirements.
[
6
]
Pursuant to CAA section 110(k)(3), the EPA may approve portions of a SIP submittal if those portions meet all the applicable CAA requirements.
Under CAA section 110(k)(4), the EPA may conditionally approve a SIP revision based on a commitment from a State to adopt specific enforceable measures by a date certain, but not later than one year from the date of approval. If the State fails to meet its commitment within one year of the final conditional approval, the conditional approval will be treated as a disapproval.
Additionally, under CAA section 110(l), the EPA cannot approve a SIP revision if it would interfere with any applicable requirement concerning attainment and reasonable further progress (RFP) (as defined by CAA section 171), or any other applicable requirement of the CAA.
[
7
]
The EPA evaluates CAA section 110(l) non-interference demonstrations on a case-by-case basis considering the circumstances of each SIP revision.

B. Comments on the August 19, 2026, Minor Source Permitting Proposed Rule
As noted above, in response to the August 19, 2026, Minor Source Permitting Proposed Rule, the EPA received three sets of adverse comments on its proposed approval of certain provisions in that Proposed Rule. The EPA summarizes and responds to those adverse comments below.
i. Comment 1
The commenter takes issue with South Carolina's noninterference demonstration underlying the EPA's CAA section 110(l) finding for Regulation 61-62.1, Section II, subparagraph II(B)(2)(h), arguing that, at the “sector level, the record does not isolate what fraction is attributable specifically to the minor sources actually exempted under this provision” and requesting that the Agency carry its noninterference finding “the last, unquantified step to the exempted sources themselves.” The commenter also states that they find the State's May 13, 2026, CAA section 110(l) demonstration “adding pollutant-by-pollutant NEI sector breakdowns and NAAQS design-value margin comparisons,” which the commenter frames as “narrowed” by SC DES's July 21, 2026, letter, as “a reasoned basis for the change” to the EPA's treatment of subparagraph II(B)(2)(h) in the August 19, 2026, Proposed Rule, relative to the January 21, 2025, proposal. However, the commenter states that “it inherits the unquantified-exempt-subset gap described above” because “the new demonstration still stops at the minor-NSR-sector level rather than the exempted-source level.” The commenter also states that the State did not “supply the technical basis for the . . . threshold expansion” in the August 8, 2014, SIP revision and that there is no “accompanying technical justification in the record before [the] EPA,” and the Agency should ask South Carolina to supply one, given that “two . . . affected pollutants . . . are ozone precursors.” The commenter further states that the 2026 Minor Source Permitting Proposed Rule “does not indicate” and that “[the] EPA should confirm that the version of subparagraph II(B)(2)(h) actually being approved matches what was . . . noticed for comment . . . or provide an additional comment period.” The EPA summarizes and addresses these individual comments in Comments 1a through 1c, below.
1. Comment 1a
The commenter argues that “the record isolates the specific nonpoint sector that includes minor sources regulated under the state's minor NSR program . . . [b]ut . . . does not isolate” the fraction attributable to the minor sources exempt under subparagraph II(B)(2)(h). The commenter adds that the “EPA repeatedly states only that exempt sources comprise `an even smaller,' unquantified fraction of the already-isolated sector total.” The commenter points to NO
X
, volatile organic compound (VOC), and carbon monoxide (CO) percent contributions to total 2020 National Emissions Inventory (NEI) emissions for certain nonpoint sectors identified in the Proposed Rule and states that the “EPA should require, or independently derive,” minor source-specific, rather than minor-NSR-sector-specific emissions percentages “before relying on this demonstration in a final action.”
2. Response 1a
The EPA disagrees with Comment 1a. The NEI is a comprehensive and detailed estimate of, in part, criteria pollutant and criteria precursor air emissions released every three years, based primarily on data provided by State, Local, and Tribal agencies for sources in their jurisdictions, supplemented by data developed by the EPA. As noted in the Proposed Rule, stationary sources subject to the State's minor NSR program and any sources qualifying for exemption from the program, including those exempt under Regulation 61-62.1, Section II, subparagraph II(B)(2)(h), fall into the nonpoint source category. NEI nonpoint sources include emissions estimates for sources which are individually too small in magnitude to report as point sources and typically too small, numerous, or difficult to inventory using methods for other classes of sources.
[
22
]
As the State explains in its CAA section 110(l) demonstration, South Carolina's State emissions inventory is limited to major sources, and not all minor stationary source emissions are accounted for in its NEI (
i.e.,
directly reported). This is because minor stationary sources do not trigger “point source” reporting requirements and are generally accounted for in the nonpoint inventory. However, as explained in the August 19, 2026, Proposed Rule, the EPA finds that the available 2020 NEI data, which the State divides by source category, then further by sector, indicates that the proportion of emissions that would be automatically exempt under the exemption thresholds in subparagraph II(B)(2)(h) comprise a very small portion of overall emissions in the State. Further, of the limited portion of 2020 NEI emissions attributable to permitted and exempt minor stationary sources, the subset of potentially exempt minor stationary sources comprises an even smaller fraction, as the commenter notes.
Although the commenter takes issue that “the record does not isolate” the fraction specifically attributable to minor sources exempt under these thresholds, the EPA evaluates CAA section 110(l) non-interference demonstrations on a case-by-case basis considering the circumstances of each SIP revision.
[
23
]
In this case, it is not necessary to derive and evaluate source-specific emissions estimates in lieu of sector-specific emissions estimates, as the commenter states. As discussed in detail in the Proposed Rule, the Agency has evaluated the change to Regulation 61-62.1, Section II, subparagraph II(B)(2)(h) in the SIP to include the addition of the threshold exemptions for certain sources of sulfur dioxide (SO
2
), NO
X
, and CO and the slightly increased exemption threshold for certain sources of particulate matter (PM), in light of, in part, the State's NAAQS attainment
(
printed page 73454)
history, long-term and recent air quality design values and margins between those design values and the NAAQS, and 2020 NEI data for pollutants and precursors. For the reasons stated therein, the EPA has determined that the added or revised exemption thresholds will not interfere with any applicable requirement or RFP, as defined in section 171, or any other applicable requirement of the CAA, and that the State has articulated the basis for setting the scope of its minor NSR program pursuant to CAA section 110(a)(2)(C) and
40 CFR 51.160(e)
.
[
24
]
Therefore, under CAA section 110(k)(3), the Agency is required to approve the changes to subparagraph II(B)(2)(h) submitted in South Carolina's SIP revisions through April 24, 2020.

25

X
