3. Comment 2b
The commenter states that “[p]eriodic testing creates an inherent compliance loophole,”
i.e.,
that “industrial facilities frequently optimize operations, adjust fuel mixes, or throttle production specifically for the scheduled day of a stack test, yielding emissions data that fails to reflect routine, variable operations.” The commenter states that the “EPA should require South Carolina to prioritize [CEMS] wherever technically and economically feasible,” framing CEMS as “the only reliable, 24/7 accountability necessary to verify that industrial sources are continuously complying with NO
X
emission limits and protecting local ozone and [PM] attainment standards.” The commenter further states that, “[w]here periodic stack testing or parametric monitoring is permitted, the [S]tate must incorporate mandatory, unannounced audit testing protocols.”
4. Response 2b
The EPA disagrees that CEMS provides “the only reliable . . . accountability necessary to verify” that sources are in continuous compliance with “NO
X
emission limits” and that “local ozone and [PM] attainment standards” are protected. Continuous monitoring systems (CMS) include CEMS, continuous opacity monitoring systems (COMS), and continuous parametric monitoring systems (CPMS).
[
80
]
Federal requirements, including SIP-approved requirements, can necessitate periodic or continuous monitoring to demonstration compliance and ensure practicable enforceability. Under Regulation 61-62.5, Standard No. 5.2, in Section IV, new affected sources are either subject to
40 CFR part 60
, and any applicable NO
X
monitoring requirements therein, or to CEMS, PEMS, or manufacturer's certification requirements, and/or source testing provisions under Section IV. If the Agency takes final action approving a corrective SIP revision consistent with the commitment in the State's May 13, 2026, conditional approval request and supplement, the CEMS and source testing requirements applicable to certain new affected sources will apply without being subject to the State's discretion. If the State fails to submit the corrective revisions to which it has committed within the one-year conditional approval timeframe, the conditional approval will become a disapproval.
[
81
]
Where the commenter takes issue with the State's addition of parametric monitoring requirements to Regulation 61-62.5, Standard No. 5.2, applicable to certain new affected boilers and turbines under Section IV, as explained in the 2026 Proposed Rule, CEMS and PEMS are each designed to assess continuous compliance, and the use of PEMS can provide more flexible and less expensive options than CEMS for demonstrating compliance of regulated sources, while providing “reasonable assurance of compliance.”
[
82
]
Possible considerations a source could factor into account when requesting PEMS in lieu of CEMS include cost and space. The key indicators,
i.e.,
parameters, that are monitored have an established and measured relationship with the underlying operating conditions that represent compliance with the applicable emission limits or control requirements. With respect to the added parametric monitoring requirements applicable to certain large boilers in lieu of CEMS in certain circumstances under paragraph IV(A)(1), PEMS to measure NO
X
and oxygen or carbon dioxide must be “installed, calibrated, maintained, and operated in accordance with approved methods in Regulation 61-62.60,” which is where South Carolina incorporates the Federal NSPS regulations by reference, and sources subject to CEMS and PEMS are required to submit equivalent excess emissions and monitoring systems performance reports semiannually. These reports require detailed descriptions of any excess emissions and the circumstances surrounding excess emissions events, along with descriptions of periods during which the CMS was inoperative. For the added parametric monitoring requirements applicable to certain turbines, those requirements depend on source characteristics,
e.g.,
NO
X
control technology, and subject sources are also subject to the source testing requirements in paragraph IV(C)(3), during which the parameters continuously monitored must be evaluated “to establish acceptable values and ranges.” Subject source owners or operators are also required to develop and keep on-site a parameter monitoring plan.
Likewise, regarding the comments concerning the State's addition of stack testing requirements to Standard No. 5.2,
[
83
]
stack testing is an established CAA compliance monitoring tool across Federal regulations,
e.g.,
NSPS under
40 CFR parts 60
or NESHAPs under parts 61 and 63, used to determine a facility's compliance with emission limits, or capture or control efficiencies established pursuant to CAA requirements. Stack tests are conducted under testing conditions that are generally representative of operating conditions and which should demonstrate that a source is capable of complying with applicable emission standards at all times.
[
84 85
]
Under Regulation 61-62.5, Standard No. 5.2, Section IV, source tests “will be used to
(
printed page 73466)
show compliance with the NO
X
standard[s].” With respect to the added source testing requirements applicable to certain new affected sources,
i.e.,
smaller boilers, certain internal combustion engines and turbines, and other affected source types, Regulation 61-62.5, Standard No. 5.2, Section IV requires all source testing to be “conducted in accordance with Regulation 61-62.1, Section IV.”
As described in the 2026 Proposed Rule and above, Regulation 61-62.1, Section IV, as revised through the April 24, 2020, SIP revision, requires at subsection IV(B) that the State approve the test plan required under subsection IV(C) prior to the source conducting the test. The test plan includes the test objective at paragraph IV(C)(2), which constitutes a description of the overall purpose of the test and the citation of any State or Federal regulation or permit condition requiring the test. Additionally, under Regulation 61-62.1, subsection IV(B), the State may request any additional information related to the test plan and will deny any plan for which additional requested information is not submitted. Under Regulation 61-62.1, subsection IV(C), in addition to the test objective, the plan must include process descriptions; safety considerations; sampling and analytical procedures; sampling locations and documentation; internal quality assurance/quality control measures for applicable test methods; and final report content. Under Regulation 61-62.1, subsection IV(J), modifications to the plan must be approved before the test. Under Regulation 61-62.1, subsection IV(D), a source owner, operator, or representative must notify the State of the source test prior to the test date and provide access to the facility for source testing observation. Furthermore, Under Regulation 61-62.1, subsection IV(E), the State may request that source test samples collected be split for independent analysis or analysis in the State laboratory, and performance testing for certain methods must include a test method performance audit, if a performance audit sample is commercially available, using a blind audit sample supplied by an accredited audit sample provider and analyzed during the test in order to indicate test data bias. Regulation 61-62.1, subsection IV(E) also gives the State discretion to require subsequent remedial actions based on split samples and/or performance audit results. Regulation 61-62.1, subsection IV(G) covers noncompliant test results and requires a source owner, operator, or representative to submit a written plan including interim actions to minimize emissions pending a demonstration of compliance, corrective actions taken or proposed to return the source to compliance, the intended method used to demonstrate source compliance,
e.g.,
retest and proposed date, and any changes necessary to the site-specific test plan before the retest. Under Regulation 61-62.1, subsection IV(H), a source owner, operator, or representative or source test consultant must provide access to the analytical laboratory for observation of instrument calibrations and field and audit sample analyses, and, under Regulation 61-62.1, subsection IV(I), the State may inspect the source(s) tested. Thus, the State has the authority and the ability to oversee the test plan and testing, to audit the tests, and to inspect the source(s) being tested.
As explained in the 2026 Source Testing and NO
X
Control Proposed Rule, the State's added parametric monitoring requirements under Regulation 61-62.5, Standard No. 5.2 in Section IV, applicable to certain turbines, serve to demonstrate compliance with the NO
X
emission limits and/or control requirements in Standard No. 5.2. With respect to the State's added source testing requirements and the PEMS requirements, to which it has committed to add for certain large boilers, in Section IV, if South Carolina fulfills its commitment in line with the May 13, 2026, commitment letter and supplement, and if the EPA approves the corrective SIP revision under CAA section 110(k)(4), those SIP-strengthening requirements would no longer be subject to the State's discretion. For the reasons described in the 2026 Proposed Rule and in this action, the EPA disagrees that: (1) it should “push[ ] for 24/7 continuous monitoring” and require the State to “prioritize [CEMS] wherever technically and economically feasible,” in lieu of other,
i.e.,
parametric monitoring and source testing, monitoring methods; (2) periodic testing requirements, such as those added to Regulation 61-62.5, Standard No. 5.2, in Section IV applicable to certain sources create “an inherent compliance loophole” whereby facilities can “optimize operations, adjust fuel mixes, or throttle production specifically for the . . . day of a stack test, yielding emissions data that fails to reflect routine, variable operations”; and (3) for periodic stack testing or parametric monitoring, the State “must incorporate mandatory, unannounced audit testing protocols.”
With respect to the commenter's statement that periodic testing requirements create “an inherent compliance loophole,” as explained above: (1) source testing is an established compliance tool used to determine a facility's compliance or capture or control efficiencies; (2) under Regulation 61-62.1, Section IV, source test conditions can dictate permit emission or production rate limits, and (3) under Regulation 61-62.5, Standard No. 5.2, Section IV, source tests “will be used to show compliance with the NO
X
standard[s].” Furthermore, in Standard No. 5.2, certain sources,
i.e.,
certain turbines also subject to PEMS, as noted above, as well as internal combustion engines, are subject to additional source testing provisions. These provisions require, with respect to turbines, monitoring of continuously monitored parameters during testing “to establish acceptable values and ranges” which will be evaluated continuously, and, with respect to internal combustion engines, source owners or operators to operate affected engines within parameter(s) established during the most recent compliant source test. A State-issued summary of that test must be maintained with the engine's required permit.
With respect to the commenter's statement concerning unannounced audit testing for sources subject to periodic source testing or parametric monitoring requirements, as noted above, new affected sources subject to parametric monitoring under Standard No. 5.2 without concurrent applicable source testing requirements,
i.e.,
certain large boilers, are required to submit detailed excess emissions reports semiannually. For sources subject to source testing requirements in Standard No. 5.2, and therefore Regulation 61-62.1, Section IV, Regulation 61-62.1, subsection IV(E) provides for test method performance audits, if relevant samples are commercially available from an accredited provider. Furthermore, as described above, under Regulation 61-62.1, the State may request any test plan-related information not already provided and can inspect the source(s) tested; observe the test itself, as well as instrument calibrations, and field and audit sample analyses; and independently analyze test samples. Finally, Regulation 61-62.1, Section II(O) requires each facility to allow SC DES to: (1) “enter the facility where emissions-related activity is conducted, or where records are kept under the conditions of the permit”; (2) “have access to and copy . . . any records that must be kept under the conditions of the permit”; (3) “[i]nspect any facilities, equipment (including
(
printed page 73467)
monitoring and air pollution control equipment), practices, or operations regulated or required”; and (4) “sample or monitor, at reasonable times, substances or parameters for the purpose of assuring compliance with the permit or applicable requirements.”
5. Comment 2c
The commenter cites “the absence of rigorous, legally enforceable timelines to address and correct operational deficiencies identified during tune-ups” and states that requirements to perform tune-ups are “meaningless if a facility is not legally bound to fix sub-optimal combustion efficiency, high carbon monoxide markers, or elevated NO
X
emissions within a strict window.” The commenter claims that the “EPA must require South Carolina to amend its rule to establish a hard, legally enforceable deadline, not to exceed 30 days from the completion of a tune-up report, for a facility to complete and verify corrective actions following any failed or sub-optimal diagnostic check.” The commenter also claims that “any exceedance discovered during a tune-up must be treated as a reportable deviation rather than corrected under a shroud of administrative discretion.”
6. Response 2c
The commenter's state that “a recurring flaw across . . . SIP frameworks is the absence of rigorous, legally enforceable timelines to address and correct operational deficiencies during . . . tune-ups” is outside the scope of 2026 Source Testing and Control of NO
X
Proposed Rule. As explained in the 2026 Source Testing and NO
X
Control Proposed Rule, the State's changes to its tune-up requirements applicable to new affected sources are consistent with or comparable to the SIP-approved tune-up requirements. The changes also clarify tune-up requirements applicable to existing affected sources. The EPA, therefore, evaluated the overall changes to the State's SIP-approved tune-up requirements for sources covered by Standard No. 5.2.
Regarding the commenter's claim that tune-up requirements are “meaningless if a facility is not legally bound to fix sub-optimal combustion efficiency, high carbon monoxide markers, or elevated NOx emissions within a strict window,” the EPA notes that the purpose of conducing tune-up activities is to optimize combustion efficiency, so the actions taken in support of this objective are generally completed during the process.
[
86
]
The State's tune-up requirements in Regulation 61-62.5, Standard No. 5.2 represent routine maintenance that helps to ensure optimal functioning of the combustion units,
[
87
]
so the EPA finds that the aim of the required tune-ups is to “fix sub-optimal combustion efficiency.”
Moreover, and regarding the commenter's contention that “any exceedance discovered during a tune-up must be treated as a reportable deviation,” Standard No. 5.2 requires that all tune-up records be maintained on-site for inspection by DES for five years and tune-up plans be maintained.
[
88
]
Additionally, Regulation 61-62.1, Section V,
Credible Evidence,
provides at Section V(A), that “[t]he monitoring data collected and records of operations would serve as the basis for a source to certify compliance, and could be used by the Department as direct evidence of an enforceable violation of the underlying emission limitation or standard.” Therefore, the State has access to the records supporting those activities and the ability to review information generated during tune-ups. Furthermore, exceedances of emission limits are not allowed under the State's SIP. Additionally, as noted in the August 19, 2026, Proposed Rule and this action, the State's regulations at issue,
i.e.,
Regulation 61-62.1, Section IV and Regulation 61-62.5, Standard No. 5.2, contain MRR and source testing requirements for subject sources to demonstrate compliance with applicable requirements, including Federal and SIP requirements. Regulation 61-62.5, Standard No. 5.2 requires specific excess emissions reporting for units with CEMS. South Carolina also requires excess emissions reporting for units without CEMS via a required standard permit condition at Regulation 61-62.1, Section II, subparagraph (J)(1)(c). Therefore, to the extent a tune-up activity identifies a performance issue that has caused excess emissions, sources are required to include the relevant information in reporting.
For the reasons discussed above, the EPA rejects the commenter's contention that it “must require South Carolina . . . to establish a . . . legally enforceable deadline, not to exceed 30 days from the completion of a tune-up report, for a facility to complete and verify corrective actions following any failed or sub-optimal diagnostic check” and the inference that the State's tune-up requirements under Standard No. 5.2 reflect “loopholes” with respect to “equipment tune-up timelines.” As noted above, the corrective actions supporting the tune-up are generally conducted in sync with the required tune-up, and the State has established other monitoring and testing requirements more specifically intended to assess compliance with the requirements of Standard No. 5.2, although it has the ability to access and assess the tune-up records, as needed.

Department of the Interior
Fish and Wildlife Service
[Docket No. FWS-R8-ES-2026-3994; FXES11130800000-267-FF08E00000]
AGENCY:
Fish and Wildlife Service, Interior.
ACTION:
Notice of availability; and request for comments.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (Service) invites the public, as well as local, State, Tribal, and Federal agencies, to comment on recovery permit applications to conduct activities intended to enhance the propagation and survival of endangered species under section 10(a)(1)(A) of the Endangered Species Act (ESA). With some exceptions, the ESA prohibits activities affecting ESA-listed species unless the Service issues a federal authorization, such as a permit, to allow for those activities. Prior to issuing 10(a)(1)(A) permits for endangered species the Service must invite public comment and consider any information received during the public comment period. We will consider all information received during the public comment period before issuing any of the requested permits.
DATES:
Comments will be accepted on or before December 16, 2026. Comments submitted electronically using the Federal eRulemaking Portal (see
ADDRESSES
, below) must be received by 11:59 p.m. eastern time on the closing date.
To ensure your comment is received and considered, you must submit it using one of the methods identified in the
ADDRESSES
section of this document. Comments submitted through any method not authorized in this document, or sent to an address not listed here, will not be considered.
ADDRESSES:
Comment submission:
All submissions must include the docket number [FWS-R8-ES-2026-3994] for this document. You must submit comments using one of the following methods:
Electronic submission:
Federal eRulemaking Portal at:

The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (Service) invites the public to comment on applications for permits under section 10(a)(1)(A) of the Endangered Species Act of 1973, as amended (ESA;
16 U.S.C. 1531
et seq.
), and our regulations in the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) at
50 CFR part 17
. Any documents or other information submitted with the applications will be available for public review, subject to the requirements of the Privacy Act of 1974, as amended (
5 U.S.C. 552a
) and the Freedom of Information Act (
5 U.S.C. 552
).
Background
With some exceptions, the Act prohibits certain activities with listed species, including the take of listed wildlife unless a Federal permit is issued that authorizes such activities. A recovery permit issued by the Service under section 10(a)(1)(A) of the Act authorizes otherwise prohibited take of listed species by the permittee while engaging in activities that are conducted for scientific purposes that promote recovery of the species or for the enhancement of propagation or survival of the species in the wild. The Service regulations implementing the Act's prohibitions and permitting requirements for listed species are set forth in
50 CFR part 17
.
Permit Applications Available for Review and Comment
Section 10(c) of the Act requires the Service to publish notice of each application in the
Federal Register
and to invite interested parties to submit written data, views, or arguments before we take final action on the permit application. Accordingly, we invite comments on these applications. The comments and recommendations that will be most useful, and likely to influence agency decisions, are those supported by quantitative information or studies. An interested party opposed to a recovery permit's issuance may object during the comment period by following the requirements in
50 CFR 17.22(d)
and request notification of the final action. The Service will follow the procedures in that section regarding notification of interested parties who file objections to issuance of permits.

AGENCY:

ACTION:
Temporary final rule.
SUMMARY:
The Coast Guard is establishing a temporary safety zone for certain navigable waters of the Miami Marine Stadium Basin in connection with the FRL Inaugural Invitational eFoil Exhibition Race. This safety zone is necessary to protect personnel, vessels, and the marine environment from potential hazards associated with the eFoil races. This rule prohibits entry of vessels or persons into this safety zone unless authorized by the Captain of the Port Sector Miami or its designated representative.
DATES:
This rule is effective from 8 a.m. until 9 p.m. on November 15, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
To view available documents, go to
https://www.regulations.gov
and search for USCG-2026-1162.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
If you have questions about this rule, contact MST2 Elliot Cortes, Sector Miami Waterways Management Division, U.S. Coast Guard; telephone 786-295-9051, or email
SectorMiamiWaterways@uscg.mil
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Table of Abbreviations
CFR Code of Federal Regulations
COTP Captain of the Port
DHS Department of Homeland Security
FR Federal Register
NPRM Notice of proposed rulemaking
§ Section
U.S.C. United States Code
II. Background and Authority
On August 26, 2026, an organization notified the Coast Guard that it will be conducting an eFoil exhibition race from 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. on November 15, 2026. The races will take place within Miami Marine Stadium. The safety zone would cover all navigable waters within 100 yards of the race area.
On October 19, 2026, the Coast Guard published a notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) titled, “Safety Zone: FRL Inaugural Invitational eFoil Exhibition Race, Miami Marine Stadium Basin, Miami, FL in the
Federal Register
(
91 FR 66033
). In the NPRM, we stated why we issued the NPRM and invited comments on our proposed regulatory action related to the races.
On November 5, 2026, the Coast Guard published a correction to the NPRM in the
Federal Register
(
91 FR 69736
). The correction changed the comment deadline from November 18, 2026, to November 6, 2026. The correction explained that the original comment deadline fell after the proposed enforcement period and that the revised deadline would allow the Coast Guard to consider timely submitted comments before determining whether to issue a final rule for the scheduled event.
The Coast Guard is issuing this rule under the authority in
46 U.S.C. 70034
. The (Captain of the Port (COTP) has determined that potential hazards associated with the eFoil races, including high speed watercraft activity, present a safety concern for persons, vessels, and the marine environment from in the vicinity of the event. This rule is necessary to protect personnel, vessels, and the marine environment in the navigable waters of the safety zone.
Because of the event is scheduled for November 15, 2026, the Coast Guard finds good cause under
5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3)
for making this rule effective less than 30 days after publication in the
Federal Register
. Delaying the effective date would be impracticable and contrary to the public interest because the safety zone is necessary on the date of the event to protect persons, vessels, and the marine environment from potential hazards associated with eFoil race operations.
III. Discussion of Comments and the Rule
During the comment period that ended on November 6, 2026, the Coast Guard received one comment raising multiple concerns regarding the proposed safety zone. The Coast Guard addresses those concerns below.
The commenter stated that the November 18, 2026, comment deadline published in the NPRM was after the proposed November 15, 2026, event date and would prevent public feedback from informing the Coast Guard's decision before the event. The Coast Guard acknowledges that the original comment deadline occurred after the proposed enforcement period. On November 5, 2026, the Coast Guard published a correction to the NPRM that changed the comment deadline to November 6, 2026.
91 FR 69736
. The correction provided an expedited comment period that allowed interested persons an opportunity to comment while allowing the Coast Guard sufficient time to review timely submitted comments and determine whether a final rule was necessary before the scheduled event. The Coast Guard considered the comment received on the NPRM, along with any other timely submitted comments, before issuing this rule.
The commenter stated that the NPRM described the proposed safety zone as affecting a small area for “a few hours,” which was inconsistent with the proposed 13-hour enforcement period from 8 a.m. until 9 p.m. The Coast Guard acknowledges that the phrase “a few hours” did not accurately describe the proposed enforcement period. This final rule specifies that the safety zone will be enforced from 8 a.m. until 9 p.m. on November 15, 2026. The Coast Guard has also revised the discussion of small entity impacts in section IV.A of this preamble to reflect the full enforcement period.
The commenter stated that the proposed 100-yard buffer did not provide sufficient detail regarding the safety zone boundaries or demonstrate that the race area would fit safely within the regulated area. The regulatory text in both the NPRM and this final rule identifies the regulated area using four coordinates based on the World Geodetic System 1984 datum. The designated approximately 310-meter by 310-meter safety zone in the southeast portion of the Miami Marine Stadium Basin provides an ample buffer for the dual 70-meter by 160-meter race-course layout, with approximately 75 meters of clearance at the ends and 120 meters on the sides. In addition, because the basin entrance near Rickenbacker Marina is approximately 1.3 kilometers from the race area, vessel transit outside the safety zone will remain unobstructed. The Coast Guard will publish a Marine Safety Information Bulletin containing the georeferenced buoy coordinates for the event area. The Coast Guard has determined that the regulated area described in
33 CFR 165.T07-1162
is necessary to protect persons, vessels, and the marine environment from potential hazards associated with the event.
The commenter stated that eFoil racing presents hazards, including high-speed collisions, impact trauma, and lithium-ion battery failures, and expressed concern that the NPRM did not describe emergency response, race stop, or battery safety procedures. The Coast Guard recognizes that eFoil race operations may present hazards to race participants, spectators, and other
(
printed page 73446)
persons or vessels in the vicinity of the event. The event sponsor is responsible for race operations and will provide active in water recovery and event safety coverage, including one jet ski, three safety boats, a City of Miami Fire Rescue dive boat, and Miami Marine Patrol assets. The Coast Guard's role is limited to enforcing the outer perimeter of the safety zone. Racing will be suspended immediately if primary safety coverage is compromised. The safety zone established by this rule provides a controlled area around the event and is intended to reduce the risk of injury, vessel collision, and other hazards associated with the race.
The commenter stated that the NPRM did not include detailed budget, staffing, or cost benefit information regarding Coast Guard enforcement of the event. This safety patrol is a nonrecurring, single-day operation that will use standard, pre-allocated Coast Guard resources and U.S. Coast Guard Auxiliary volunteer assets integrated into Sector Miami's routine weekend operations. The Coast Guard does not anticipate that enforcement of this safety zone will degrade regional search-and-rescue capabilities. Because this rule is not a significant regulatory action under
Executive Order 12866
, a formal cost-benefit analysis is not required. Local safety vessels, police officers, and liability insurance are funded by the event sponsor. In addition, as discussed in section IV.A of this preamble, the Coast Guard certifies under
5 U.S.C. 605(b)
that this rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities. Vessels will be able to safely transit around the regulated area, and vessels may request permission to enter the safety zone from the COTP or a designated representative.
The commenter raised concerns regarding localized environmental effects, including battery-charging risks, anchoring effects on sensitive marine habitats, and marine debris recovery. The Coast Guard considered these concerns as part of its environmental review. All race craft are electric, reducing the risk of fuel spills associated with gasoline powered race craft. The event sponsor has incorporated measures to avoid or minimize environmental effects, including use of bare bottom anchoring to avoid seagrass, shore-based battery swap and containment procedures, and protected species observation and race hold procedures. The event plan also provides for the removal of marine debris generated by the event.
The Coast Guard completed a Record of Environmental Consideration for this action and determined that the temporary safety zone is categorically excluded from further environmental review under paragraph L60(a) of Appendix A, Table 1 of DHS Instruction Manual 023-01-001-01, Rev. 1. The Record of Environmental Consideration concluded that the action is not expected to result in significant adverse environmental impacts and does not involve extraordinary circumstances that would preclude use of the categorical exclusion. A Record of Environmental Consideration supporting this determination is available in the docket.
This rule establishes a temporary safety zone from 8 a.m. until 9 p.m. on November 15, 2026. The safety zone includes the navigable waters described in § 165.T07-1162. During the enforcement period, no vessel or person may enter the safety zone without permission from the COTP or a designated representative.
IV. Regulatory Analyses
We developed this rule after considering numerous statutes and Executive orders related to rulemaking. Below we summarize our analyses based on a number of these statutes and Executive orders.
A. Impact on Small Entities
The Regulatory Flexibility Act of 1980 (RFA),
5 U.S.C. 601-612
, as amended, requires Federal agencies to consider the potential impact of regulations on small entities during rulemaking. The term “small entities” comprises small businesses, not-for-profit organizations that are independently owned and operated and are not dominant in their fields, and governmental jurisdictions with populations of less than 50,000. Section 605 of the RFA allows an agency to certify a rule, in lieu of preparing an analysis, if the rulemaking is not expected to have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities.
The Coast Guard certifies that, although some small entities may intend to transit the safety zone above, this rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities. Vessel traffic will be able to safely transit around this safety zone. This safety zone will only impact a small, designated area for one day from 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. It is during a time when vessel traffic is normally high. In addition, the Coast Guard will issue a Broadcast Notice to Mariners via VHF FM marine channel 16, which will allow small entities to adjust their transit plans, and the rule allows vessels to request permission to enter the zone from the COTP.
Under section 213(a) of the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act of 1996 (
Pub. L. 104-121
), if this rule will affect your small business, organization, or governmental jurisdiction and you have questions, contact the person listed in the
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
section.
The National Ombudsman resolves concerns of uneven or excessive federal regulatory enforcement. Reviews are confidential and do not waive the right to pursue administrative appeals or any other legal action. Contact 1-888-REG-FAIR (1-888-734-3247) or
Ombudsman@SBA.gov
.
B. Collection of Information
This rule will not call for a new collection of information under the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (
44 U.S.C. 3501-3520
).
C. Federalism and Indian Tribal Governments
We have analyzed this rule under
Executive Order 13132
, Federalism, and have determined that it is consistent with the fundamental federalism principles and preemption requirements described in that Order.
Also, this rule does not have tribal implications under
Executive Order 13175

(a) Comments Due Date
The FAA must receive comments on this airworthiness directive (AD) by December 31, 2026.
(b) Affected ADs
None.
(c) Applicability
This AD applies to all Airbus Helicopters Deutschland GmbH (AHD) Model MBB-BK 117 C-1 and MBB-BK 117 C-2 helicopters, certificated in any category, with Air Comm Corporation (ACC) air-conditioning system part number (P/N) EC145-7040-1 installed in accordance with FAA Supplemental Type Certificate No. SR00601DE.
(d) Subject
Joint Aircraft System Component (JASC) Code 2100, Air conditioning system.
(e) Unsafe Condition
This AD was prompted by reports of excessive corrosion on the condenser inlet duct, which caused the internal support wire helix to break and protrude and impinge the tail rotor (TR) drive shaft. The FAA is issuing this AD to detect and prevent failure of the TR drive shaft. The unsafe condition, if not addressed, could result in failure of the TR drive shaft and loss of control of the helicopter.
(f) Compliance
Comply with this AD within the compliance times specified, unless already done.
(g) Required Actions
Within 7 days after the effective date of this AD and thereafter at intervals not to exceed 50 hours time-in-service or 3 months, whichever occurs first, accomplish the following actions:
(1) Inspect the TR drive shaft in the location below the ACC condenser air inlet duct assembly (duct assembly) for any protruding wire helix or wear. If there is any protruding wire helix or any wear on the TR drive shaft, before further flight, replace the TR drive shaft, in accordance with a method approved by the Manager, International Validation Branch, FAA; or European Union Aviation Safety Agency; or AHD's Design Organization Approval (DOA). If approved by the DOA, the approval must include the DOA-authorized signature.
(2) Inspect the exterior and interior installation and condition of the ACC duct assembly by accomplishing the following actions:
(i) Inspect the exterior of the ACC duct assembly for broken helix wire and bulging. If the helix wire is broken, or if there is any bulging at the bottom areas over the TR drive shaft, before further flight, replace the ACC duct assembly with a new, zero-hour, and never installed ACC duct assembly.
(ii) With moderate pressure, squeeze and flex the duct by hand to ensure the duct returns to its circular shape. If the duct does not return to the original circular shape, before further flight, replace the ACC duct assembly with a new, zero-hour, and never installed ACC duct assembly.
(iii) Inspect (using a borescope) the interior of the ACC duct assembly for corrosion of the wire helix, or if the inner silicone lining is separating, bubbling, or peeling away from the wire helix. If there is any corrosion of the wire helix, or if the inner silicone lining is separating, bubbling, or peeling away from the wire helix, before further flight, replace the ACC duct assembly with a new, zero-hour, and never installed ACC duct assembly.
(h) Special Flight Permits
Special flight permits as described in
14 CFR 21.197
and
21.199
, are not allowed.
(i) Alternative Methods of Compliance (AMOCs)

14 CFR 39.19
. In accordance with
14 CFR 39.19
, send your request to your principal inspector or local Flight Standards District Office, as appropriate. If sending information directly to the manager of the West Certification Branch, send it to the attention of the person identified in paragraph (j) of this AD and email to:
AMOC@faa.gov
.
(2) Before using any approved AMOC, notify your appropriate principal inspector, or lacking a principal inspector, the manager of the local flight standards district office/certificate holding district office.

WCB-COS@faa.gov

Airbus Helicopters:
Docket No. FAA-2026-13814; Project Identifier MCAI-2026-00037-R.
(a) Comments Due Date

(b) Affected ADs
This AD replaces AD 2025-24-01, Amendment 39-23196 (

, December 8, 2025) (AD 2025-24-01).
(c) Applicability
This AD applies to all Airbus Helicopters Model EC 155 B and EC 155 B1 helicopters, certificated in any category, as identified in European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) AD 2026-0011, dated January 15, 2026 (EASA AD 2026-0011).
(d) Subject
Joint Aircraft System Component (JASC) Code 5620, Passenger compartment windows; 5630, Door windows.
(e) Unsafe Condition
This AD was prompted by a determination that the required forces to jettison the windows exceed the maximum jettisoning effort requirements. The FAA is issuing this AD to prevent the inability to jettison the window(s) during an emergency. The unsafe condition, if not addressed, could result in a reduced capability to evacuate helicopter occupants during an emergency and injury to helicopter occupants.
(f) Compliance
Comply with this AD within the compliance times specified, unless already done.
(g) Required Actions
Except as specified in paragraphs (h) and (i) of this AD: Comply with all required actions and compliance times specified in, and in accordance with, EASA AD 2026-0011.

SUMMARY:
This notice announces public meetings of the Technical Pipeline Safety Standards Committee, also known as the Gas Pipeline Advisory
(
printed page 73638)
Committee (GPAC), and the Technical Hazardous Liquid Pipeline Safety Standards Committee, also known as the Liquid Pipeline Advisory Committee (LPAC). The meetings will be held to discuss the notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM), titled “Repair Criteria for Hazardous Liquid and Gas Transmission Pipelines.”
DATES:
The GPAC will meet on Wednesday, December 2, 2026, beginning at 9:00 a.m. ET, until approximately 2:30 p.m. ET. The LPAC will meet on Wednesday, December 2, 2026, beginning at approximately 2:45 p.m. ET, until approximately 5:30 p.m. ET, and on Thursday, December 3, 2026, beginning at 9:00 a.m. ET, until approximately 4:30 p.m. ET. The meetings may end earlier or later than published times depending on when each committee completes its review. Members of the public may attend these meetings virtually and are asked to register on the meeting website at
https://primis-meetings.phmsa.dot.gov/​
no later than November 27, 2026. Individuals who require accommodations because of a disability must notify Joseph Berry by email at
joseph.berry1@dot.gov
by that date as well.
ADDRESSES:
Advisory committee members will participate in the meetings in person at the U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT), 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590. PHMSA will provide a virtual format for members of the public. The agendas, registration details, location, times of the meetings, and virtual access instructions will be posted at
https://primis-meetings.phmsa.dot.gov/​
.
Presentations will be available on the meeting website and at
https://www.regulations.gov
in docket number PHMSA-2025-0019.

Members of the public who wish to submit a written statement for consideration by the GPAC or LPAC may do so by November 18, 2026. PHMSA will also accept written comments after the meetings if received no later than December 30, 2026. Submit comments to docket number PHMSA-2025-0019 using any of the following methods and identifying the docket number on the top of the first page:
On
https://www.regulations.gov
,
follow instructions to “submit a comment.”
By mail or hand delivery to Docket Management System: U.S. Department of Transportation, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590-0001. Hand delivery is available between 9:00 a.m. and 5:00 p.m. ET, Monday through Friday, except Federal holidays. Submit two copies if you submit your comment by mail and include a self-addressed stamped postcard if you wish to receive confirmation of receipt.
Comments may be viewed in the docket on
https://www.regulations.gov
.

https://www.dot.gov/​privacy
.

Joseph Berry by phone at 720-601-3577 or by email at
joseph.berry1@dot.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Information on the Committees
The GPAC and LPAC are statutorily required advisory committees that provide PHMSA and the Secretary of Transportation with recommendations on proposed standards for the transportation of gas and hazardous liquid by pipelines. Established in accordance with
49 U.S.C. 60115
and the Federal Advisory Committee Act of 1972 (FACA,
5 U.S.C. Ch. 10
), the committees are tasked with reviewing and providing recommendations on the technical feasibility, reasonableness, cost-effectiveness, and practicability of PHMSA's proposed changes to the gas and hazardous liquid pipeline safety regulations. Each committee consists of 15 members, with membership evenly divided among Federal and State governments, regulated industry, and the public.
II. Meeting Agenda
The GPAC will meet on Wednesday, December 2, 2026, and the LPAC will meet on Wednesday, December 2, 2026, and Thursday, December 3, 2026, to discuss the NPRM titled “Repair Criteria for Hazardous Liquid and Gas Transmission Pipelines.”
[
1
]
The GPAC and LPAC will review the NPRM and supporting regulatory analyses, including the preliminary regulatory impact analyses, environmental assessments, and other materials pertaining to the NPRM provided in the public docket. The agendas are subject to change. Following the meetings, PHMSA will evaluate the GPAC and LPAC recommendations and consider comments received and relevant information from the meeting reports in developing the final rule.
III. Public Participation
The meetings will be accessible virtually. All participants must register through the official meeting website. PHMSA also will record the meetings and post records to the public docket.
Though verbal statements from members of the public will not be permitted during the meetings, PHMSA invites written comments. Members of the public who wish to submit any written statement for consideration by the committees may do so by November 18, 2026. PHMSA also will accept written comments after the meetings if received by December 30, 2026.
Individuals should check the meeting website or contact Joseph Berry regarding any possible changes. PHMSA is not always able to publish a notice in the
Federal Register
quickly enough to provide timely notice regarding last-minute issues that impact a previously announced advisory committee meeting.

49 CFR 1.97
.

AGENCY:
Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA), Department of Transportation (DOT).
ACTION:
Notice of applications for exemption; request for comments.
SUMMARY:
FMCSA announces receipt of applications from five individuals for an exemption from the prohibition in the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Regulations (FMCSRs) against operation of a commercial motor vehicle (CMV) by persons with a current clinical diagnosis of myocardial infarction, angina pectoris, coronary insufficiency, thrombosis, or any other cardiovascular disease of a variety known to be accompanied by syncope (transient loss of consciousness), dyspnea (shortness of breath), collapse, or congestive heart failure. If granted, the exemption would enable the individual with an ICD to operate CMVs in interstate commerce.
DATES:
Comments must be received on or before December 16, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
You may submit comments identified by Docket No. FMCSA-2026-0064 using any of the following methods:
Federal eRulemaking Portal:
Go to
www.regulations.gov
,
insert the docket number (FMCSA-2026-0064) in the keyword box and click “Search.” Next, choose the only notice listed, and click on the “Comment” button. Follow the online instructions for submitting comments.
Mail:
Dockets Operations, U.S. Department of Transportation, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, W58-213, Washington, DC 20590-0001.
Hand Delivery or Courier:
Dockets Operations, U.S. Department of Transportation, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, W58-213, Washington, DC 20590-0001, between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m., Monday through Friday, except Federal holidays.
Fax:
(202) 493-2251.
To avoid duplication, please use only one of these four methods. See the “Public Participation” portion of the
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION
section for instructions on submitting comments.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Ms. Christine A. Hydock, Chief, Medical Programs Division, FMCSA, DOT, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590-0001; (202) 366-4001;
fmcsamedical@dot.gov
.
Office hours are 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. ET Monday through Friday, except Federal holidays.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Public Participation
A. Submitting Comments
If you submit a comment, please include the docket number for this notice (FMCSA-2026-0064), indicate the specific section of this document to which each comment applies, and provide a reason for each suggestion or recommendation. You may submit your comments and material online or by fax, mail, or hand delivery, but please use only one of these means. FMCSA recommends that you include your name and a mailing address, an email address, or a phone number in the body of your document so that FMCSA can contact you if there are questions regarding your submission.
To submit your comment online, go to
https://www.regulations.gov/​docket/​FMCSA-2026-0064
.
Next, choose the only notice listed, click the “Comment” button, and type your comment into the text box on the following screen. Choose whether you are submitting your comment as an individual or on behalf of a third party and then submit.
If you submit your comments by mail or hand delivery, submit them in an unbound format, no larger than 8
                    1/2
                     by 11 inches, suitable for copying and electronic filing. FMCSA will consider all comments and material received during the comment period.
B. Confidential Business Information (CBI)
CBI is commercial or financial information that is both customarily and actually treated as private by its owner. Under the Freedom of Information Act (
5 U.S.C. 552
), CBI is exempt from public disclosure. If your comments responsive to the notice contain commercial or financial information that is customarily treated as private, that you actually treat as private, and that is relevant or responsive to the notice, it is important that you clearly designate the submitted comments as CBI. Please mark each page of your submission that constitutes CBI as “PROPIN” to indicate it contains proprietary information. FMCSA will treat such marked submissions as confidential under the Freedom of
(
printed page 73633)
Information Act, and they will not be placed in the public docket of the notice. Submissions containing CBI should be sent to Sarah Stella, Chief, Regulatory Development Division, Office of Policy, FMCSA, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590-0001 or via email at
sarah.stella@dot.gov
.
At this time, you need not send a duplicate hardcopy of your electronic CBI submissions to FMCSA headquarters. Any comments FMCSA receives not specifically designated as CBI will be placed in the public docket for this notice.
C. Viewing Comments
To view comments, go to
www.regulations.gov
,
insert the docket number (FMCSA-2026-0064) in the keyword box and click “Search.” Next, choose the only notice listed, and click “Browse Comments.” If you do not have access to the internet, you may view the docket online by visiting Dockets Operations in room W58-213 of the DOT West Building, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590-0001, between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m. ET Monday through Friday, except Federal holidays.
D. Privacy Act
In accordance with
49 U.S.C. 31315(b)(6)
, DOT solicits comments from the public on the exemption request. DOT posts these comments, including any personal information the commenter provides, to
www.regulations.gov
,
as described in the system of records notice DOT/ALL-14 FDMS (Federal Docket Management System), which can be reviewed under the “Department Wide System of Records Notices” link at
https://www.transportation.gov/​individuals/​privacy/​privacy-act-system-records-notices
.
The comments are posted without edit and are searchable by the name of the submitter.
II. Legal Basis
FMCSA has authority under
49 U.S.C. 31136(e)
and
31315(b)
to grant exemptions from the FMCSRs. FMCSA must publish a notice of each exemption request in the
Federal Register
(
49 CFR 381.315(a)
). The Agency must provide the public an opportunity to inspect the information relevant to the application, including the applicant's safety analysis. The Agency must provide an opportunity for public comment on the request.
The Agency reviews the application, safety analyses, and public comments submitted and determines whether granting the exemption would likely achieve a level of safety equivalent to, or greater than, the level of safety that would be achieved absent such exemption, pursuant to the standard set forth
49 U.S.C. 31315(b)(1)
. The Agency must publish its decision in the
Federal Register
(
49 CFR 381.315(b)
). If granted, the notice will identify the regulatory provision from which the applicant will be exempt, the effective period, and all terms and conditions of the exemption (
49 CFR 381.315(c)(1)
). If the exemption is denied, the notice will explain the reason for the denial (
49 CFR 381.315(c)(2)
). The exemption may be renewed (
49 CFR 381.300(b)
). FMCSA grants medical exemptions from the FMCSRs for a 2-year period to align with the maximum duration of a driver's medical certification.
III. Background
The physical qualification standard for drivers regarding cardiovascular diseases and loss of consciousness provides that a person is physically qualified to drive a CMV if that person has “no current clinical diagnosis of myocardial infarction, angina pectoris, coronary insufficiency, thrombosis, or any other cardiovascular disease of a variety known to be accompanied by syncope, dyspnea, collapse, or congestive cardiac failure” (
49 CFR 391.41(b)(4)
). To assist in applying this standard, FMCSA publishes guidance for medical examiners (MEs) in the form of medical advisory criteria in Appendix A to 49 CFR part 391.
[
1
]
The advisory criteria for
49 CFR 391.41(b)(4)
indicates that ICDs are installed to address an ongoing underlying cardiovascular condition and that syncope or collapse is likely to occur as a result of both the underlying cardiovascular condition as well as when the ICDs discharge. Therefore, ICDs are medically disqualifying. In April 2007, FMCSA published an evidence report titled, “Cardiovascular Disease and Commercial Motor Vehicle Driver Safety,” presenting findings regarding cardiovascular disease and CMV driver safety.
[
2
]
In December 2014, FMCSA published a research report titled, “Implantable Cardioverter Defibrillators and the Impact of a Shock in a Patient When Deployed,” that provided evidence regarding the potential impact of ICD deployment and how it may interfere with the safe operation of a CMV.
[
3
]
The Agency considers the medical advisory criteria, the April 2007 evidence report, the December 2014 research report, the application, any public comments received, and the individual's medical information in deciding whether to grant the exemption.
The five individuals listed in this notice have requested an exemption from
49 CFR 391.41(b)(4)
. Accordingly, the Agency will evaluate the qualifications of each applicant to determine whether granting the exemption will achieve the required level of safety mandated by statute.
IV. Qualifications of Applicants
Ron Bledsoe
Ron Blesdoe is a class C driver's license holder in Texas. A letter from Mr. Blesdoe's cardiologist reports that his ICD was implanted on October 26, 2023, for a history of dilated cardiomyopathy. Mr. Blesdoe's cardiologist also reports that his ICD has never deployed, and his underlying heart condition is stable. Mr. Bledsoe has experienced no heart failure symptoms and no exertional limitations since the ICD was implanted.
Wes Bryant
Wes Bryant is a class A driver's license holder in Tennessee. concerning each proposed collection of information, including each proposed extension of an existing collection of information, and to allow 60 days for public comment. https://www.regulations.gov
and press the “Search” button, then proceed as follows:
1. Under Refine Documents Results—check the box to “Only show documents open for comment”;
2. Under Agency—select “See More” and check the box for “Commodity Futures Trading Commission,” then press the Apply button;
3. Identify this notice in the list of CFTC documents open for comment, press the “Comment” button to open the submission form, and follow the instructions on the form.
Alternatively, if you are viewing this notice on
www.federalregister.gov
,
click the “Submit A Public Comment” button at the top of the page to open the comment form. Follow the instructions on the form to submit your comment to

are encouraged.

FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT

17 CFR 145.9
for requesting confidential treatment under the Freedom of Information Act (“FOIA”) of information submitted to the Commission.

Under the PRA,
44 U.S.C. 3501
et seq.,
Federal agencies must obtain approval from the Office of Management and Budget (“OMB”) for each collection of information they conduct or sponsor. “Collection of information” is defined in
44 U.S.C. 3502(3)
and
5 CFR. 1320.3(c)
and includes agency requests or requirements that members of the public submit reports, keep records, or provide information to a third party. Section 3506(c)(2)(A) of the PRA,
44 U.S.C. 3506(c)(2)(A)
, requires Federal agencies to provide a 60-day notice in the
Federal Register
concerning each proposed collection of information, including each proposed extension of an existing collection of information, before submitting the collection to OMB for approval. To comply with this requirement, the CFTC is publishing notice of the proposed extension of the currently approved collection of information listed below. An agency may not conduct or sponsor, and a person is not required to respond to, a collection of information unless it displays a currently valid OMB control number.
[
1
]
Title:
Implementing the Whistleblower Provisions of Section 23 of the Commodity Exchange Act, OMB Control Number 3038-0082. This is a request for extension of a currently approved information collection.
Abstract:
Section 23 of the Commodity Exchange Act,
7 U.S.C. 26
, directs that the Commission establish a fund from which to pay awards of 10 to 30 percent of sanctions collected from successful enforcement of covered judicial or administrative actions, or related actions, to individuals who provide information that leads to the successful enforcement of an action in which sanctions exceeding $1,000,000 are obtained. Section 23(c) establishes procedures for the determination or denial of an award. Commission Rules 165.3 and 165.7 implement these statutory provisions.
[
2
]
Rule 165.3(a) requires the submission of information to the Commission on a Form TCR. The Form TCR, “Tip, Complaint, or Referral,” and the instructions thereto, are designed to capture basic identifying information about a complainant and elicit sufficient information to determine whether the conduct alleged suggests a violation of the Commodity Exchange Act. Rule 165.7(b)(1) requires the submission of information to the Commission on a Form WB-APP. The Form WB-APP, “Application for Award for Original Information Provided Pursuant to Section 23 of the Commodity Exchange Act,” and the instructions thereto, are designed to elicit sufficient information to determine whether and to what extent a claimant qualifies for a whistleblower award.
With respect to the collection of information, the CFTC invites comments on:
Whether the proposed collection of information is necessary for the proper performance of the functions of the Commission, including whether the information will have a practical use;
The accuracy of the Commission's estimate of the burden of the proposed collection of information, including the validity of the methodology and assumptions used;
Ways to enhance the quality, usefulness, and clarity of the information to be collected; and
Ways to minimize the burden of collection of information on those who are to respond, including through the use of appropriate automated electronic, mechanical, or other technological collection techniques or other forms of information technology;
e.g.,
permitting electronic submission of responses.
Burden Statement:
The respondent burden for this collection is estimated to be as follows:
Respondents/Affected Entities:
Individuals.

FAA-2026-4426.
Petitioner:
Blue Vigil, LLC.
Section(s) of 14 CFR Affected:
§§ 107.12 and 107.19.
Description of Relief Sought:
Blue Vigil, LLC seeks relief to operate the Blue Vigil AL1000 Autonomous Aerial Light system, a tethered unmanned aircraft system (UAS), weighing less than 55 pounds (lbs.), without a certificated remote pilot-in-command (PIC). The AL1000 is a permanently tethered, fully integrated aerial lighting system used to position a high-intensity Light-Emitting Diode (LED) array above access-controlled worksites for nighttime illumination. The system is physically and programmatically incapable of intentional horizontal movement, operates only within a system-defined operating cylinder, and is limited to a maximum operating height of 110 feet above ground level (AGL) in Class G airspace. Operations would occur only within physically access-controlled worksites, with the system base positioned at least 50 feet from boundaries adjacent to areas accessible to the general public, and with a designated Site Responsible Operator maintaining continuous visual line of sight (VLOS).

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
CPSC seeks to renew the following currently approved collection of information:
Title:
Contests, Challenges, and Awards.
OMB Number:
3041-0151.
Type of Review:
Renewal of collection.
Frequency of Response:
On occasion.
Affected Public:
Contestants, award nominees, award nominators.
General Description of Collection:
The Commission establishes contests, challenges, and awards to increase the public's knowledge and awareness of safety hazards. The Commission also recognizes through awards certain individuals, firms, and organizations that work to address issues related to consumer product safety. The information to be collected from contestants and award nominees or nominators includes contact and background information necessary to conduct a contest or award program. Limited background or biographical information similar to data found on a resume, such as a nominee's education and work experience, may be requested for some contests or awards. Additionally, substantive entries such as essays, posters, drawings, or videos may be requested for contestants and award nominees.
Estimated Number of Respondents:
CPSC estimates that there will be 500 contest or award participants each year.
Estimated Time per Response:
The estimated time to complete a contest or award submission is five hours per participant.
Total Estimated Annual Burden:
Based on CPSC's estimates that there will be 500 participants who require five hours each to complete their submissions, CPSC estimates that the total annual burden of this collection is 2,500 hours. The annualized cost to respondents for the information collection is approximately $123,650 (2,500 hours × $49.46/hr.), as estimated from total compensation data available from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, “Employer Costs for Employee Compensation,” June 2026, Table 1, Total compensation for all civilian workers:
https://www.bls.gov/​news.release/​archives/​ecec_​09092026.htm
.
Request for Comments:
The Commission solicits written comments from all interested persons about the proposed collection of information. The Commission specifically solicits information relevant to the following topics:
whether the collection of information described above is necessary for the proper performance of the Commission's functions, including whether the information would have practical utility;
whether the estimated burden of the proposed collection of information is accurate;
whether the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected could be enhanced; and
whether the burden imposed by the collection of information could be minimized by use of automated, electronic or other technological collection techniques, or other forms of information technology.
